presentation: Acanthosis nigricans — insulin resistance in an obese adolescent
stem:
A 14-year-old boy is brought to his GP by his mother because of dark, thickened skin on the back of his neck and in both armpits, which has developed gradually over the past year. Scrubbing the skin has made no difference. He has no thirst, polyuria or weight loss. His BMI is 34 kg/m² (above the 99th centile) and his father has type 2 diabetes. The affected skin is hyperpigmented and velvety, with no scale, itch or inflammation.

Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Skin scrapings for fungal microscopy
options.B: Check his blood glucose today
options.C: Prescribe topical tretinoin cream
options.D: Refer for a skin biopsy
options.E: Reassure and advise on skin hygiene

correct_answer: B. Check his blood glucose today
why_correct: Velvety hyperpigmentation of the neck and flexures in an obese adolescent is acanthosis nigricans, a cutaneous marker of insulin resistance. Together with obesity and a family history of type 2 diabetes, NICE lists it as a feature that should make you think of type 2 diabetes, so he needs his blood glucose checked now rather than treatment of the skin. In children, diabetes is confirmed using plasma glucose (WHO criteria), not HbA1c, which Diabetes UK advises is not appropriate for diagnosing diabetes in any child or young person. If the glucose is raised, or diabetes is otherwise suspected, he should be discussed with and referred to the paediatric diabetes team on the same day, who will confirm the diagnosis and its type. The skin usually improves with weight loss and better insulin sensitivity. Source: NICE NG18 Diabetes (type 1 and type 2) in children and young people, 2015 (updated 2023), recommendations 1.1.2–1.1.5; Diabetes UK Diagnostic criteria for diabetes.
why_wrong: A. The velvety, non-scaly, non-itchy skin is not a fungal infection, so scrapings miss the real problem. C. Topical retinoids may soften the skin but treat the sign and leave the metabolic cause uninvestigated. D. Benign acanthosis nigricans is a clinical diagnosis and does not need histology. E. It is not caused by poor hygiene, and reassurance alone misses possible type 2 diabetes.
pearl: Acanthosis nigricans in an obese young person is insulin resistance written on the skin — check for type 2 diabetes.
thinking: Velvety dark skin in neck and axillae  ↓  obese adolescent, family history of T2DM  ↓  acanthosis nigricans  ↓  marker of insulin resistance: think type 2 diabetes  ↓  check blood glucose now (plasma glucose criteria in children, not HbA1c)  ↓  raised or suspected diabetes: same-day paediatric diabetes team
exam_trap: Treating the skin (antifungal, retinoid, hygiene advice) instead of looking for the metabolic cause.
takeaway: Acanthosis nigricans in an obese adolescent: check blood glucose and involve the paediatric diabetes team the same day if it is raised; HbA1c is not used to diagnose diabetes in children.
notes: Re-keyed after clinical review (Oct 2026): previously keyed 'Measure his HbA1c'. NICE NG18 fetched 8 Oct 2026: 1.1.2 same-day referral to a multidisciplinary paediatric diabetes team for suspected type 1 diabetes; 1.1.3 confirm using WHO plasma glucose criteria; 1.1.4 assume type 1 unless strong indications of type 2; 1.1.5 think of type 2 with obesity, strong family history and acanthosis nigricans. Diabetes UK diagnostic criteria page (fetched 8 Oct 2026) lists 'ALL children and young people' as a situation where HbA1c is not appropriate for diagnosis. Some local pathways (e.g. NHS Highland) use HbA1c for suspected type 2 in young people, so no HbA1c option is offered as a distractor to avoid a second defensible answer.

presentation: Malignant acanthosis nigricans — occult gastric cancer
stem:
A 64-year-old man sees his GP because of velvety, dark thickening of the skin in his armpits, groins and around his neck, which has appeared and spread rapidly over the past 2 months. His palms have also become thickened with exaggerated ridges. He has lost 8 kg in 3 months without trying and reports early fullness and upper abdominal discomfort after meals. His BMI is 22 kg/m² and he takes no regular medicines. Abdominal examination is normal.

Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Check HbA1c and review in 3 months
options.B: Routine referral to dermatology
options.C: Topical urea cream and review in 6 weeks
options.D: Test for H. pylori and start a PPI
options.E: Suspected cancer pathway referral

correct_answer: E. Suspected cancer pathway referral
why_correct: Rapid-onset, extensive acanthosis nigricans in a slim older adult, especially with thickened ridged palms ('tripe palms') and weight loss, suggests malignant acanthosis nigricans, which is most often associated with gastric adenocarcinoma. He also meets NICE criteria for a suspected cancer pathway referral for stomach cancer: aged 55 or over with weight loss and upper abdominal pain or dyspepsia. Source: NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral, 2015 (amended 2025); Hong Kong Med J 2023 case review of malignant acanthosis nigricans.
why_wrong: A. Insulin resistance does not explain sudden, florid acanthosis nigricans with weight loss in a man of normal weight, and a 3-month delay is unsafe. B. A routine dermatology referral delays investigation of the likely internal cancer. C. A keratolytic treats only the skin and ignores the red-flag weight loss. D. Test-and-treat for H. pylori is for uncomplicated dyspepsia, not dyspepsia with weight loss at 55 or over.
pearl: Sudden acanthosis nigricans in a thin older adult, especially with tripe palms, is a paraneoplastic sign until proven otherwise — think stomach.
thinking: Rapid, widespread acanthosis nigricans  ↓  tripe palms, not obese  ↓  weight loss + early satiety + upper abdominal pain, age 64  ↓  suspect malignant acanthosis nigricans from gastric adenocarcinoma  ↓  NG12: suspected cancer pathway referral for upper GI endoscopy
exam_trap: Attributing the skin change to insulin resistance and checking HbA1c, as you would in an obese patient.
takeaway: Sudden acanthosis nigricans with weight loss in an older adult needs urgent investigation for gastric cancer.
notes: NICE pages returned 403 to the fetch tool; NG12 2025 wording ("suspected cancer pathway referral") confirmed via the BSG summary and an NG12 mirror. Presentation P180 chosen as the skin sign is what is tested; P217 Weight loss is a defensible alternative.

presentation: Livedo reticularis with recurrent miscarriage — antiphospholipid syndrome
stem:
A 32-year-old woman attends the recurrent miscarriage clinic after three consecutive miscarriages at 7, 8 and 9 weeks' gestation. Two years ago she had a deep vein thrombosis of the left leg. She has no joint pain, mouth ulcers or photosensitive rash. On examination there is a persistent, net-like, violaceous mottling over her thighs and knees that remains when she is warm. Her blood pressure is 118/74 mmHg and urinalysis is normal.

Which blood tests are most appropriate to confirm the likely underlying diagnosis?

options.A: Lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin antibodies
options.B: Factor V Leiden and prothrombin gene mutation testing
options.C: Antinuclear antibody and complement levels
options.D: Protein C, protein S and antithrombin activity levels
options.E: Karyotyping of both partners

correct_answer: A. Lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin antibodies
why_correct: Persistent livedo reticularis with recurrent first-trimester miscarriage and a previous venous thrombosis points to antiphospholipid syndrome. Women with recurrent miscarriage should be tested for lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin antibodies, and a positive result must be confirmed on two occasions at least 12 weeks apart. Confirmed antiphospholipid syndrome changes management in a future pregnancy (aspirin plus low-molecular-weight heparin). Source: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 17 Recurrent Miscarriage, 2023.
why_wrong: B. Inherited thrombophilia testing is not recommended for recurrent first-trimester miscarriage and does not explain livedo reticularis. C. ANA and complement support a diagnosis of lupus, but she has no lupus features and they do not diagnose antiphospholipid syndrome. D. Protein C, protein S and antithrombin are inherited thrombophilia tests that do not explain her pattern of disease. E. Parental karyotyping is not routinely recommended and does not explain her thrombosis or skin sign.
pearl: Livedo reticularis + thrombosis + pregnancy loss = antiphospholipid syndrome until the antibodies say otherwise.
thinking: Three first-trimester miscarriages  ↓  previous DVT  ↓  persistent livedo reticularis  ↓  antiphospholipid syndrome  ↓  lupus anticoagulant + anticardiolipin antibodies, repeat at 12 weeks
exam_trap: Choosing an inherited thrombophilia screen because of the previous DVT.
takeaway: Recurrent miscarriage with livedo reticularis or thrombosis: test lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin antibodies, repeated at 12 weeks.
notes: Anti-beta-2-glycoprotein I deliberately left out of the keyed option because the RCOG 2023-based NHS guideline says it is not routinely tested. Condition: C370 kept as the slot target and it names livedo reticularis; C086 (coagulation disorders including thrombophilia) is a defensible alternative because APS is an acquired thrombophilia. Presentation P181 (livedo as a rash pattern).

presentation: Pyoderma gangrenosum in ulcerative colitis — avoid debridement (pathergy)
stem:
A 38-year-old woman with ulcerative colitis, which is currently flaring with five loose stools a day, is referred by the surgical team with an ulcer on her right shin. It began 3 weeks ago as a painful pustule after she knocked her leg and has enlarged rapidly to 6 cm despite 10 days of oral flucloxacillin. It is extremely painful, with a ragged, undermined, violaceous edge and a purulent base. A wound swab grew mixed skin flora. A similar lesion last year became much larger after surgical debridement. Her ankle–brachial pressure index is 1.0.

Which is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Wide surgical debridement of the ulcer
options.B: IV flucloxacillin and benzylpenicillin
options.C: Split-thickness skin graft to the ulcer
options.D: High-dose oral prednisolone
options.E: Multilayer compression bandaging

correct_answer: D. High-dose oral prednisolone
why_correct: A rapidly enlarging, very painful ulcer with an undermined violaceous edge in a patient with active ulcerative colitis, which worsened after previous surgery (pathergy), is pyoderma gangrenosum. Extensive or rapidly progressive disease needs systemic immunosuppression; in the UK STOP GAP trial oral prednisolone (0.75 mg/kg/day) and ciclosporin were equally effective, and prednisolone will also treat her colitis flare. Treatment should be planned with dermatology and the gastroenterology team managing her colitis. Pyoderma gangrenosum is an inflammatory (neutrophilic) ulcer rather than an infection, but the wound should still be assessed for superadded infection, which would need treating alongside the immunosuppression. Surgery and debridement should be avoided while it is active, unless there is a specific specialist-led reason, because trauma extends the ulcer. Source: Ormerod et al, STOP GAP trial, BMJ 2015; DermNet pyoderma gangrenosum.
why_wrong: A. Debridement causes pathergy and enlarges an active pyoderma gangrenosum ulcer, as happened last year. B. The ulcer is driven by inflammation rather than infection: it has enlarged despite antibiotics and the swab grew only mixed skin flora, so more antibiotics will not control it, although superadded infection should still be looked for. C. Grafting during active disease leads to graft failure and new ulcers at the donor site. E. Compression is for venous ulcers, does not treat the inflammation and is likely to worsen a pathergic ulcer.
pearl: An ulcer that gets worse after debridement is pyoderma gangrenosum until proven otherwise — treat the immune system, not the wound.
thinking: Rapidly enlarging painful ulcer, undermined violaceous edge  ↓  active UC, started after minor trauma  ↓  worsened after previous debridement (pathergy)  ↓  pyoderma gangrenosum  ↓  systemic steroid (or ciclosporin), no surgery
exam_trap: Treating it as an infected wound that needs more antibiotics or debridement.
takeaway: Pyoderma gangrenosum: systemic immunosuppression such as oral prednisolone, and avoid surgical debridement.
notes: No current NICE/BAD guideline for PG; based on UK RCT (STOP GAP) and DermNet. Small, localised PG would be treated with potent topical steroid/tacrolimus first, so the stem specifies extensive, rapidly progressive disease plus an IBD flare to make systemic steroid unambiguous.

presentation: Necrobiosis lipoidica — association with diabetes
stem:
A 29-year-old woman sees her GP about patches on both shins that have slowly enlarged over a year. Examination shows well-demarcated, shiny, yellow-brown plaques with a red-brown rim, a thin atrophic centre and visible telangiectasia. They are not itchy and there is no rash elsewhere. She is otherwise well and takes no regular medicines.

Which condition is most strongly associated with this skin finding?

options.A: Graves disease
options.B: Sarcoidosis
options.C: Diabetes mellitus
options.D: Crohn disease
options.E: Chronic venous insufficiency

correct_answer: C. Diabetes mellitus
why_correct: Shiny, yellow-brown, atrophic plaques with telangiectasia and a red rim on both shins are necrobiosis lipoidica. It is strongly associated with diabetes mellitus (type 1 and type 2), and a substantial proportion of affected people have diabetes or prediabetes, so she should be tested for diabetes. Lesions can ulcerate after minor trauma. Source: DermNet necrobiosis lipoidica, 2023.
why_wrong: A. Graves disease causes pretibial myxoedema, which gives firm, waxy, orange-peel plaques, not atrophic yellow plaques with telangiectasia. B. Sarcoidosis causes erythema nodosum (tender red nodules) or lupus pernio, not this picture. D. Crohn disease is associated with erythema nodosum and pyoderma gangrenosum on the shins. E. Chronic venous insufficiency causes haemosiderin staining and lipodermatosclerosis around the ankles, with oedema and varicose veins.
pearl: Yellow, shiny, atrophic shin plaques with telangiectasia = necrobiosis lipoidica = check for diabetes.
thinking: Bilateral shin plaques  ↓  yellow-brown, shiny, atrophic, telangiectasia  ↓  necrobiosis lipoidica  ↓  associated with diabetes mellitus  ↓  test for diabetes
exam_trap: Confusing it with pretibial myxoedema and choosing Graves disease.
takeaway: Necrobiosis lipoidica on the shins is associated with diabetes mellitus.
notes: Stem deliberately omits a diabetes history so the question tests the association rather than giving it away.

presentation: Dry gangrene of a toe — chronic limb-threatening ischaemia
stem:
A 74-year-old man who smokes 20 cigarettes a day sees his GP because the tip of his left second toe has turned black over 3 weeks. For 2 months he has had pain in the left foot at night, eased by hanging the leg over the side of the bed. The toe is black, dry, shrivelled and cold with a clear line of demarcation; there is no swelling, discharge, spreading redness or crepitus. Left foot pulses are absent. He is afebrile, with a heart rate of 82 bpm, and is otherwise well. He does not have diabetes.

Which is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Sharp debridement of the toe in the surgery
options.B: Moist hydrogel dressings to soften the toe
options.C: Dry dressing and urgent vascular referral
options.D: Oral co-amoxiclav and review in one week
options.E: Compression bandaging and routine referral

correct_answer: C. Dry dressing and urgent vascular referral
why_correct: Rest pain with a dry, demarcated, black toe and absent pulses is chronic limb-threatening (critical) ischaemia with dry gangrene. The toe should be kept clean and dry, and he needs urgent assessment by the vascular team, who will image the limb and consider revascularisation before any amputation; dead tissue in an unperfused foot will not heal. UK standards expect specialist review within 2 working days of referral for stable tissue loss. Source: NICE CG147 Peripheral arterial disease, 2012 (updated 2020); Vascular Society PAD Quality Improvement Framework, 2022.
why_wrong: A. Removing dead tissue from an unperfused foot creates a non-healing wound, and any debridement or amputation should follow vascular assessment. B. Moist dressings can turn stable dry gangrene into wet, infected gangrene. D. There are no signs of infection, and antibiotics do nothing for the ischaemia that needs urgent assessment. E. Compression is dangerous in an ischaemic limb, and a routine referral is too slow for tissue loss.
pearl: Dry gangrene: keep it dry, keep your scalpel away, and get the vascular team to restore blood flow first.
thinking: Rest pain eased by dependency  ↓  dry, black, demarcated toe, absent pulses  ↓  chronic limb-threatening ischaemia with dry gangrene  ↓  no infection or sepsis  ↓  keep dry + urgent vascular assessment for revascularisation
exam_trap: Debriding or applying moist dressings to the black toe before blood flow has been assessed.
takeaway: Dry gangrene in peripheral arterial disease: keep it dry and refer urgently to vascular surgery.
notes: Patient deliberately non-diabetic to keep this on the PAD pathway rather than NG19. The NHS Tayside formulary does allow trained practitioners to sharp-debride the demarcation zone, so option A is framed as debridement in the GP surgery before vascular assessment.

presentation: Stable dry gangrene of a toe — conservative care when revascularisation is not appropriate
stem:
An 88-year-old woman in a care home has a black, dry, shrivelled left third toe with a clear line of demarcation, which has developed over 6 weeks. She has severe heart failure, is housebound and is moderately frail. The vascular multidisciplinary team has reviewed her and judged that she is not fit for angioplasty or bypass; she has capacity and has said she does not want an amputation. There is no swelling, discharge, spreading redness or crepitus. She is afebrile, her observations are normal and her foot pain is controlled with regular paracetamol and low-dose morphine.

Which is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Keep it dry and offloaded, with analgesia and review
options.B: Toe amputation under local anaesthetic this week
options.C: Moist hydrogel dressings to debride the dead tissue
options.D: Prophylactic oral antibiotics until the toe separates
options.E: Refer for below-knee amputation to prevent spread

correct_answer: A. Keep it dry and offloaded, with analgesia and review
why_correct: This is stable, uninfected dry gangrene in a frail woman who is not a candidate for revascularisation, after a vascular MDT decision and in line with her own informed wishes. The appropriate plan is individualised conservative (and, as needed, palliative) care: keep the toe clean and dry, protect the foot from pressure, control pain, and arrange regular planned review of the foot by the care home nurses, podiatry and her GP. Staff and the patient should have clear instructions to seek urgent medical help if swelling, discharge, spreading redness, fever or any systemic illness develops, because these signal conversion to wet gangrene. With this care the dead toe may demarcate and separate on its own (auto-amputation). Surgery on an unperfused foot is unlikely to heal and she has declined it. Source: NICE CG147 Peripheral arterial disease, 2012 (updated 2020); StatPearls Gangrene (NCBI Bookshelf), updated 2025.
why_wrong: B. Without revascularisation the amputation wound is unlikely to heal, and she has declined amputation. C. Moist dressings soften dry gangrene and risk turning it into wet, infected gangrene. D. There is no infection, and long-term prophylactic antibiotics add side effects and resistance without benefit. E. Stable dry gangrene is not spreading, major amputation needs an MDT decision, and she has capacity and has declined it.
pearl: Stable dry gangrene that cannot be revascularised: keep it dry, offload it, control pain, review it regularly and safety-net for wet change.
thinking: Dry, black, demarcated toe, no infection, systemically well  ↓  vascular MDT: not fit for revascularisation  ↓  capacitous patient declines amputation  ↓  individualised conservative care: keep dry and clean, offload, analgesia, planned review  ↓  safety-net for swelling, discharge, redness, fever; toe may separate on its own
exam_trap: Reflexively choosing surgical removal of the dead toe when the foot cannot be revascularised and the patient has declined surgery.
takeaway: Stable dry gangrene not suitable for revascularisation: individualised conservative care (dry, offloaded, analgesia, planned review) with clear safety-netting for wet change, guided by the MDT and the patient's wishes.
notes: Replaces the earlier MG007 (septic wet diabetic foot) so that MG007, MG008 and MG009 do not all teach IV antibiotics plus urgent surgery. Distinct from MG006, where the patient has not yet been assessed and needs urgent vascular referral: here the MDT has already decided against revascularisation. NICE CG147 1.6.1 (vascular MDT assessment) and 1.6.11 (no major amputation unless the MDT has considered all revascularisation options) were checked. StatPearls 2025 describes auto-amputation of dry gangrene, and NHS Tayside says to keep dry gangrene dry. Presentation P042 (black, painful toe); P088 Frailty is a defensible alternative.

presentation: Dry gangrene converting to wet gangrene — recognition
stem:
A 78-year-old man is an inpatient on the vascular ward awaiting angiography for chronic limb-threatening ischaemia of his right leg. On admission his right fourth and fifth toes were black, dry and shrivelled, with a clear line of demarcation. Over the past 24 hours the forefoot has become swollen, and the skin around the toes has developed blisters, a foul-smelling brown discharge and dusky discolouration that fades into the surrounding skin with no clear edge. There is no crepitus. He is newly confused, with a temperature of 38.4°C, heart rate 108 bpm and blood pressure 112/70 mmHg.

Which is the most appropriate interpretation and next step?

options.A: Stable dry gangrene: keep dry and await angiography
options.B: Cellulitis: start oral antibiotics and mark the margin
options.C: Dependent oedema: elevate the leg and review in the morning
options.D: Infected wound: swab it and await culture results
options.E: Wet gangrene: IV antibiotics and urgent surgical review

correct_answer: E. Wet gangrene: IV antibiotics and urgent surgical review
why_correct: Dry gangrene is cold, shrivelled and sharply demarcated with no discharge and little systemic upset. New swelling, blistering, foul discharge, a poorly demarcated spreading edge and fever with confusion mean the necrotic tissue has become infected: wet gangrene. This is a surgical emergency needing broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and urgent surgical review for debridement or amputation to control the source; uncontrolled infection is an indication to operate before revascularisation. Source: StatPearls Gangrene (NCBI Bookshelf), updated 2025; Vascular Society PAD Quality Improvement Framework, 2022.
why_wrong: A. The swelling, blisters, discharge, loss of demarcation and fever show this is no longer stable dry gangrene, and waiting for angiography allows infection to spread. B. Oral antibiotics for cellulitis ignore the infected dead tissue, which needs IV antibiotics and surgical source control. C. Oedema does not cause blisters, foul discharge, fever or confusion. D. A swab result will not change the immediate need for IV antibiotics and surgery, and waiting delays treatment.
pearl: Dry gangrene that becomes swollen, wet, smelly and poorly demarcated, with a fever, has turned wet — call the surgeons now.
thinking: Known dry, demarcated toe gangrene  ↓  new swelling, blisters, foul discharge, edge no longer demarcated  ↓  fever, tachycardia, new confusion  ↓  conversion to wet (infected) gangrene  ↓  IV antibiotics + urgent surgical debridement/amputation
exam_trap: Assuming a patient with known dry gangrene is still stable and simply waiting for the planned angiography.
takeaway: Swelling, blistering, discharge, a poorly demarcated edge and systemic upset mean wet gangrene: IV antibiotics and urgent surgery.
notes: Replaces the earlier Fournier gangrene draft, which duplicated DS130. Tests telling wet from dry gangrene (conversion on the ward) rather than definitive septic management (MG007) or gas gangrene (MG009). No crepitus is stated, to exclude gas gangrene. Presentation P198 (swollen foot); P056 Deteriorating patient is a defensible alternative.

presentation: Gas gangrene (clostridial myonecrosis) after a contaminated wound
stem:
A 34-year-old man is admitted 2 days after a crush injury to his left calf from farm machinery; the deep, soil-contaminated laceration was sutured closed at a minor injuries unit. He now has severe calf pain, out of proportion to the appearance. The calf is tense and swollen, with bronze-brown skin, haemorrhagic blisters and a thin, foul-smelling brown discharge. There is crepitus on palpation. His temperature is 38.8°C, heart rate 128 bpm and blood pressure 90/54 mmHg. An X-ray shows gas along the muscle planes.

Which is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy before any debridement
options.B: IV antibiotics and urgent surgical debridement
options.C: IV antibiotics alone and surgical reassessment in 24 hours
options.D: Remove sutures and pack the wound on the ward
options.E: MRI of the leg before deciding on treatment

correct_answer: B. IV antibiotics and urgent surgical debridement
why_correct: A deep, soil-contaminated crush wound closed primarily, followed by severe pain, bronze skin, haemorrhagic bullae, crepitus, gas in muscle planes and shock, is gas gangrene (clostridial myonecrosis, usually Clostridium perfringens). Treatment is immediate high-dose IV antibiotics and urgent, radical surgical debridement of all dead muscle, with a repeat look within 24 hours and amputation if needed. Empirical antibiotics should follow the local protocol for necrotising soft-tissue infection, which usually means broad-spectrum cover (regimens vary, for example piperacillin with tazobactam) with clindamycin to suppress toxin production, narrowed with microbiology advice, for example to benzylpenicillin with clindamycin, once clostridial infection is confirmed. Source: NHS Lothian antimicrobial guideline Severe soft tissue infection including suspected necrotising fasciitis, 2024; Clostridial myonecrosis case report and literature review, Infection (Springer), 2024.
why_wrong: A. Hyperbaric oxygen is at most an adjunct and must never delay surgical debridement. C. Antibiotics cannot reach necrotic, poorly perfused muscle, so delaying surgery allows rapid spread and death. D. Opening the wound on the ward does not remove the dead muscle that is producing toxin. E. The diagnosis is already clear clinically and on X-ray, and further imaging only delays surgery.
pearl: Crepitus, bronze skin and pain out of proportion after a dirty wound = gas gangrene; antibiotics plus theatre, never antibiotics alone.
thinking: Deep soil-contaminated crush wound closed primarily  ↓  severe pain, bronze skin, haemorrhagic bullae, crepitus, gas on X-ray  ↓  shock  ↓  clostridial myonecrosis (gas gangrene)  ↓  broad-spectrum IV antibiotics per local necrotising infection protocol (with clindamycin) + urgent radical debridement
exam_trap: Choosing hyperbaric oxygen or antibiotics alone and delaying surgery.
takeaway: Gas gangrene: IV antibiotics and urgent surgical debridement of all dead muscle.
notes: No specific UK guideline on gas gangrene found; management verified against a 2024 peer-reviewed review/case report. Presentation P198 (swollen limb); P179 Skin laceration/injury is a defensible alternative.

presentation: Sliding hiatus hernia — risk factor (raised intra-abdominal pressure)
stem:
A 58-year-old man has gastroscopy because his heartburn and regurgitation have continued despite 8 weeks of a full-dose proton pump inhibitor. It shows a 3 cm sliding hiatus hernia with mild oesophagitis and no Barrett oesophagus. He works as a taxi driver, takes ibuprofen most days for knee pain, and drinks about 20 units of alcohol a week. He had an appendicectomy as a teenager. His BMI is 36 kg/m² and his waist circumference is 118 cm.

Which factor has most likely contributed to his hiatus hernia?

options.A: Regular ibuprofen use
options.B: Helicobacter pylori infection
options.C: Alcohol intake of 20 units a week
options.D: Central obesity
options.E: Previous appendicectomy

correct_answer: D. Central obesity
why_correct: A sliding hiatus hernia develops when the gastro-oesophageal junction is pushed up through a widened diaphragmatic hiatus, and raised intra-abdominal pressure is one of the main mechanisms. Obesity, especially central obesity, is a well-recognised risk factor, along with increasing age, pregnancy and ascites, which all raise intra-abdominal pressure. With a BMI of 36 kg/m² and a waist of 118 cm, his central obesity is the most likely contributor, and weight loss is also one of the most useful lifestyle measures for his reflux. Source: Hiatus hernia, Patient.info professional reference (updated 2024); Hiatus hernia, NHS website.
why_wrong: A. NSAIDs damage the gastric and duodenal mucosa and cause ulcers, but they do not widen the hiatus or push the stomach up. B. Helicobacter pylori causes gastritis and peptic ulcer disease and is not a cause of hiatus hernia. C. Alcohol can worsen reflux symptoms by relaxing the lower oesophageal sphincter, but it does not cause the hernia itself. E. An appendicectomy decades ago does not affect the diaphragmatic hiatus; previous surgery around the gastro-oesophageal junction is the relevant surgical risk factor.
pearl: Anything that pushes up from below — central obesity, pregnancy, ascites — favours a sliding hiatus hernia.
thinking: Sliding hiatus hernia on gastroscopy  ↓  mechanism: widened hiatus + raised intra-abdominal pressure  ↓  BMI 36, waist 118 cm = central obesity  ↓  NSAIDs, H. pylori and alcohol affect mucosa or reflux, not the hiatus  ↓  central obesity
exam_trap: Choosing a factor that worsens reflux or damages the mucosa (alcohol, NSAIDs, H. pylori) instead of one that raises intra-abdominal pressure.
takeaway: Central obesity raises intra-abdominal pressure and is a key risk factor for sliding hiatus hernia.
notes: Replaces the earlier MG010 (chest X-ray recognition), which duplicated GF016. New angle: risk factor and mechanism (raised intra-abdominal pressure) for sliding hiatus hernia; does not overlap MG011 (initial lifestyle + PPI management), MG012 (types/volvulus risk) or MG013 (Cameron lesions). Gastroscopy after a failed PPI trial is consistent with NICE CG184 referral for persistent symptoms. Presentation X: heartburn/regurgitation has no GMC presentation entry. Appendicectomy chosen as the surgical distractor because previous gastro-oesophageal surgery is itself a recognised risk factor (Patient.info).

presentation: Sliding hiatus hernia with reflux — initial management
stem:
A 46-year-old man sees his GP with three months of heartburn and acid regurgitation, worse after large meals and when lying flat. A CT scan for renal colic last year reported a small sliding hiatus hernia. He has no difficulty swallowing, vomiting, weight loss or gastrointestinal bleeding, and his full blood count is normal. His BMI is 31 kg/m², and he drinks about 30 units of alcohol a week. He asks whether he needs an operation to repair the hernia.

What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Lifestyle advice and a full-dose PPI for 4 weeks
options.B: Referral to upper GI surgeons for laparoscopic hernia repair
options.C: Suspected cancer pathway referral for endoscopy
options.D: Regular domperidone 10 mg three times daily
options.E: Barium swallow to measure the hernia size

correct_answer: A. Lifestyle advice and a full-dose PPI for 4 weeks
why_correct: A small sliding hiatus hernia is common and does not need repair in itself; what matters is treating his reflux symptoms. NICE advises lifestyle advice (weight loss, cutting down alcohol, avoiding late large meals, raising the head of the bed) and a full-dose proton pump inhibitor for 4 weeks for reflux-type dyspepsia without alarm features. Surgery (laparoscopic fundoplication) is only considered later for confirmed reflux that responds to acid suppression when the patient does not want, or cannot tolerate, long-term treatment. Source: NICE CG184 Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease and dyspepsia in adults, 2014 (updated 2019).
why_wrong: B. NICE reserves anti-reflux surgery for confirmed GORD after a trial of acid suppression, so operating first-line on a small sliding hernia is not appropriate. C. He is under 55 with no dysphagia, weight loss, bleeding or anaemia, so he does not meet suspected cancer pathway criteria for endoscopy. D. Domperidone is restricted by the MHRA to short-term relief of nausea and vomiting because of cardiac risk and has no role in reflux. E. Measuring the hernia would not change management, because treatment is guided by symptoms, not hernia size.
pearl: Treat the reflux, not the hernia: a small sliding hiatus hernia is a finding, not an indication for surgery.
thinking: Typical reflux symptoms  ↓  known small sliding hiatus hernia  ↓  no alarm features, age under 55  ↓  lifestyle advice + full-dose PPI for 4 weeks  ↓  surgery only for confirmed GORD after PPI response if long-term therapy unwanted
exam_trap: Assuming a hiatus hernia that causes reflux needs surgical repair before medical treatment has been tried.
takeaway: Sliding hiatus hernia with reflux and no alarm features: lifestyle measures and a PPI first.
notes: Condition kept as Hiatus hernia (C168) because the patient's question and the key decision are about whether the hernia itself needs repair; Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (C148) is an equally defensible alternative. Presentation X: heartburn/regurgitation has no GMC presentation entry (Chest pain would be forced). NICE pages returned 403 to the fetcher; CG184 wording was confirmed via a mirror (medthority). '4 weeks' used rather than '4 or 8 weeks' because without endoscopy NICE treats this as uninvestigated dyspepsia (1-month PPI). H. pylori test-and-treat deliberately not used as a distractor because NICE allows it as an alternative first step.

presentation: Para-oesophageal (type III) hiatus hernia — types and volvulus risk
stem:
A 66-year-old woman has a CT chest for a cough that persisted after a chest infection; the cough has now settled. The report describes a type III (mixed) para-oesophageal hiatus hernia, with the gastro-oesophageal junction and about a quarter of the stomach lying above the diaphragm. She has mild fullness after large meals but no heartburn, difficulty swallowing, vomiting or weight loss, and her haemoglobin is normal. She is fit and active and plays golf twice a week.

Which statement about her hernia is most accurate?

options.A: It is the commonest type of hiatus hernia seen in adults
options.B: Her gastro-oesophageal junction remains below the diaphragm
options.C: It is more prone to volvulus than a sliding hernia
options.D: It needs no referral unless heartburn fails to settle on a PPI
options.E: Its main risk is Barrett oesophagus, needing yearly endoscopy

correct_answer: C. It is more prone to volvulus than a sliding hernia
why_correct: Hiatus hernias are classified by the position of the gastro-oesophageal junction and what has herniated: type I (sliding, about 95%) moves the junction up, type II has the fundus rolling up beside a normally placed junction, type III combines both, and type IV includes other organs. Types II to IV are para-oesophageal hernias, in which the stomach can rotate within the chest, so they carry a greater risk of gastric volvulus, obstruction, strangulation and perforation than uncomplicated sliding hernias. Because of this, even mildly symptomatic para-oesophageal hernias in fit patients are referred for a surgical opinion on elective repair, and patients are told to seek emergency help for sudden severe pain or retching without vomiting. Source: SAGES Guidelines for the Management of Hiatal Hernia, 2013; SAGES Laparoscopic Hiatal Hernia Repair (patient and clinician information).
why_wrong: A. Sliding (type I) hernias make up about 95% of hiatus hernias, so a para-oesophageal hernia is the less common type. B. In a type III hernia the gastro-oesophageal junction is displaced above the diaphragm along with the stomach; it stays in place only in type II. D. Management of a para-oesophageal hernia is driven by its mechanical risk, not heartburn, and even mild symptoms in a fit patient justify a surgical opinion. E. Barrett oesophagus is linked to long-standing reflux, not to the hernia type, and a hiatus hernia alone is not an indication for yearly endoscopy.
pearl: Sliding hernias mainly cause reflux; para-oesophageal hernias are more prone to twisting — refer and safety-net for volvulus.
thinking: Type III = GEJ and stomach above diaphragm  ↓  types II–IV are para-oesophageal  ↓  stomach can rotate in the chest  ↓  risk of volvulus, strangulation and perforation  ↓  surgical opinion on elective repair + safety-net for sudden pain or unproductive retching
exam_trap: Treating every hiatus hernia like a sliding hernia and judging it only by reflux symptoms.
takeaway: Para-oesophageal hiatus hernias carry a greater risk of volvulus and strangulation than sliding hernias, so even mildly symptomatic fit patients should be referred for a surgical opinion.
notes: Replaces the earlier MG012 (Borchardt triad), which duplicated GF018. Tests knowledge of hernia types (GEJ position, prevalence) and the volvulus/strangulation risk that distinguishes para-oesophageal from sliding hernias; it avoids the diagnosis (MG010/GF016), reflux management (MG011), Cameron lesions (MG013) and acute volvulus (GF018) angles. Presentation P104 because the hernia was found on a CT done for another reason; the mild post-prandial fullness is minor.

presentation: Cameron lesions in a large hiatus hernia — recurrent iron-deficiency anaemia
stem:
A 71-year-old woman has had recurrent iron-deficiency anaemia for 18 months and has needed two blood transfusions, despite taking ferrous sulfate and omeprazole 20 mg twice daily throughout. She also has fullness in her chest and breathlessness after meals. Gastroscopy shows a large mixed hiatus hernia, with about 8 cm of stomach above the diaphragm and linear erosions in the gastric folds at the level of the diaphragm. Colonoscopy and coeliac serology are normal. She is otherwise fit and active.

What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Double the omeprazole dose and continue oral iron
options.B: Capsule endoscopy to examine the small bowel
options.C: Repeat colonoscopy with random colonic biopsies
options.D: Regular intravenous iron infusions indefinitely
options.E: Referral for elective laparoscopic hernia repair

correct_answer: E. Referral for elective laparoscopic hernia repair
why_correct: Linear erosions in the gastric folds where a large hiatus hernia passes through the diaphragm are Cameron lesions, a recognised cause of chronic occult blood loss and iron-deficiency anaemia. She has transfusion-requiring anaemia despite iron and twice-daily PPI, plus post-prandial symptoms from the hernia, so medical treatment has failed. Symptomatic para-oesophageal and mixed hernias are usually considered for repair, so she should be referred to an upper GI surgeon to assess her for elective laparoscopic repair, which in a fit patient can treat both the anaemia and her symptoms; the final decision rests on that specialist assessment and her own choice. Source: SAGES Guidelines for the Management of Hiatal Hernia, 2013; Li et al., Cameron ulcer systematic review, Frontiers in Medicine 2025.
why_wrong: A. She is already on full PPI and iron and still needs transfusions, so more of the same medical treatment has failed. B. Small bowel investigation is for anaemia with no cause found on gastroscopy and colonoscopy, and here a cause has been found. C. Her colonoscopy was normal and random biopsies look for microscopic colitis in diarrhoea, not for a source of blood loss. D. Lifelong IV iron replaces losses without treating the bleeding lesion or her hernia symptoms in a patient fit for surgery.
pearl: Iron-deficiency anaemia with a large hiatus hernia: look for Cameron lesions at the diaphragmatic pinch.
thinking: Recurrent IDA needing transfusion  ↓  large mixed hiatus hernia + linear erosions at diaphragm = Cameron lesions  ↓  colonoscopy and coeliac negative  ↓  failed iron + high-dose PPI, plus hernia symptoms, fit patient  ↓  elective laparoscopic repair
exam_trap: Sending her for small bowel capsule endoscopy as if the anaemia were unexplained, when the gastroscopy has already shown the cause.
takeaway: Symptomatic large hiatus hernia with Cameron lesions and refractory anaemia: refer for surgical assessment for elective repair.
notes: Focus said 'para-oesophageal'; stem uses 'mixed' (type III) hernia, which is the commonest large para-oesophageal type in practice and falls under the same SAGES repair recommendation. Condition C168 rather than Anaemia (C020) because the tested decision is hernia repair; presentation P018 Anaemia.

presentation: Adrenal incidentaloma — exclude hormone excess
stem:
A 54-year-old man has an unenhanced CT of the kidneys, ureters and bladder for suspected renal colic. No stone is seen, but there is an incidental 2.6 cm left adrenal mass. The radiologist reports that it is homogeneous, smooth-edged and measures 6 Hounsfield units, consistent with a benign lipid-rich adenoma. His blood pressure is 128/78 mmHg, serum potassium is 4.2 mmol/L, and he has no features of Cushing syndrome. He has no history of cancer.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Reassure and discharge without further tests
options.B: Overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test
options.C: CT-guided percutaneous biopsy of the left adrenal mass
options.D: Repeat adrenal CT scan in 6 to 12 months
options.E: Referral to surgeons for laparoscopic left adrenalectomy

correct_answer: B. Overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test
why_correct: An adrenal mass under 4 cm that is homogeneous and 10 Hounsfield units or less on unenhanced CT is a benign adenoma and needs no further imaging, but every incidentaloma still needs assessment for hormone excess. The European guideline recommends an overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test in all patients to look for autonomous cortisol secretion, which is common, often clinically silent and linked to hypertension, diabetes and fractures. Metanephrines are reserved for masses that do not look like benign adenomas, and an aldosterone-to-renin ratio for those with hypertension or hypokalaemia, so neither is needed first here. Source: European Society of Endocrinology/ENSAT clinical practice guideline on adrenal incidentalomas, 2023.
why_wrong: A. A benign imaging appearance does not exclude hormone secretion, so he still needs biochemical testing before discharge. C. Adrenal biopsy is not part of routine work-up and is only considered in selected patients with a history of extra-adrenal cancer after phaeochromocytoma is excluded. D. A homogeneous mass of 10 Hounsfield units or less is benign and needs no repeat imaging, whatever its size. E. Surgery is not indicated for a small, benign-looking adenoma unless hormone excess or suspicious features are found.
pearl: Imaging tells you whether an adrenal incidentaloma is benign; only biochemistry tells you whether it is functioning.
thinking: Incidental adrenal mass  ↓  under 4 cm, homogeneous, ≤10 HU = benign adenoma, no more imaging  ↓  still check function in everyone  ↓  normotensive, normal potassium, benign appearance  ↓  overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test
exam_trap: Reassuring and discharging because the CT looks benign, forgetting that a benign adenoma can still secrete cortisol.
takeaway: Every adrenal incidentaloma needs a 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test, even when it looks benign.
notes: ESE 2023 recommends metanephrines only for masses that are not clearly benign (the abstract wording is looser than the recommendation text), so metanephrines were not offered as an option to avoid a second defensible answer. The stem specifies an unenhanced CT so the HU value is valid.

presentation: Incidental solid pulmonary nodule — BTS risk-based pathway
stem:
A 67-year-old woman has a CT pulmonary angiogram for suspected pulmonary embolism, which is negative. It shows an incidental 11 mm solid, spiculated nodule in the right upper lobe. She is an ex-smoker with a 40 pack-year history and has no previous chest imaging for comparison. She is well and fit for further investigation. The radiologist calculates a Brock model malignancy risk of 24%.

According to British Thoracic Society guidance, what is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.A: No further imaging is required
options.B: Repeat CT chest in 3 months
options.C: Repeat CT chest in 12 months
options.D: PET-CT scan
options.E: CT-guided percutaneous biopsy

correct_answer: D. PET-CT scan
why_correct: The BTS guideline discharges solid nodules under 5 mm (or under 80 mm³), uses CT surveillance for nodules of 5 to 8 mm, and applies the Brock model to nodules of 8 mm or more. When the Brock risk is 10% or more and the nodule is large enough to be assessed, the next step is PET-CT, whose result feeds into the Herder model to guide biopsy, surgery or surveillance. With an 11 mm spiculated nodule and a Brock risk of 24%, PET-CT is indicated. Source: British Thoracic Society Guidelines for the Investigation and Management of Pulmonary Nodules, 2015.
why_wrong: A. Solid nodules can be discharged only if they are under 5 mm (or under 80 mm³), have clearly benign features such as benign calcification or a typical perifissural appearance, or have been stable over the surveillance period, and this 11 mm spiculated nodule has none of these. B. A 3-month CT is used for 6 to 8 mm nodules or for nodules of 8 mm or more with a Brock risk below 10%. C. A 12-month CT is for small 5 to 6 mm nodules and would dangerously delay assessment of a probable cancer. E. Biopsy usually follows PET-CT and Herder risk assessment rather than replacing them, and PET-CT also helps stage the disease.
pearl: BTS nodule rule: under 5 mm discharge, 5 to 8 mm surveillance, 8 mm or more Brock, and Brock 10% or more means PET-CT.
thinking: Incidental solid nodule  ↓  11 mm = 8 mm or more, so apply Brock  ↓  Brock 24% = 10% or more  ↓  PET-CT  ↓  then Herder model to decide biopsy, surgery or surveillance
exam_trap: Choosing interval CT surveillance by size alone without applying the Brock risk threshold for nodules of 8 mm or more.
takeaway: Solid nodule of 8 mm or more with Brock risk of 10% or more: PET-CT next.
notes: Distinct from existing N299, which only asks the generic approach to an incidental nodule; this item tests the specific BTS size/Brock thresholds. Brock score is given in the stem so candidates do not need to calculate it. Condition C198 Incidental finding rather than Lung cancer (C229) because the tested decision is the incidental nodule pathway, not a confirmed cancer.

presentation: Incidental simple renal cyst (Bosniak I)
stem:
A 58-year-old man has a contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen for suspected diverticulitis, which confirms mild uncomplicated sigmoid diverticulitis. The scan also shows an incidental 3.5 cm cyst in the right kidney. It contains homogeneous fluid of 8 Hounsfield units, with a thin smooth wall and no septa, calcification, solid component or enhancing nodule. His blood pressure and renal function are normal, and urinalysis shows no blood. He asks what should be done about the cyst.

What is the most appropriate management of the renal cyst?

options.A: Reassure him that no follow-up is needed
options.B: Repeat renal ultrasound scan in 12 months
options.C: Suspected cancer pathway referral to urology
options.D: Percutaneous aspiration of the cyst fluid
options.E: MRI scan of the kidneys to characterise it

correct_answer: A. Reassure him that no follow-up is needed
why_correct: A renal cyst with homogeneous water-density fluid (−9 to 20 Hounsfield units), a thin smooth wall and no septa, calcification or enhancing solid tissue is a Bosniak I simple cyst. Simple renal cysts are very common, especially with age, and are benign with no meaningful malignant potential. No imaging follow-up or referral is needed, and he can be reassured. Source: Bosniak classification of cystic renal masses, version 2019 (Silverman et al., Radiology 2019).
why_wrong: B. Interval imaging is used for Bosniak IIF cysts, not for a simple Bosniak I cyst. C. A suspected cancer pathway referral is for a solid or complex renal mass (Bosniak III or IV), not a simple cyst. D. Aspiration is reserved for large cysts causing symptoms such as pain or obstruction, and this cyst is incidental. E. The contrast CT has already fully characterised the cyst as simple, so MRI adds nothing.
pearl: Water density, thin wall, nothing inside: a Bosniak I cyst is benign and needs no follow-up.
thinking: Incidental renal cyst on contrast CT  ↓  water attenuation, thin smooth wall, no septa, calcification or enhancement  ↓  Bosniak I simple cyst  ↓  benign  ↓  reassure, no follow-up
exam_trap: Arranging interval imaging or urology referral 'to be safe' for a cyst that is already fully characterised as simple.
takeaway: Bosniak I simple renal cyst: reassure, no follow-up.
notes: Focus specified ultrasound; sharpened to contrast-enhanced CT because the Bosniak classification (including v2019) is defined on CT/MRI and its use on ultrasound is contested, which would make the 'no follow-up' answer arguable. Condition C198 (Incidental finding); simple renal cyst has no specific GMC entry and Polycystic kidney disease (C316) would be wrong.

presentation: Incidental imaging finding — duty to inform and ensure follow-up
stem:
A 63-year-old man has been treated for mild acute pancreatitis and is ready for discharge. While writing his discharge summary, an FY1 doctor reads the full report of his admission CT abdomen. The final line notes an incidental 9 mm solid nodule in the partly imaged left lower lobe and recommends a dedicated CT chest. Nobody has mentioned this to the patient, who has full capacity and is keen to go home.

What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Leave it for the GP to act on from the copied report
options.B: Discharge him and ask the consultant to write to him
options.C: Explain the finding and ensure follow-up is arranged
options.D: Avoid mentioning it to prevent unnecessary anxiety
options.E: Tell his wife first so that she can break the news gently

correct_answer: C. Explain the finding and ensure follow-up is arranged
why_correct: GMC guidance requires doctors to give patients the information they want or need about their condition, including uncertainties, and to make sure information needed for ongoing care is shared and that a named clinician or team takes responsibility. The FY1 should explain the finding honestly and proportionately, discuss it with a senior, and ensure the recommended CT chest is requested or clearly handed over, with the plan and who is responsible written in the discharge summary. Incidental findings that are only noted in a report are a well-known cause of missed diagnoses. Source: GMC Good medical practice, 2024 (paragraphs 28 and 65).
why_wrong: A. Relying on the GP to spot a line in a copied report risks the finding being missed and passes on responsibility without a clear handover. B. Discharging without telling him leaves him uninformed, and an unspecified future letter is not a safe follow-up plan. D. Withholding information to avoid worry is not justified for a patient with capacity and could delay a cancer diagnosis. E. Sharing his information with his wife before him breaches confidentiality unless he has agreed to it.
pearl: If you find it, you own it until someone else clearly does: tell the patient and close the loop.
thinking: Incidental finding in a report  ↓  patient has capacity and has not been told  ↓  GMC: give information patients need, share it for ongoing care  ↓  tell him, involve a senior  ↓  arrange or hand over follow-up with named responsibility, document in discharge summary
exam_trap: Assuming the GP will pick up the finding from the copied report, so the hospital does not need to act.
takeaway: Incidental findings must be explained to the patient and follow-up arranged with clear ownership before discharge.
notes: Focus mentioned candour; the statutory/professional duty of candour applies when something has gone wrong, which is not the case here, so the item rests on GMC Good medical practice 2024 paras 28 (information to patients) and 65 (continuity of care) instead. Condition C198 kept because the question is genuinely about managing an incidental finding (MAPPING_RULES exception); a strict reviewer could argue NONE (communication/professional practice), but the validator and brief allow the target here.

presentation: Septic shock with multi-organ dysfunction — critical care referral
stem:
A 72-year-old woman is admitted to the medical ward with community-acquired pneumonia. She received intravenous co-amoxiclav and clarithromycin within an hour of arrival. Six hours later she is drowsy. Her blood pressure is 82/46 mmHg, heart rate 122 beats per minute, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 92% on 4 L/min oxygen. She has passed 40 mL of urine in the last 4 hours. She has now received 1,000 mL of crystalloid in 250 mL boluses with no improvement, and the medical registrar is at the bedside. Repeat bloods show creatinine 214 micromol/L (78 micromol/L on admission), platelets 61 × 10⁹/L (232 × 10⁹/L on admission), bilirubin 52 micromol/L and venous lactate 4.9 mmol/L. She was fully independent before admission and has no treatment escalation plan limiting care.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Give a further 2,000 mL crystalloid bolus over 30 minutes
options.B: Transfuse one adult dose of platelets
options.C: Change antibiotics to IV meropenem and review in 24 hours
options.D: Start IV hydrocortisone and continue ward-based care
options.E: Refer to critical care for vasopressor and organ support

correct_answer: E. Refer to critical care for vasopressor and organ support
why_correct: She has septic shock with failure of several organ systems: circulatory (hypotension despite fluids), renal (acute kidney injury and oliguria), haematological (falling platelets), hepatic (rising bilirubin) and neurological (drowsiness), with a raised lactate. This is multi-organ dysfunction, and she has not responded to fluid resuscitation. NICE advises getting senior advice once 1,000 mL has been given without improvement, discussing vasopressors with the critical care team, and referring a high-risk patient who does not respond within 1 hour of an intervention to critical care. Source: Suspected sepsis in people aged 16 or over: recognition, assessment and early management, NICE NG253, 2025 (updated 2026).
why_wrong: A. Large further fluid boluses after fluid-refractory hypotension risk pulmonary oedema and delay the vasopressor support she needs. B. Thrombocytopenia here reflects sepsis-related organ dysfunction, and platelets are not routinely transfused without bleeding or a planned procedure. C. Her antibiotics are appropriate and were given promptly; changing them does nothing for her failing circulation, and waiting 24 hours is unsafe. D. Steroids are only considered in shock already needing vasopressors, and she needs critical care rather than continued ward care.
pearl: Sepsis plus failure of two or more organs that does not respond to fluids is a critical care problem, not a ward problem.
thinking: Pneumonia with sepsis  ↓  hypotension despite 1,000 mL fluid  ↓  AKI + oliguria, falling platelets, rising bilirubin, drowsy, lactate 4.9  ↓  multi-organ dysfunction (septic shock)  ↓  no ceiling of care  ↓  refer to critical care for vasopressors and organ support
exam_trap: Giving more and more fluid on the ward instead of recognising fluid-refractory shock that needs vasopressors.
takeaway: Fluid-refractory sepsis with several failing organs: refer to critical care for organ support.
notes: NICE NG51 has been replaced by NG253 (2025, updated Sept 2026); NG253 uses 250 mL boluses up to 1,000 mL then senior advice, and vasopressor decisions with critical care. Differs from existing GF040 (initial escalation call) by testing recognition of fluid-refractory multi-organ dysfunction with the registrar already present.

presentation: Severe acute pancreatitis with persistent organ failure — critical care
stem:
A 51-year-old man is on day 3 of an admission with alcohol-related acute pancreatitis. Despite intravenous fluids, his blood pressure has been 80–88/48–52 mmHg for 2 days, his urine output has been under 15 mL per hour for the past 12 hours, and his creatinine has risen from 88 to 296 micromol/L. His oxygen saturation is 93% on 4 L/min oxygen. He is afebrile, bilirubin is normal and ultrasound shows no gallstones or bile duct dilatation. CT shows 30% pancreatic necrosis with no gas.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Start IV meropenem to prevent infection of the pancreatic necrosis
options.B: Admit to critical care for circulatory and renal support
options.C: Arrange urgent ERCP with biliary sphincterotomy
options.D: Arrange emergency laparotomy and pancreatic necrosectomy
options.E: Keep him nil by mouth and start total parenteral nutrition

correct_answer: B. Admit to critical care for circulatory and renal support
why_correct: Organ failure lasting more than 48 hours defines severe acute pancreatitis, and he now has persistent circulatory and renal failure. Treatment is supportive, so the priority is admission to critical care for organ support such as vasopressors and renal replacement therapy. Sterile necrosis on day 3 needs no specific intervention. Source: Pancreatitis, NICE NG104, 2018 (updated 2020).
why_wrong: A. NICE advises against prophylactic antimicrobials in acute pancreatitis, and he has no sign of infected necrosis. C. ERCP is for gallstone pancreatitis with cholangitis or ongoing bile duct obstruction, and this is alcohol-related with a normal bilirubin and undilated ducts. D. Early open necrosectomy carries high mortality, and sterile necrosis on day 3 is not an indication for surgery. E. NICE advises against routine nil by mouth and recommends enteral nutrition first, with parenteral nutrition only if enteral feeding fails or is contraindicated.
pearl: Severe pancreatitis is defined by organ failure lasting over 48 hours, and its treatment is organ support.
thinking: Acute pancreatitis day 3  ↓  hypotension for 2 days despite fluids + oliguric AKI  ↓  persistent (>48 h) organ failure = severe pancreatitis  ↓  sterile necrosis, no cholangitis  ↓  supportive care in critical care for organ support
exam_trap: Reaching for antibiotics or an intervention on the pancreas when the patient's failing organs need support first.
takeaway: Persistent organ failure in pancreatitis: critical care organ support; no prophylactic antibiotics.
notes: Condition could also defensibly be C011 Acute pancreatitis; C251 kept as the slot target because the tested point is recognising and supporting multi-organ failure. Distinct from exemplar DF041 (ARDS in pancreatitis): this one tests circulatory and renal failure and the futility of antibiotics/necrosectomy/ERCP.

presentation: Frail older patient with progressive multi-organ failure — ceiling of care
stem:
A 91-year-old woman who lives in a nursing home is admitted with urosepsis. She has advanced dementia, needs help with all personal care and her Clinical Frailty Scale score is 8. After 48 hours of intravenous antibiotics and fluids she is worsening: blood pressure 78/42 mmHg, she has passed no urine for 10 hours, creatinine has risen from 96 to 388 micromol/L and lactate is 5.2 mmol/L. She is drowsy and lacks capacity to make decisions about her treatment. Her son is at the bedside. There is no advance decision, lasting power of attorney or treatment escalation plan.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Refer to critical care for intubation and vasopressor support
options.B: Arrange urgent haemodialysis for her anuric acute kidney injury
options.C: Ask her son to decide whether she goes to intensive care
options.D: Senior best-interests ceiling of care, consulting her son
options.E: Continue full active treatment and review at the next ward round

correct_answer: D. Senior best-interests ceiling of care, consulting her son
why_correct: She has progressive multi-organ failure despite 48 hours of treatment, on a background of advanced dementia and very severe frailty, so a treatment escalation plan is needed now. Her frailty score informs this decision but does not by itself decide it: the plan must weigh her overall clinical situation, the likely benefits and burdens of intubation, vasopressors and dialysis, and what is known of her previous wishes, values and beliefs. She lacks capacity and has no advance decision or lasting power of attorney, so under the Mental Capacity Act 2005 the senior clinician responsible for her care makes the decision in her best interests, after consulting her son about what she would have wanted. The agreed and documented plan may set a ceiling of care, for example ward-based treatment without intubation or dialysis, and should cover symptom control. Source: Treatment and care towards the end of life: good practice in decision making, GMC, 2010 (updated 2022); Mental Capacity Act 2005, section 4.
why_wrong: A. Escalating to invasive ventilation and vasopressors without considering her frailty, wishes and likely benefit is not in her best interests by default. B. Dialysis is a form of organ support whose appropriateness must be decided within the ceiling-of-care discussion, not started reflexively. C. Without a lasting power of attorney her son is not the decision maker, and he must not be given the impression that he is. E. She is deteriorating now, and delaying the plan risks inappropriate emergency escalation or an unplanned death.
pearl: Relatives without a lasting power of attorney are consulted, not asked to decide.
thinking: 91, CFS 8, advanced dementia  ↓  worsening shock, anuria, rising lactate despite 48 h treatment  ↓  weigh likely benefits and burdens of organ support, not frailty score alone  ↓  lacks capacity, no advance decision or LPA  ↓  senior clinician decides in best interests after consulting son about her wishes  ↓  agree and document a ceiling of care
exam_trap: Asking the son to choose whether his mother goes to intensive care, as though he were the legal decision maker.
takeaway: Frail patient with progressive multi-organ failure: senior-led treatment escalation plan, made in best interests after consulting family.
notes: Presentation could also defensibly be P088 Frailty; P056 chosen because the stem's presenting problem is deterioration. NICE NG253 rec 1.8.12 also asks for a shared decision on escalation, taking account of treatment escalation plans, before vasopressors.

presentation: Sepsis — recognising evolving organ dysfunction
stem:
A 64-year-old man attends the emergency department with 2 days of fever, rigors and dysuria. His temperature is 39.4°C, heart rate 104 beats per minute and blood pressure 118/72 mmHg. He is alert. He is started on intravenous antibiotics for suspected urosepsis, and his blood results are reviewed. A routine GP blood test 5 days ago, before he became unwell, showed a creatinine of 82 micromol/L.

Which result most strongly indicates that he is developing organ dysfunction?

options.A: Creatinine 186 micromol/L
options.B: C-reactive protein 284 mg/L
options.C: White cell count 21.4 × 10⁹/L
options.D: Neutrophil count 18.6 × 10⁹/L
options.E: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 78 mm/h

correct_answer: A. Creatinine 186 micromol/L
why_correct: His creatinine has risen from 82 to 186 micromol/L within 5 days, more than a 50% rise within 7 days, which meets the NICE (KDIGO-based) definition of acute kidney injury: a sign that infection is now causing organ hypoperfusion and dysfunction. NICE sepsis guidance uses acute kidney injury or a lactate over 2 mmol/L as evidence of hypoperfusion and advises treating such patients as high risk. The other results show inflammation but say nothing about whether an organ is failing. Source: Suspected sepsis in people aged 16 or over: recognition, assessment and early management, NICE NG253, 2025 (updated 2026); Acute kidney injury: prevention, detection and management, NICE NG148, 2019 (recommendation 1.3.1).
why_wrong: B. A very high C-reactive protein reflects the size of the inflammatory response, not organ failure. C. A raised white cell count is part of the host response to infection and is not organ dysfunction. D. Neutrophilia shows a bacterial response but gives no information about organ perfusion. E. A raised ESR is a non-specific marker of inflammation and is not used to judge organ dysfunction.
pearl: Inflammatory markers show the size of the fire; creatinine, lactate, urine output, platelets, bilirubin and conscious level show which organs are burning.
thinking: Suspected urosepsis  ↓  which result shows an organ failing, not just inflammation?  ↓  creatinine 82 → 186 within 5 days = >50% rise within 7 days = acute kidney injury  ↓  renal dysfunction = evidence of hypoperfusion  ↓  treat as high risk and monitor closely
exam_trap: Picking the most dramatic inflammatory number (CRP 284) as the sign of severity.
takeaway: In sepsis, AKI (or a raised lactate or new oliguria) signals organ dysfunction; CRP and white cells do not.
notes: Condition C363 Sepsis: the question tests recognition of organ dysfunction (AKI) in suspected sepsis; C251 Multi-organ dysfunction syndrome is not used because only one organ is failing. NICE NG253 (published Nov 2025, last updated Sep 2026) uses lactate over 2 mmol/L or acute kidney injury as evidence of hypoperfusion. Lactate deliberately left out of the options to avoid two correct answers. After clinical review (Oct 2026) the baseline was moved from 3 months to 5 days before presentation so the rise meets NICE NG148 1.3.1 (50% or greater rise known or presumed within 7 days; checked at source 8 Oct 2026).

presentation: Pyrexia of unknown origin — classical definition
stem:
A 46-year-old woman has had evening temperatures of 38.4–38.8°C for 10 days. Her full blood count, urea and electrolytes, liver function tests, urine culture, blood cultures and chest X-ray are normal. A junior doctor documents 'pyrexia of unknown origin' in her notes.

Which is the classical definition of pyrexia of unknown origin?

options.A: Above 37.5°C on several occasions for over 1 week, with no cause after investigation
options.B: Above 38.3°C on several occasions for over 1 week, with no cause after investigation
options.C: Above 38.3°C on several occasions for over 3 weeks, with no cause after investigation
options.D: Above 37.5°C on several occasions for over 3 weeks, even before any investigation is done
options.E: Above 38.3°C continuously for over 6 months, with no cause after full investigation

correct_answer: C. Above 38.3°C on several occasions for over 3 weeks, with no cause after investigation
why_correct: Classical pyrexia of unknown origin is a temperature above 38.3°C on several occasions, during an illness lasting more than 3 weeks, with no diagnosis after appropriate investigation (originally 1 week in hospital, now usually a set of outpatient or inpatient tests). Her temperatures are high enough, but 10 days is too short to meet the definition. Many short fevers are self-limiting viral illnesses, which is why the time limit exists. Source: Pyrexia of unknown origin, Patient.info professional reference (reviewed 2024); Investigating and managing pyrexia of unknown origin in adults, BMJ, 2010.
why_wrong: A. Both the temperature (37.5°C) and duration (1 week) are too low; this would label many self-limiting viral fevers as PUO. B. The temperature is right, but 1 week is too short, which is the error made by the junior doctor here. D. The definition needs a failure to find a cause after investigation, not just a long fever. E. The fever does not have to be continuous, and 6 months is far longer than the 3 weeks required.
pearl: PUO = 38.3°C, 3 weeks, still no answer after proper investigation.
thinking: Fever 38.4–38.8°C  ↓  only 10 days  ↓  classical PUO needs >38.3°C on several occasions  ↓  >3 weeks of illness  ↓  no cause after appropriate investigation  ↓  she does not yet meet the definition
exam_trap: Calling any fever without an obvious source after a week 'PUO'.
takeaway: Classical PUO: >38.3°C on several occasions, >3 weeks, undiagnosed after appropriate investigation.
notes: No NICE/CKS guidance defines PUO; definition taken from Petersdorf–Beeson as given in Patient.info (2024) and BMJ 2010 clinical review. Options worded to avoid the inpatient-week vs 3-day/3-visit variants.

presentation: Pyrexia of unknown origin — HIV testing
stem:
A 34-year-old man has had fevers up to 38.7°C, night sweats and 5 kg weight loss over 4 weeks. Examination shows small, non-tender cervical and axillary lymph nodes and nothing else. Full blood count shows lymphocytes 0.8 × 10⁹/L. Urea and electrolytes, liver function tests, urine culture, three sets of blood cultures and chest X-ray are normal. He has not been tested for HIV before.

Which investigation should be offered next?

options.A: Bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy
options.B: Excision biopsy of an axillary lymph node
options.C: Whole-body FDG-PET-CT scan
options.D: Temporal artery biopsy
options.E: HIV antigen and antibody test

correct_answer: E. HIV antigen and antibody test
why_correct: Unexplained fever is an HIV indicator condition, and an HIV test should be offered early in the work-up of pyrexia of unknown origin to everyone, whatever their perceived risk. His fever, night sweats, weight loss, lymphadenopathy and lymphopenia make HIV, and HIV-related infection or lymphoma, important possibilities. A fourth-generation antigen and antibody test is simple and cheap and directs the rest of the investigation. Source: HIV testing: increasing uptake among people who may have undiagnosed HIV, NICE NG60, 2016 (updated 2025); NICE quality standard QS157, statement 3, 2017.
why_wrong: A. Bone marrow examination is invasive and is kept for later, for example unexplained cytopenias or suspected haematological malignancy once simpler tests are done. B. Lymph node biopsy may be needed, but only after simple non-invasive tests such as HIV serology. C. PET-CT is a later-line test that cannot replace a basic HIV test. D. Temporal artery biopsy is for suspected giant cell arteritis, which is very unlikely at 34 with no headache or jaw claudication.
pearl: Every patient with a pyrexia of unknown origin needs an HIV test — early, and without a risk assessment first.
thinking: 4 weeks of fever, sweats, weight loss  ↓  lymphadenopathy + lymphopenia  ↓  first-line tests negative  ↓  unexplained fever is an HIV indicator condition  ↓  offer an HIV test now, before invasive tests
exam_trap: Jumping to invasive biopsies or advanced imaging before a simple HIV test.
takeaway: In PUO, offer an HIV test early to everyone.
notes: NICE QS157 lists 'unexplained fever' among HIV indicator conditions; BHIVA/BASHH/BIA 2020 testing guideline (review scheduled) and Salisbury NHS list include PUO. Strictly he has 4 weeks of fever with first-line tests negative, so the label PUO is reasonable.

presentation: Inpatient fever with no source — drug fever
stem:
A 71-year-old man is on day 12 of an admission for community-acquired pneumonia, which has improved after a 5-day course of amoxicillin that finished 7 days ago. During the admission he was also started on allopurinol for recurrent gout and omeprazole without a clear indication. For the last 5 days he has had temperatures of 38.4–38.8°C but feels well, and his heart rate is 76 beats per minute when febrile. There is no rash. Eosinophils are 1.1 × 10⁹/L, liver function tests are normal and C-reactive protein is 38 mg/L. Repeat chest X-ray shows resolving consolidation. He has no diarrhoea. Three sets of blood cultures and urine culture are negative, and cannula sites are clean.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Stop the new drugs and assess for DRESS
options.B: Start IV piperacillin with tazobactam
options.C: Start oral prednisolone 40 mg once daily
options.D: Arrange a bone marrow aspirate and trephine
options.E: Give regular paracetamol and continue all medicines

correct_answer: A. Stop the new drugs and assess for DRESS
why_correct: A well patient with a new fever in hospital, a relatively slow pulse, eosinophilia, and no source on a thorough infection screen suggests a drug reaction. Allopurinol is a recognised cause of drug fever and of DRESS (drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms), and omeprazole has no clear indication, so both new medicines should be stopped. Fever with eosinophilia after starting allopurinol can be an early hypersensitivity reaction before any rash appears, so monitoring the temperature alone is not enough: he needs a clinical reassessment of skin, mucous membranes, lymph nodes and observations, and repeat blood tests including full blood count and film, liver function, renal function and urinalysis to look for organ involvement. Escalate to a senior and dermatology if a rash, rising eosinophils or organ involvement develops, and report the reaction via the Yellow Card scheme. Simple drug fever usually settles within about 48–72 hours of stopping the culprit. Source: DermNet Drug hypersensitivity syndrome (DRESS); Pyrexia of unknown origin, Patient.info professional reference (reviewed 2024); Investigating and managing pyrexia of unknown origin in adults, BMJ, 2010.
why_wrong: B. Empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics in a stable patient with no infective source obscure the diagnosis and expose him to further drug reactions. C. Steroids can mask the cause and are not started without a diagnosis; they are considered by specialists if a severe hypersensitivity syndrome such as DRESS is confirmed. D. Bone marrow examination is invasive and premature when stopping the probable culprit drugs has not yet been tried. E. Treating the fever while continuing the probable culprit drugs leaves the cause in place and risks a more severe reaction such as DRESS.
pearl: Well, febrile, relatively bradycardic and eosinophilic on new drugs: stop what is new and non-essential, and look actively for DRESS.
thinking: Inpatient fever for 5 days  ↓  well, relative bradycardia, eosinophilia  ↓  full infection screen negative, pneumonia resolving  ↓  recently started allopurinol + omeprazole  ↓  drug fever or early DRESS  ↓  stop new drugs, reassess skin and organs, repeat FBC, LFTs, renal function, escalate if worsening
exam_trap: Starting broad-spectrum antibiotics for every inpatient fever without looking at the drug chart.
takeaway: Unexplained inpatient fever with eosinophilia on new drugs: stop the likely culprits and assess for DRESS and organ involvement, not just the temperature.
notes: Condition could defensibly be C015 Adverse drug effects, as drug fever is the diagnosis being tested; C338 kept as slot target because the question is framed as an unexplained (nosocomial) fever work-up. Strictly this is a nosocomial fever rather than classical PUO (duration under 3 weeks). After clinical review (Oct 2026) the key was reworded from 'Stop allopurinol and omeprazole and monitor his temperature' to include active assessment for DRESS and organ involvement; 'the new drugs' means allopurinol and omeprazole (amoxicillin has already finished). No rash and normal LFTs are stated so that the presentation is not yet established DRESS needing specialist treatment.

presentation: Pyrexia of unknown origin — next investigation after negative first-line tests
stem:
A 38-year-old woman has had fevers of up to 38.6°C on most days for 4 weeks, with fatigue and 3 kg weight loss. She is haemodynamically stable, eating and drinking. A detailed history and repeated examination have found no focus, and there is no heart murmur. Full blood count shows haemoglobin 108 g/L with normal white cells and platelets. C-reactive protein is 62 mg/L. Urea and electrolytes, liver function tests, thyroid function, urinalysis and urine culture, three sets of blood cultures, HIV test, autoimmune screen and chest X-ray are normal or negative. She has no recent travel.

Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Start empirical IV ceftriaxone
options.B: CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis
options.C: Start a trial of oral prednisolone
options.D: Bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy
options.E: Diagnostic laparoscopy and peritoneal biopsy

correct_answer: B. CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis
why_correct: She now meets the definition of classical pyrexia of unknown origin and is stable, with a raised C-reactive protein. The history, repeated examination, baseline blood tests and microbiology have been completed and give no clue to direct a specific test, so the most useful next step is cross-sectional imaging of the chest, abdomen and pelvis, chosen to look for occult infection (such as an abscess), malignancy (such as lymphoma or a solid tumour) or inflammatory disease, which then directs further tests. In other patients the next test is guided by any clinical clues, and FDG-PET-CT may follow if CT does not help. Empirical antibiotics and steroids are avoided in stable patients because they can mask the cause and delay diagnosis. Source: Investigating and managing pyrexia of unknown origin in adults, BMJ, 2010; Pyrexia of unknown origin, Patient.info professional reference (reviewed 2024).
why_wrong: A. Empirical antibiotics in a stable, non-neutropenic patient rarely cure PUO and can make cultures negative and delay the diagnosis. C. A steroid trial can mask lymphoma, infection and vasculitis and is discouraged without a diagnosis. D. Bone marrow examination is invasive and is kept for cytopenias or when non-invasive imaging has not found a cause. E. Surgical exploration is a last resort, not a step before non-invasive imaging.
pearl: In stable PUO, investigate before you treat: CT first, then PET-CT if needed — not empirical antibiotics or steroids.
thinking: Fever >38.3°C for 4 weeks, stable  ↓  history, repeated examination, first-line bloods, cultures, HIV, autoimmune screen and CXR unrevealing  ↓  raised CRP, mild anaemia, no localising clue  ↓  classical PUO  ↓  CT chest, abdomen and pelvis to look for occult infection, malignancy or inflammation  ↓  avoid empirical antibiotics/steroids
exam_trap: Starting empirical antibiotics or steroids in a stable patient to 'see if it settles'.
takeaway: Stable PUO with a completed, unrevealing first-line assessment: CT chest/abdomen/pelvis to look for an occult cause, then PET-CT if needed.
