notes: PET-CT deliberately omitted from the options because some centres may use it at this point (BMJ 2010 supports early FDG-PET if CRP raised), which could make two answers defensible. No NICE guideline covers PUO. Differs from existing GF045, where CT was already negative and the answer was to withhold empirical treatment.

presentation: Papilloedema — urgent brain imaging before lumbar puncture
stem:
A 47-year-old man attends the emergency department with a 3-week history of headache that is getting steadily worse. It is worst when he wakes in the morning and when he lies flat, and he has vomited on waking twice this week. He has no fever, neck stiffness or rash. His blood pressure is 134/82 mmHg. Neurological examination is normal, but fundoscopy shows bilateral swollen optic discs with blurred margins.

Which is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.A: Lumbar puncture with opening pressure measurement
options.B: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein
options.C: MRI brain on the suspected cancer pathway within 2 weeks
options.D: Urgent same-day CT scan of the head
options.E: Formal visual field testing by an optometrist

correct_answer: D. Urgent same-day CT scan of the head
why_correct: A progressive headache that is worse on waking and lying flat, with morning vomiting and bilateral optic disc swelling, means raised intracranial pressure until proven otherwise. He needs urgent brain imaging the same day (CT, or MRI if immediately available) to look for a mass lesion, hydrocephalus or venous sinus thrombosis. Lumbar puncture is only considered after imaging has excluded a space-occupying lesion, because it can precipitate herniation. Source: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension consensus guidelines (Mollan et al., JNNP, 2018); UHB raised intracranial pressure pathway.
why_wrong: A. A lumbar puncture before imaging risks brain herniation if there is a mass lesion or obstructive hydrocephalus. B. Inflammatory markers are used for suspected giant cell arteritis, which does not cause bilateral disc swelling with a positional headache. C. Papilloedema with features of raised pressure is an emergency, so a 2-week pathway is too slow. E. Visual fields are useful for monitoring but do not identify the cause and would delay urgent imaging.
pearl: Papilloedema plus a positional morning headache: image the brain today, and never needle the spine first.
thinking: Headache worse on waking and lying flat + morning vomiting  ↓  bilateral swollen discs = papilloedema  ↓  raised intracranial pressure until proven otherwise  ↓  exclude mass, hydrocephalus or venous sinus thrombosis  ↓  urgent same-day brain imaging, then consider lumbar puncture
exam_trap: Jumping straight to lumbar puncture to measure the opening pressure before the brain has been imaged.
takeaway: Papilloedema needs urgent same-day neuroimaging before any lumbar puncture.

presentation: Papilloedema versus optic neuritis — distinguishing features
stem:
A 29-year-old woman sees her GP with a 6-week history of daily headaches. Her optometrist has written to say that he saw optic disc swelling during a routine eye test. The GP is trying to decide whether the disc swelling is more likely to be papilloedema or optic neuritis.

Which additional finding would most support papilloedema rather than optic neuritis?

options.A: Pain on moving the eyes
options.B: Normal visual acuity and colour vision
options.C: A relative afferent pupillary defect
options.D: A central scotoma on visual field testing
options.E: Disc swelling affecting one eye only

correct_answer: B. Normal visual acuity and colour vision
why_correct: In papilloedema the optic nerve fibres keep working in the early stages, so visual acuity, colour vision and pupil responses are usually normal; the field defect is an enlarged blind spot. Optic neuritis damages the nerve directly, giving reduced acuity, red desaturation, a central scotoma, a relative afferent pupillary defect and often pain on eye movement. Papilloedema is also usually bilateral, while optic neuritis is usually unilateral. Source: GPnotebook, Comparison of papilloedema and papillitis (2025).
why_wrong: A. Pain on eye movement is typical of optic neuritis, not papilloedema. C. A relative afferent pupillary defect shows optic nerve dysfunction in one eye, which fits optic neuritis. D. A central scotoma is the classic field defect in optic neuritis; papilloedema gives an enlarged blind spot. E. One-sided disc swelling points away from papilloedema, which is usually bilateral.
pearl: Swollen discs that see well are papilloedema; a swollen disc that sees badly is optic neuritis.
thinking: Optic disc swelling  ↓  ask: is nerve function preserved?  ↓  normal acuity, colour vision and pupils  ↓  nerve working despite swelling  ↓  papilloedema (raised intracranial pressure), not optic neuritis
exam_trap: Assuming a swollen disc with good vision cannot be serious — preserved acuity is typical of early papilloedema.
takeaway: Papilloedema: usually bilateral, with normal acuity, colour vision and pupils early on.
notes: NICE CKS (optic neuritis) returned HTTP 403 from this environment; features were checked against GPnotebook (UK) and LITFL.

presentation: Transient visual obscurations — symptom of papilloedema
stem:
A 23-year-old woman with a body mass index of 38 kg/m² has had daily headaches for 6 weeks. Several times a day, when she stands up after bending down, the vision in both eyes greys out for a few seconds and then returns fully. Her lying and standing blood pressures show no postural drop. Visual acuity is 6/6 in both eyes and she has no floaters, flashing lights or eye pain.

What is the most likely cause of her visual episodes?

options.A: Amaurosis fugax from emboli in the carotid arteries
options.B: Visual aura from migraine with aura
options.C: Orthostatic hypotension on standing up
options.D: Posterior vitreous detachment in both eyes
options.E: Transient visual obscurations from papilloedema

correct_answer: E. Transient visual obscurations from papilloedema
why_correct: Brief greying or blacking out of vision in one or both eyes for seconds, brought on by standing up or bending, is the typical description of transient visual obscurations. They happen when a swollen optic disc is briefly under-perfused and are a symptom of papilloedema. In a young woman with a raised BMI and daily headaches, idiopathic intracranial hypertension is the likely cause, and she needs fundoscopy and urgent assessment. Source: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension consensus guidelines (Mollan et al., JNNP, 2018).
why_wrong: A. Amaurosis fugax is usually one-sided, lasts minutes and occurs in older people with vascular risk factors. B. Migraine aura usually builds up over 5 to 60 minutes with positive features such as zigzags, not seconds-long greying on posture change. C. Orthostatic hypotension is unlikely as there is no postural blood pressure drop. D. Posterior vitreous detachment causes floaters and flashes, not brief bilateral greying of vision.
pearl: Seconds-long greying of vision on standing or bending means look at the discs.
thinking: Seconds-long bilateral greying of vision  ↓  triggered by standing or bending  ↓  no postural blood pressure drop  ↓  transient visual obscurations  ↓  papilloedema (likely idiopathic intracranial hypertension) — check fundi urgently
exam_trap: Putting posture-related visual greying down to postural hypotension without checking the optic discs.
takeaway: Transient visual obscurations are a red-flag symptom of papilloedema.

presentation: Fundoscopic features of papilloedema
stem:
A 38-year-old woman attends the emergency department with a 2-week history of headache that is worse in the morning and when she coughs. She has felt nauseated on waking. Her visual acuity is 6/6 in both eyes. The foundation doctor examines her fundi with an ophthalmoscope.

Which set of fundoscopic findings would most strongly indicate papilloedema?

options.A: Blurred margins, absent venous pulsation, disc haemorrhages
options.B: Enlarged optic cup with a thin neuroretinal rim
options.C: Pale, flat optic disc with sharp margins
options.D: Cherry-red spot at the macula with a pale retina
options.E: Arteriovenous nipping with silver-wiring of the retinal arterioles

correct_answer: A. Blurred margins, absent venous pulsation, disc haemorrhages
why_correct: Papilloedema is optic disc swelling caused by raised intracranial pressure. On fundoscopy the disc margins become blurred and the disc raised, the veins become engorged, and flame-shaped haemorrhages can appear around the disc; these findings are usually bilateral. Spontaneous venous pulsations are usually lost, but they are also absent in some healthy people, so this sign is not diagnostic on its own: the diagnosis rests on the overall appearance of the disc in a patient whose symptoms suggest raised pressure. Source: Life in the Fast Lane, That optic disc doesn't look right (2025); GPnotebook, Papilloedema (2025).
why_wrong: B. A large cup with a thin rim is the appearance of glaucomatous optic neuropathy. C. A pale, flat disc with sharp margins is optic atrophy, which can follow long-standing papilloedema but is not active swelling. D. A cherry-red spot with a pale retina is central retinal artery occlusion, which causes sudden painless visual loss. E. Arteriovenous nipping and silver-wiring are signs of chronic hypertensive retinopathy, not raised intracranial pressure.
pearl: Blurred, raised margins with peripapillary haemorrhages make the case for a swollen disc; absent venous pulsation supports it but never proves it alone.
thinking: Headache worse in the morning and on coughing  ↓  suspect raised intracranial pressure  ↓  look at the disc  ↓  blurred margins + absent venous pulsation + disc haemorrhages  ↓  papilloedema
exam_trap: Confusing a pale, sharp optic disc (optic atrophy) with active disc swelling.
takeaway: Papilloedema shows blurred, raised disc margins, loss of venous pulsation and peripapillary haemorrhages.
notes: Existing Q12719 asks for the single most characteristic finding (swollen optic discs); this item tests recognition of the full fundoscopic pattern against other disc and retinal appearances. Absent spontaneous venous pulsation is also seen in some healthy people, so it is presented as part of a set, not alone. NICE CKS returned HTTP 403 here; fundoscopic features were checked against GPnotebook (UK) and LITFL (Australian, secondary).

presentation: Unilateral tinnitus with asymmetric hearing loss — imaging when MRI is contraindicated
stem:
A 61-year-old man with a permanent pacemaker that is not MRI-conditional is seen in the ear, nose and throat (ENT) clinic; cardiology have confirmed that he cannot have an MRI scan. He has had 6 months of constant, non-pulsatile tinnitus in his right ear and mild unsteadiness. Otoscopy is normal. Pure tone audiometry shows a right sensorineural hearing loss that is 25 decibels worse than the left at two adjacent frequencies. Facial nerve function is normal.

Given that MRI is not possible, which is the most appropriate investigation?

options.A: Non-contrast CT scan of the head, including the posterior fossa
options.B: Repeat pure tone audiometry in 12 months
options.C: Contrast-enhanced CT of the internal auditory meati
options.D: Carotid artery duplex ultrasound scan
options.E: Auditory brainstem response testing alone

correct_answer: C. Contrast-enhanced CT of the internal auditory meati
why_correct: Unilateral tinnitus with an asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss and unsteadiness raises the possibility of a vestibular schwannoma, so the internal auditory meati need imaging. MRI of the internal auditory meati is the first-line investigation and should be used whenever MRI is suitable. This man cannot have MRI because his pacemaker is not MRI-conditional, and for people who are unable to have MRI, NICE recommends contrast-enhanced CT of the internal auditory meati instead. Source: Tinnitus: assessment and management (NICE NG155, 2020, rec 1.4.6); Hearing loss in adults (NICE NG98, 2018).
why_wrong: A. A non-contrast CT of the head can miss a small vestibular schwannoma in the internal auditory canal. B. Waiting 12 months delays the diagnosis of a possible tumour when imaging is already indicated. D. Carotid duplex is relevant to pulsatile tinnitus, but his tinnitus is non-pulsatile. E. Auditory brainstem response testing is less sensitive than imaging for small tumours and does not replace it.
pearl: No MRI possible? Contrast-enhanced CT of the internal auditory meati is the NICE fallback.
thinking: Unilateral non-pulsatile tinnitus + asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss  ↓  possible vestibular schwannoma  ↓  MRI of internal auditory meati first-line  ↓  MRI contraindicated (non-conditional pacemaker)  ↓  contrast-enhanced CT of internal auditory meati
exam_trap: Choosing a plain non-contrast CT head, which is not designed to show a small tumour in the internal auditory canal.
takeaway: Investigate unilateral tinnitus with asymmetric hearing loss with MRI of the internal auditory meati, or contrast-enhanced CT if MRI is not possible.
notes: The slot's original focus (MRI IAM for unilateral tinnitus with asymmetric SNHL) is already covered by existing DF009, so this item sharpens the angle to the NICE NG155 alternative when MRI is contraindicated. Condition labelled vestibular schwannoma as the lesion being excluded; P097 Hearing loss would also be defensible but the slot target is Tinnitus.

presentation: Pulsatile tinnitus with headache — check fundi for idiopathic intracranial hypertension
stem:
A 26-year-old woman with a body mass index of 36 kg/m² sees her GP with 2 months of a whooshing noise in both ears that keeps time with her heartbeat. She also has daily headaches that are worse when she wakes and when she bends over. She has no hearing loss, vertigo or ear pain. Otoscopy is normal.

Which examination is most important to perform at this consultation?

options.A: Fundoscopy to look for optic disc swelling
options.B: Auscultation of the neck for a carotid bruit
options.C: Rinne and Weber tuning fork tests
options.D: Palpation of the temporal arteries
options.E: Dix–Hallpike positional manoeuvre

correct_answer: A. Fundoscopy to look for optic disc swelling
why_correct: Pulsatile tinnitus with a headache that is worse on waking and bending in a young woman with a raised BMI strongly suggests idiopathic intracranial hypertension. The key examination is fundoscopy, because papilloedema confirms raised intracranial pressure, makes the situation urgent and threatens sight. If papilloedema is present she needs same-day referral for brain imaging and further assessment. Source: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension consensus guidelines (Mollan et al., JNNP, 2018); Tinnitus: assessment and management (NICE NG155, 2020).
why_wrong: B. A carotid bruit is worth listening for in pulsatile tinnitus, but it does not assess the raised intracranial pressure suggested by her headache. C. Tuning fork tests assess hearing loss, which she does not have. D. Temporal artery palpation is for giant cell arteritis, which is very unlikely at 26. E. The Dix–Hallpike manoeuvre tests for benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, and she has no vertigo.
pearl: Pulsatile tinnitus plus headache in a young woman: look at the discs before anything else.
thinking: Pulsatile tinnitus + headache worse on waking and bending  ↓  young woman with raised BMI  ↓  suspect idiopathic intracranial hypertension  ↓  fundoscopy for papilloedema  ↓  if present: same-day referral for imaging
exam_trap: Treating pulsatile tinnitus purely as an ear problem and forgetting to examine the optic discs.
takeaway: In pulsatile tinnitus with headache, always examine the fundi for papilloedema.
notes: Existing Q336 and Q697 ask for the diagnosis after imaging and lumbar puncture; this item tests the first bedside step at the GP stage.

presentation: Bilateral tinnitus with gradual hearing loss — audiological assessment
stem:
A 74-year-old man sees his GP because of ringing in both ears for about a year. His wife says he has the television on loudly, and he struggles to follow conversation in noisy places. The tinnitus is the same in both ears, is not pulsatile and does not stop him sleeping. He has no vertigo, ear pain, discharge or neurological symptoms. Otoscopy shows clear ear canals and normal eardrums.

Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Reassure him that no follow-up is needed
options.B: Request MRI of the internal auditory meati
options.C: Prescribe betahistine for three months
options.D: Refer him for an audiological assessment
options.E: Refer him to ENT to be seen within 24 hours

correct_answer: D. Refer him for an audiological assessment
why_correct: Bilateral, symmetrical tinnitus with gradual hearing difficulty in an older adult is most likely due to age-related hearing loss. NICE recommends that everyone with tinnitus is offered an audiological assessment, and that adults with hearing difficulties have wax and infection excluded and then an audiological assessment. Hearing aids, if needed, often improve the tinnitus as well as communication. Source: Tinnitus: assessment and management (NICE NG155, 2020); Hearing loss in adults (NICE NG98, 2018).
why_wrong: A. Reassurance alone leaves a hearing loss that is affecting communication unassessed and untreated. B. MRI of the internal auditory meati is for unilateral or asymmetric tinnitus or hearing loss, or tinnitus with neurological or otological features; symmetrical tinnitus with gradual bilateral hearing loss does not need a scan. C. NICE advises against betahistine for tinnitus. E. Referral within 24 hours is for hearing loss that developed suddenly in the past 30 days, not gradual loss over a year.
pearl: Symmetrical tinnitus with gradual hearing loss needs a hearing test, not a scan.
thinking: Bilateral symmetrical non-pulsatile tinnitus  ↓  gradual hearing difficulty in an older adult  ↓  no red flags, wax excluded  ↓  likely age-related hearing loss  ↓  audiological assessment (hearing aids if needed)
exam_trap: Ordering an MRI for symmetrical tinnitus with no red flags.
takeaway: Offer an audiological assessment to people with tinnitus; image only when the features suggest a structural cause.
notes: Condition X: the likely underlying condition (age-related hearing loss/presbycusis) has no GMC condition entry. P097 Hearing loss would also fit the presentation, but the slot target is Tinnitus.

presentation: Cisplatin ototoxicity — new tinnitus and high-frequency hearing loss
stem:
A 66-year-old man with muscle-invasive bladder cancer is having his third cycle of neoadjuvant chemotherapy with gemcitabine and cisplatin. He reports a new high-pitched ringing in both ears and finds it harder to hear his grandchildren. Audiometry shows a new bilateral high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss compared with his baseline test. His other medicines are ondansetron, dexamethasone and lansoprazole.

Which medicine is most likely to be responsible?

options.A: Gemcitabine
options.B: Cisplatin
options.C: Ondansetron
options.D: Dexamethasone
options.E: Lansoprazole

correct_answer: B. Cisplatin
why_correct: Cisplatin causes dose-related, cumulative ototoxicity that presents as tinnitus and high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss, often in both ears. Audiometry is recommended before treatment and again if hearing symptoms develop, and important deterioration may need a dose change or stopping the drug. The oncology team should be told before the next cycle. Source: Cisplatin 1 mg/ml Sterile Concentrate Summary of Product Characteristics (emc, current).
why_wrong: A. Gemcitabine mainly causes bone marrow suppression, flu-like symptoms and rashes, not ototoxicity. C. Ondansetron commonly causes headache and constipation but is not ototoxic. D. Dexamethasone causes hyperglycaemia, insomnia and mood change rather than hearing loss. E. Lansoprazole is not associated with tinnitus or sensorineural hearing loss.
pearl: Platinum chemotherapy plus new tinnitus means cisplatin ototoxicity until proven otherwise.
thinking: New bilateral tinnitus + high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss  ↓  during chemotherapy  ↓  which drug is ototoxic?  ↓  cisplatin (cumulative, dose-related)  ↓  audiometry and inform oncology before the next cycle
exam_trap: Blaming the antiemetics because they are the medicines most often linked with side effects.
takeaway: Cisplatin is ototoxic: new tinnitus or high-frequency hearing loss needs audiometry and an oncology review.
notes: BNF and NICE CKS pages returned HTTP 403 from this environment; the cisplatin facts were checked against the UK Summary of Product Characteristics on emc instead.

presentation: Tinnitus-related distress with high suicide risk — crisis mental health referral
stem:
A 52-year-old man sees his GP with constant tinnitus in both ears for 8 months. He cannot sleep, has stopped working and says the noise has made his life unbearable. He tells the GP he has saved up 60 co-codamol tablets and plans to take them all this weekend while his wife is away. He has not told anyone else. He is not intoxicated, and there are no other neurological or ear symptoms.

Which is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.A: Refer for tinnitus-related CBT via the local pathway
options.B: Start sertraline and review him in two weeks
options.C: Refer to audiology for tinnitus support and advice
options.D: Refer to ENT to be seen within two weeks
options.E: Refer immediately to the crisis mental health team

correct_answer: E. Refer immediately to the crisis mental health team
why_correct: He has a clear plan, the means already gathered, a set time and a period when he will be alone, which together indicate a high risk of suicide. NICE recommends that people with tinnitus associated with a high risk of suicide are referred immediately to a crisis mental health team for assessment, with a safe place provided while they wait. In practice this means he should not be left alone while the assessment is arranged, and removing his access to the 60 co-codamol tablets should be discussed and agreed with him (involving his wife if he consents). Tinnitus or audiology referrals must not delay this, and tinnitus management can continue once his immediate safety has been addressed. Source: Tinnitus: assessment and management (NICE NG155, 2020, rec 1.2.1); Self-harm: assessment, management and preventing recurrence (NICE NG225, 2022, rec 1.11.7 on safety planning and restricting access to lethal means; written for people who have self-harmed, its principles apply here).
why_wrong: A. Tinnitus-related CBT is helpful for ongoing distress but cannot manage an immediate suicide risk. B. Starting an antidepressant with a two-week review leaves him unsafe this weekend, and gives no immediate risk management. C. Audiology tinnitus support does not address an imminent risk to his life. D. A two-week ENT referral is for distress without high suicide risk, so it is too slow here.
pearl: Tinnitus with a suicide plan is a psychiatric emergency first and an ear problem second.
thinking: Distressing tinnitus  ↓  suicidal thoughts with plan, means, timing and isolation  ↓  high suicide risk  ↓  immediate referral to crisis mental health team and keep him safe  ↓  continue tinnitus care afterwards
exam_trap: Focusing on treating the tinnitus and referring routinely while missing the immediate suicide risk.
takeaway: Tinnitus with high suicide risk needs immediate referral to a crisis mental health team.
notes: Condition X: what is tested is acute suicide-risk management in tinnitus-related distress; no GMC condition genuinely represents this (not established depression, no self-harm act). P196 Suicidal thoughts would also be a defensible presentation, but the slot target is Tinnitus.

presentation: Cervical radiculopathy — C6 root
stem:
A 52-year-old man who works as a plasterer has had three weeks of right-sided neck pain that shoots down the outside of his forearm into his thumb and index finger, which feel numb and tingly. On examination, shoulder abduction is full strength. Elbow flexion and wrist extension are weak at 4/5 on the right. The biceps and supinator (brachioradialis) reflexes are reduced on the right, and the triceps reflex is normal. There is reduced pinprick sensation over the right thumb. Gait and lower limb examination are normal.

Which nerve root is most likely affected?

options.A: C6
options.B: C5
options.C: C7
options.D: C8
options.E: C5 and C6 together

correct_answer: A. C6
why_correct: Sensory change in the thumb and index finger, weakness of elbow flexion and wrist extension, and a reduced biceps and supinator reflex point to the C6 root. Normal shoulder abduction argues against C5, and a normal triceps reflex argues against C7. Source: Cervical radiculopathy (Clinical Intelligence), British Journal of General Practice, 2018.
why_wrong: B. A C5 lesion causes weak shoulder abduction and sensory loss over the lateral upper arm (regimental badge area), and his shoulder abduction is normal. C. A C7 lesion causes weak elbow extension, a reduced triceps reflex and middle finger sensory change. D. A C8 lesion affects finger flexion and the little finger and medial forearm. E. A combined C5 and C6 lesion would also weaken shoulder abduction, which is normal here.
pearl: C6 'six-shooter': the thumb and index finger make a pistol, and C6 supplies the thumb, wrist extensors and the supinator reflex.
thinking: Neck pain radiating into the arm = radiculopathy  ↓  Thumb and index finger sensory change  ↓  Weak elbow flexion and wrist extension, normal shoulder abduction  ↓  Reduced biceps and supinator reflexes, triceps normal  ↓  C6 root
exam_trap: Choosing C5 because the biceps reflex is reduced, ignoring the normal shoulder abduction and the thumb sensory loss.
takeaway: Thumb numbness, weak wrist extension and a reduced supinator reflex localise to C6.
notes: NICE CKS pages returned 403 to automated fetch; C6 features were confirmed from the BJGP 2018 Clinical Intelligence article.

presentation: Foot drop — L5 radiculopathy vs common peroneal palsy
stem:
A 47-year-old man has had two weeks of low back pain radiating down the outside of his left leg. For the last five days he has been catching his left toes on the pavement. On examination, left ankle dorsiflexion and big toe extension are 3/5. Left ankle inversion is also weak at 4/5, and left hip abduction is weak at 4/5. Ankle eversion is mildly weak. Knee and ankle reflexes are normal and equal. There is reduced sensation over the dorsum of the left foot. There is no saddle anaesthesia and bladder and bowel function are normal.

Where is the lesion most likely to be?

options.A: Common peroneal nerve at the fibular head
options.B: Sciatic nerve in the thigh
options.C: L5 nerve root
options.D: S1 nerve root
options.E: Deep peroneal nerve in the leg

correct_answer: C. L5 nerve root
why_correct: Foot drop with weak ankle inversion (tibialis posterior, tibial nerve) and weak hip abduction (gluteus medius, superior gluteal nerve) cannot be explained by a single peripheral nerve, but all of these muscles share the L5 root. Back pain radiating down the leg and normal reflexes also fit an L5 radiculopathy. Source: Mermelstein, Barbosa and Kaski, Neurological gait assessment, Practical Neurology 2024;24:11–21 (and its published correction on hip abduction); Foot drop, WikiMSK.
why_wrong: A. A common peroneal palsy causes foot drop and weak eversion but spares ankle inversion and hip abduction, which are supplied by other nerves. B. The sciatic nerve does not supply gluteus medius, so hip abduction would be normal, and the ankle reflex may be reduced. D. An S1 lesion causes weak plantar flexion, lateral foot sensory loss and a reduced ankle reflex, not foot drop. E. A deep peroneal lesion causes weak dorsiflexion with a small area of numbness between the first and second toes, and spares inversion, eversion and the hip.
pearl: Foot drop: test inversion and hip abduction — if either is weak, look at the L5 root, not the fibular head.
thinking: Foot drop (weak dorsiflexion)  ↓  Also weak inversion (tibial nerve) and hip abduction (superior gluteal nerve)  ↓  More than one peripheral nerve involved, all L5 myotome  ↓  Radicular back pain, normal reflexes  ↓  L5 radiculopathy
exam_trap: Assuming every foot drop is a common peroneal palsy without testing ankle inversion and hip abduction.
takeaway: Foot drop with weak inversion or hip abduction points to L5, not the common peroneal nerve.
notes: Kept distinct from existing Q11624 (identify root from dorsiflexion weakness); this tests root vs peripheral nerve localisation.

presentation: Cervical radiculopathy without red flags — initial management
stem:
A 44-year-old office worker sees her GP with 10 days of left neck pain spreading down the back of her arm into her middle finger, with intermittent tingling. She is otherwise well, with no fever, weight loss, history of cancer or trauma. Power, reflexes and sensation in both arms are normal. She has no leg symptoms, gait disturbance, hand clumsiness, or bladder or bowel problems. She is taking regular paracetamol and ibuprofen, which help.

What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Urgent MRI scan of the cervical spine
options.B: Plain X-ray of the cervical spine
options.C: Urgent referral to the on-call spinal surgical team
options.D: Soft cervical collar and bed rest for at least a month
options.E: Analgesia, keep active, review at 4–6 weeks

correct_answer: E. Analgesia, keep active, review at 4–6 weeks
why_correct: This is probable C7 cervical radiculopathy with no neurological deficit and no red flags, and most cases settle within weeks. Initial management is conservative, with analgesia, advice to stay active and physiotherapy if needed. She should be safety-netted to seek review urgently, before the planned review, if she develops new weakness or numbness, hand clumsiness, difficulty walking, bladder or bowel symptoms, or other red flags such as fever or weight loss. Imaging or specialist referral is considered if symptoms persist beyond 4–6 weeks, sooner if there is a neurological deficit, and urgently if there are red flags or features of myelopathy. Source: Cervical radiculopathy (Clinical Intelligence), British Journal of General Practice, 2018.
why_wrong: A. MRI is not needed at this stage because there are no red flags or neurological deficit, and incidental degenerative changes are common. B. Plain X-rays do not show nerve root compression and are not recommended for radiculopathy. C. Urgent surgical referral is for suspected myelopathy, progressive deficit or red flags, none of which she has. D. Prolonged rest and immobilisation in a collar are not recommended; she should be advised to stay active.
pearl: Radicular arm pain alone is common and usually self-limiting; it is the progressive deficit, myelopathy or red flags that need urgent action.
thinking: Neck pain with radicular arm symptoms  ↓  No weakness, normal reflexes and sensation  ↓  No red flags or myelopathy features  ↓  Natural history is good  ↓  Conservative management, review at 4–6 weeks
exam_trap: Ordering an MRI for every patient with arm pain, even without deficit or red flags.
takeaway: Cervical radiculopathy without deficit or red flags: conservative first, refer if it persists beyond 4–6 weeks.
notes: NICE CKS returned 403 to automated fetch; referral thresholds confirmed via BJGP 2018 and a secondary summary that cites CKS. The vignette deliberately has no motor deficit, because CKS/BJGP suggest earlier referral when neurology is abnormal.

presentation: Sciatica — S1 root examination findings
stem:
A 39-year-old warehouse worker has had three weeks of low back pain radiating down the back of his right thigh and calf to the outer edge of his foot. On examination, he cannot rise onto the toes of his right foot repeatedly, and plantar flexion is 4/5. The right ankle reflex is absent, and the knee reflexes are normal. Sensation is reduced over the lateral border and sole of the right foot. Ankle dorsiflexion and big toe extension are normal. Perianal sensation and bladder function are normal.

Which nerve root is most likely affected?

options.A: L4
options.B: S1
options.C: L5
options.D: L3
options.E: L5 and S1 together

correct_answer: B. S1
why_correct: Weak plantar flexion, a lost ankle reflex and numbness over the lateral border and sole of the foot are the classic S1 findings. Normal dorsiflexion and big toe extension argue against L5, and a normal knee reflex argues against L3 and L4. Source: MSD Manual Professional, Symptoms of common radiculopathies by cord level; Foot drop, WikiMSK.
why_wrong: A. An L4 lesion causes weak knee extension and ankle dorsiflexion, a reduced knee reflex and numbness over the medial shin. C. An L5 lesion causes weak dorsiflexion and big toe extension with numbness on the dorsum of the foot and normal reflexes. D. An L3 lesion causes weak hip flexion and knee extension with a reduced knee reflex and anterior thigh numbness. E. A combined L5 and S1 lesion would also weaken ankle dorsiflexion and big toe extension, which are normal here.
pearl: S1: 'stand on tiptoe, tap the Achilles, touch the little toe'.
thinking: Radicular leg pain to the lateral foot  ↓  Weak plantar flexion (calf raise)  ↓  Absent ankle reflex, knee reflex normal  ↓  Lateral border and sole numbness  ↓  S1 root
exam_trap: Choosing L5 because 'sciatica' is mentioned, without matching the weakness and reflex to the root.
takeaway: Weak plantar flexion, absent ankle jerk and lateral foot numbness = S1.
notes: Avoids duplicating existing Q11624 (L5 from dorsiflexion). NICE CKS returned 403 to automated fetch, so S1 findings were confirmed from secondary sources; reviewer may prefer to cite CKS Sciatica directly.

presentation: Polyhydramnios with a large fetus — check for gestational diabetes
stem:
A 31-year-old woman in her first pregnancy is seen at 31 weeks' gestation because her symphysis–fundal height is 36 cm. She had no risk factors for gestational diabetes at booking and was not offered glucose testing. Urinalysis at her last two appointments showed glycosuria of 1+. An ultrasound scan shows a single fetus with an abdominal circumference above the 97th centile, a deepest vertical pool of amniotic fluid of 10 cm, and no structural abnormality. Her blood pressure is 118/72 mmHg.

Which is the most appropriate investigation?

options.A: Amniocentesis for fetal karyotype and microarray
options.B: Maternal TORCH infection serology
options.C: Kleihauer test of maternal blood
options.D: 75 g 2-hour oral glucose tolerance test
options.E: Maternal HbA1c measurement to diagnose diabetes

correct_answer: D. 75 g 2-hour oral glucose tolerance test
why_correct: Polyhydramnios with a large fetus and repeated glycosuria strongly suggests gestational diabetes, because fetal hyperglycaemia causes fetal polyuria and overgrowth. Diabetes is a key treatable maternal cause, and the 75 g 2-hour oral glucose tolerance test is the recommended diagnostic test. Glycosuria of 1+ on two or more occasions is itself an indication for further testing. Source: NICE NG3 Diabetes in pregnancy (2015, updated 2020); Barnsley Hospital NHS FT Polyhydramnios guideline (2024).
why_wrong: A. Amniocentesis is considered when structural anomalies are seen, and this fetus is structurally normal and large, which points to a metabolic cause. B. TORCH serology is part of a broader screen but infection does not explain a macrosomic fetus with glycosuria. C. A Kleihauer test measures fetomaternal haemorrhage and has no role here. E. NICE recommends the 75 g 2-hour OGTT to test for gestational diabetes and advises against using HbA1c to assess the risk of it; HbA1c is measured only after diagnosis, to look for pre-existing type 2 diabetes.
pearl: Polyhydramnios plus a big baby: think maternal diabetes and do an OGTT.
thinking: Large-for-dates fundal height  ↓  Polyhydramnios + AC >97th centile, normal anatomy  ↓  Repeated glycosuria  ↓  Fetal hyperglycaemia → polyuria and overgrowth  ↓  75 g OGTT
exam_trap: Choosing HbA1c, which NICE does not use to test for gestational diabetes; the 75 g OGTT is the diagnostic test.
takeaway: Polyhydramnios with macrosomia: test for gestational diabetes with a 75 g OGTT.
notes: NG3 does not list polyhydramnios as an OGTT indication itself; the trust guideline does, and repeated 1+ glycosuria independently meets NG3 1.2.4.

presentation: Oligohydramnios with an SGA fetus — placental insufficiency
stem:
A 34-year-old woman who smokes 15 cigarettes a day is 33 weeks pregnant. Her symphysis–fundal height measures 29 cm. An ultrasound scan shows an estimated fetal weight below the 3rd centile, with the abdominal circumference falling across centiles since her last scan. The deepest vertical pool of amniotic fluid is 1.8 cm. The fetus is structurally normal. She reports normal fetal movements and has had no leakage of fluid. Her blood pressure is 124/78 mmHg and urinalysis is normal.

Which is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.A: Umbilical artery Doppler assessment
options.B: Repeat growth scan in four weeks
options.C: Amniocentesis for fetal karyotype
options.D: Daily CTG as the only surveillance
options.E: Sterile speculum examination for pooling

correct_answer: A. Umbilical artery Doppler assessment
why_correct: Severe small-for-gestational-age growth with falling abdominal circumference and oligohydramnios in a smoker points to placental insufficiency, as the fetus diverts blood away from its kidneys and produces less urine. Umbilical artery Doppler is the primary surveillance tool for the SGA fetus and guides the frequency of monitoring and the timing of birth. Source: RCOG Green-top Guideline No. 31, Small-for-gestational-age fetus and growth restricted fetus (2024).
why_wrong: B. Waiting four weeks for another growth scan is unsafe in a severely SGA fetus with oligohydramnios. C. Karyotyping is offered for severe early SGA or structural anomalies, and this fetus is structurally normal at 33 weeks. D. CTG should not be used as the only form of surveillance in an SGA fetus. E. There is no history of fluid leakage, and the growth restriction explains the reduced fluid.
pearl: Oligohydramnios plus a small baby means the placenta is failing until proven otherwise — Doppler the cord.
thinking: SFH small, EFW <3rd centile, AC falling  ↓  Oligohydramnios with no rupture of membranes  ↓  Placental insufficiency → reduced renal perfusion → less urine  ↓  Umbilical artery Doppler is the key surveillance test  ↓  Results guide monitoring and timing of birth
exam_trap: Doing a speculum for membrane rupture when there is no leakage and the small fetus explains the low fluid.
takeaway: Oligohydramnios with an SGA fetus: suspect placental insufficiency and do umbilical artery Doppler.
notes: Kept distinct from existing GF008 (normal growth, oligohydramnios from ruptured membranes). Cites RCOG GTG31 (3rd edition, BJOG 2024) and the NHS England North West FGR guideline (2025), which is based on GTG31 (2024), uses Doppler-based timing of birth and uses CTG only in combination with ultrasound assessment.

presentation: Polyhydramnios — fetal duodenal atresia (double bubble)
stem:
A 27-year-old woman is 30 weeks pregnant. Her symphysis–fundal height is 35 cm and her abdomen feels tense. Her 20-week anomaly scan was reported as normal, and a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at 26 weeks was normal. An ultrasound scan now shows polyhydramnios, with a deepest vertical pool of 11 cm. The fetal growth is on the 40th centile. In the upper fetal abdomen there are two fluid-filled structures side by side, and no fluid is seen in the bowel beyond them.

What is the most likely cause of the polyhydramnios?

options.A: Gastroschisis
options.B: Duodenal atresia
options.C: Posterior urethral valves
options.D: Bilateral renal agenesis
options.E: Pyloric stenosis

correct_answer: B. Duodenal atresia
why_correct: The two fluid-filled structures are the 'double bubble' of a dilated stomach and proximal duodenum, which is typical of duodenal atresia. The fetus cannot pass swallowed amniotic fluid along the gut to be absorbed, so fluid builds up, often becoming obvious in the third trimester. About a third of babies with duodenal atresia have Down syndrome, so this should be discussed. Source: University Hospital Southampton NHS FT, Duodenal atresia (neonatal surgery); Barnsley Hospital NHS FT Polyhydramnios guideline (2024).
why_wrong: A. Gastroschisis shows bowel floating freely outside the abdominal wall, not a double bubble. C. Posterior urethral valves block fetal urine output and cause oligohydramnios with a dilated bladder. D. Bilateral renal agenesis means no fetal urine and causes anhydramnios. E. Pyloric stenosis develops after birth, usually at 2–8 weeks, and is not an antenatal cause of polyhydramnios.
pearl: Too much fluid = the baby is not swallowing or absorbing it; too little fluid = the baby is not making urine or the placenta is failing.
thinking: Polyhydramnios at 30 weeks  ↓  Diabetes excluded, normal growth  ↓  Double bubble on scan  ↓  Upper gut obstruction → swallowed fluid not absorbed  ↓  Duodenal atresia (check for trisomy 21)
exam_trap: Choosing pyloric stenosis, which causes projectile vomiting from about 2 weeks after birth and does not cause antenatal polyhydramnios or a double bubble.
takeaway: Polyhydramnios with a double bubble on scan = fetal duodenal atresia.
notes: The question asks for the cause of polyhydramnios, so C319 is kept; duodenal atresia has no exact GMC entry (C265 Neonatal surgical emergencies covers postnatal presentation).

presentation: Anhydramnios at 20 weeks — bilateral renal agenesis and pulmonary hypoplasia
stem:
A 30-year-old woman has her routine fetal anomaly scan at 20 weeks' gestation. There is almost no amniotic fluid. The fetal bladder cannot be seen on repeated views over 45 minutes, and neither fetal kidney can be identified. The heart, head and spine look normal. She has had no leakage of fluid from the vagina and her blood pressure is normal. She is referred to fetal medicine, who confirm the findings.

Which consequence of these findings most determines the baby's outlook after birth?

options.A: Hydrops fetalis
options.B: Fetal heart failure
options.C: Limb contractures
options.D: Neonatal hyperkalaemia
options.E: Pulmonary hypoplasia

correct_answer: E. Pulmonary hypoplasia
why_correct: An absent bladder and kidneys with anhydramnios at 20 weeks indicates bilateral renal agenesis. From about 16 weeks amniotic fluid is mainly fetal urine, and the lungs need this fluid to develop. Without it, the lungs are usually severely underdeveloped, and this pulmonary hypoplasia is the main reason the condition is almost always fatal, with most babies stillborn or dying shortly after birth. Source: NHS England / NHS Fetal Anomaly Screening Programme, Bilateral renal agenesis: information for parents (GOV.UK, updated 2026).
why_wrong: A. Hydrops is caused by fetal anaemia, heart failure or infection and is not a feature of renal agenesis. B. The fetal heart is structurally normal, and renal agenesis does not cause fetal heart failure. C. Limb contractures and facial compression are part of the Potter sequence but are not what limits survival. D. Absent kidneys would cause hyperkalaemia after birth, but the lungs are usually the limiting problem, and survival long enough to need kidney replacement therapy is exceptional.
pearl: No kidneys → no urine → no amniotic fluid → poor lung growth: pulmonary hypoplasia is what usually proves fatal.
thinking: Anhydramnios at 20 weeks, no leakage  ↓  No bladder, no kidneys seen  ↓  Bilateral renal agenesis  ↓  After 16 weeks amniotic fluid is mainly fetal urine  ↓  Lungs need fluid to grow → pulmonary hypoplasia → usually fatal around birth
exam_trap: Picking renal failure as the cause of death, when it is the lungs that fail at birth.
takeaway: Severe early oligohydramnios from renal agenesis is almost always fatal, mainly because of pulmonary hypoplasia.
notes: The scan finding is a congenital abnormality, so P045 fits the presentation better than P184.

presentation: Schizoaffective disorder — mood and psychotic symptoms in the same episode
stem:
A 36-year-old man is admitted after his family find him neglecting himself. Over the past three months he has had very low mood, early morning waking, poor appetite with 6 kg weight loss, and loss of interest in everything. Starting in the same week as the low mood and continuing throughout, he has believed that a government agency inserts thoughts into his head, and he hears two voices discussing him in the third person. He was treated with an antidepressant and an antipsychotic. His mood has now been normal for four weeks, with normal sleep and appetite, but the voices and thought insertion continue unchanged. He has never had a manic episode, and there is no substance misuse.

Using ICD-11, what is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Severe depression with psychotic symptoms
options.B: Bipolar affective disorder
options.C: Schizoaffective disorder
options.D: Delusional disorder
options.E: Drug-induced psychotic disorder

correct_answer: C. Schizoaffective disorder
why_correct: ICD-11, the current WHO classification (ICD-10, still used for NHS coding, gives essentially the same definition), defines schizoaffective disorder as an episode in which the requirements for schizophrenia and for a moderate or severe depressive (or manic or mixed) episode are met in the same episode of illness, simultaneously or within a few days of each other, with symptoms lasting at least one month. He had a severe depressive episode and, starting in the same week, two core schizophrenia symptoms: thought insertion (an experience of passivity or control) and persistent third-person auditory hallucinations, for three months. His psychosis then continued after his mood recovered, which argues against psychotic depression, where psychotic symptoms are confined to the depressive episode. (The US DSM-5-TR also requires at least two weeks of psychosis without a mood episode, which he would also meet.) Source: WHO ICD-11 6A21 Schizoaffective disorder (MMS v2026-01).
why_wrong: A. In psychotic depression the psychotic symptoms occur only during the depressive episode and usually resolve with it, and they are often mood-congruent. B. Bipolar disorder needs a manic or hypomanic episode, and he has never had one. D. Delusional disorder involves persistent delusions without prominent hallucinations or other schizophrenia-type symptoms, and he has third-person voices, thought insertion and a full depressive episode. E. There is no history of substance misuse.
pearl: Schizophrenia-type symptoms and a full mood episode in the same episode of illness = schizoaffective disorder (ICD-11); psychosis that outlasts the mood episode points away from psychotic depression.
thinking: Severe depressive episode for 3 months  ↓  First-rank symptoms (thought insertion, third-person voices) starting the same week, ≥1 month  ↓  ICD-11: schizophrenia and mood requirements met in the same episode  ↓  Psychosis persists after mood recovers; no mania, no substances  ↓  Schizoaffective disorder
exam_trap: Labelling it psychotic depression without noticing that the psychosis persists after the mood has recovered.
takeaway: ICD-11: schizophrenia-type symptoms and a moderate or severe mood episode together in the same episode = schizoaffective disorder.
notes: Framework: ICD-11 (6A21), current WHO classification; ICD-10 F25 (still used for NHS coding) has an essentially equivalent same-episode definition. The vignette meets ICD-11 (schizophrenia and severe depressive episode requirements met simultaneously, onset in the same week, >1 month). DSM-5-TR additionally needs >=2 weeks of psychosis without a mood episode; the vignette also meets that, but it is mentioned only as a secondary note. Existing GF028 is a manic (bipolar-type) diagnosis question; this is a case with a depressive episode.

presentation: Schizoaffective disorder — persistent psychosis despite two antipsychotics (clozapine)
stem:
A 33-year-old man has had schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type, for six years and is under the care of his community mental health team psychiatrist. He takes lithium, and his plasma lithium level is 0.7 mmol/L. He has had no manic or depressive episode for 10 months, and his mood, sleep and energy are currently normal. However, he continues to hear voices discussing him and believes his neighbours are poisoning his water. He has had two sequential antipsychotic trials, each at an adequate dose for 8 weeks: first risperidone, then aripiprazole. Neither helped, and adherence to both was confirmed by his community nurse. His diagnosis has been reviewed, he does not use alcohol or drugs, and he has completed CBT for psychosis and family intervention.

What is the most appropriate next step in his drug treatment?

options.A: Increase lithium to a target level of 1.0 mmol/L
options.B: Add sertraline to treat residual mood symptoms
options.C: Combine risperidone with aripiprazole at full licensed doses
options.D: Clozapine, initiated by his psychiatrist, with weekly FBCs
options.E: Replace lithium with sodium valproate for mood control

correct_answer: D. Clozapine, initiated by his psychiatrist, with weekly FBCs
why_correct: His mood component is controlled, so the problem is the persistent psychosis. It has not responded to two adequate, sequential antipsychotic trials (adequate dose and duration, adherence confirmed, one a non-clozapine second-generation drug), and other causes of non-response have been reviewed. This is treatment-resistant psychosis, and clozapine should be offered. There is no NICE guideline specifically for schizoaffective disorder; the specialist team applies the schizophrenia guideline to the persistent psychotic component. Clozapine is started and supervised by a specialist, and the patient must be registered with a monitoring service, with a full blood count before starting and at least weekly for the first 18 weeks because of the risk of agranulocytosis. Source: NICE CG178 Psychosis and schizophrenia in adults (2014, last updated 2026, recs 1.5.7.1–1.5.7.2); Clozaril SmPC (emc, revised February 2026).
why_wrong: A. His mood is stable on a therapeutic lithium level, and raising it would not treat the persistent psychotic symptoms but would increase toxicity risk. B. He has no current depressive symptoms, and an antidepressant does not treat psychosis and may destabilise mood in the bipolar type. C. Combining two antipsychotics is not recommended except briefly when switching, and clozapine is the evidence-based option after two failed trials. E. Changing the mood stabiliser does not address the psychosis, and valproate carries MHRA restrictions in people under 55.
pearl: In schizoaffective disorder, ask which part is uncontrolled: stable mood with persistent psychosis after two antipsychotics means clozapine.
thinking: Schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type  ↓  Mood stable on therapeutic lithium  ↓  Psychosis persists after two sequential antipsychotic trials at adequate dose and duration (one SGA), adherence confirmed, other causes reviewed  ↓  Treatment-resistant psychosis  ↓  Psychiatrist initiates clozapine with registration and weekly FBC for 18 weeks
exam_trap: Adjusting the mood stabiliser because the diagnosis is 'affective', when it is the psychosis that has not responded.
takeaway: Psychosis in schizoaffective disorder that fails two adequate, sequential antipsychotic trials: specialist-initiated clozapine with blood monitoring.
notes: Replacement for the rejected MG044. NICE CG178 1.5.7.2 is worded for schizophrenia; it is applied here to the persistent psychotic component of schizoaffective disorder, which is standard UK practice, and CG178 covers psychosis broadly. The UK Clozaril SmPC (Feb 2026) still requires weekly counts for the first 18 weeks; later intervals are being revised in some sources (GPnotebook shows monthly after week 18), so the option deliberately says only 'weekly full blood counts'. The lithium + clozapine combination is acceptable but the reviewer may wish to note lithium can raise neutrophil counts. Reviewer R4 (optional addition): the clozapine SmPC warns that lithium with clozapine may increase the risk of neuroleptic malignant syndrome, and lithium can mask a falling neutrophil count.

presentation: Schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type — acute management
stem:
A 29-year-old woman with schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type, has stopped all her medication. She is brought to her community mental health team with a two-week history of elevated mood, pressured speech, reduced sleep and voices commenting on her actions. She is not pregnant but is sexually active and does not use contraception. She has no medical problems, and her ECG is normal. She agrees to treatment.

What is the most appropriate initial drug treatment?

options.A: Start an oral antipsychotic such as olanzapine
options.B: Start sodium valproate as a mood stabiliser
options.C: Start an SSRI antidepressant such as sertraline
options.D: Start lamotrigine as a mood stabiliser
options.E: Start oral lorazepam as the only treatment

correct_answer: A. Start an oral antipsychotic such as olanzapine
why_correct: She has a manic episode with psychotic symptoms and is not on an antipsychotic or mood stabiliser, so an antipsychotic such as olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone or haloperidol is first-line. It treats both the mania and the psychotic symptoms. A mood stabiliser such as lithium may be added for longer-term mood control, alongside psychological interventions, family support and care coordination. Source: NICE CG185 Bipolar disorder (2014, last updated 2025); NICE CG178 Psychosis and schizophrenia in adults (2014, last updated 2026).
why_wrong: B. Valproate is not first-line here. MHRA advice is not to start valproate in anyone under 55 unless two specialists independently agree there is no other effective or tolerated treatment, and a woman of childbearing potential must also meet the pregnancy prevention programme requirements. C. Antidepressants can worsen mania and do not treat psychosis. D. Lamotrigine is used to prevent bipolar depression and does not treat acute mania or psychosis. E. A benzodiazepine can help short-term agitation and sleep but does not treat the mania or psychosis on its own.
pearl: Acute mania with psychosis in schizoaffective disorder: antipsychotic first, mood stabiliser as needed, and never forget valproate's MHRA rules in women.
thinking: Schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type  ↓  Acute manic episode with psychotic symptoms  ↓  Off all medication  ↓  Antipsychotic treats both mania and psychosis  ↓  Oral antipsychotic first-line, plus psychosocial support
exam_trap: Starting valproate in a woman of childbearing potential without contraception.
takeaway: Manic relapse in schizoaffective disorder: start an antipsychotic first.
notes: There is no NICE guideline specifically for schizoaffective disorder; the answer follows NICE CG185 (mania not on antipsychotic/mood stabiliser: offer haloperidol, olanzapine, quetiapine or risperidone) and CG178, consistent with MSD Manual (second-generation antipsychotic first for bipolar type).

presentation: Antipsychotic physical health monitoring at 12 weeks
stem:
A 34-year-old man with schizoaffective disorder started olanzapine 12 weeks ago. His mood and psychotic symptoms have improved. He has gained 5 kg since starting treatment and says he is always hungry. He smokes 10 cigarettes a day and takes no other medicines. He attends his community mental health team for his 12-week review.

Which checks are most appropriate at this review?

options.A: Serum lithium level and thyroid function
options.B: Full blood count with absolute neutrophil count only
options.C: Liver function tests and serum prolactin level only
options.D: No further checks until his one-year review
options.E: Weight, blood pressure, HbA1c and lipid profile

correct_answer: E. Weight, blood pressure, HbA1c and lipid profile
why_correct: Antipsychotics, especially olanzapine, cause weight gain, diabetes and dyslipidaemia, which add to the high cardiovascular risk in people with psychosis. NICE recommends checking weight (weekly for 6 weeks, then at 12 weeks, 1 year and annually), and pulse, blood pressure, fasting glucose or HbA1c and lipids at 12 weeks, 1 year and then annually. The 12-week review is not the end of monitoring, and his 5 kg weight gain should be acted on now: he should be offered a combined healthy eating and physical activity programme, his antipsychotic choice reviewed with him, and help to stop smoking. Source: NICE CG178 Psychosis and schizophrenia in adults (2014, last updated 2026).
why_wrong: A. Lithium levels and thyroid function are monitored in people taking lithium, which he is not. B. Neutrophil monitoring is mandatory for clozapine, not olanzapine. C. Prolactin is checked before starting an antipsychotic, but prolactin and liver tests on their own miss the metabolic risks that matter most at 12 weeks. D. Waiting a year misses the 12-week review recommended by NICE, when early metabolic change can be treated.
pearl: Antipsychotic check at 12 weeks: weight, BP and pulse, HbA1c or fasting glucose, and lipids.
thinking: Schizoaffective disorder on olanzapine  ↓  12-week review, 5 kg weight gain  ↓  Antipsychotics cause metabolic syndrome  ↓  NICE: weight, BP/pulse, glucose/HbA1c, lipids at 12 weeks  ↓  Act on results and support smoking cessation
exam_trap: Choosing the full blood count because of clozapine monitoring, when the key risk with olanzapine is metabolic.
takeaway: Monitor weight, blood pressure, HbA1c and lipids at 12 weeks after starting an antipsychotic.
notes: CG178 is written for psychosis and schizophrenia; its antipsychotic monitoring recommendations (1.3.6.1 baseline including prolactin; 1.3.6.4 weight, pulse/BP, glucose or HbA1c and lipids at 12 weeks) are routinely applied in schizoaffective disorder. Condition C015 Adverse drug effects: the question tests monitoring for antipsychotic metabolic adverse effects (weight gain already present), not anything specific to schizoaffective disorder.

presentation: Multi-organ dysfunction syndrome after major trauma
stem:
A 34-year-old man is in the intensive care unit 4 days after a motorcycle collision. He had a pelvic fracture and a splenic laceration, needed a splenectomy and received a massive transfusion on the day of injury; he has had no blood products since day 1. He is now intubated, with bilateral infiltrates on chest X-ray and a PaO2/FiO2 ratio of 18 kPa. His urine output has been under 0.3 mL/kg/hour for 24 hours and his creatinine has risen from 82 to 315 micromol/L, so haemofiltration is being started. His platelet count has fallen to 41 × 10⁹/L and his INR is 2.1. Blood cultures and line-tip cultures are negative and no source of infection has been found.

Which term best describes his condition?

options.A: Systemic inflammatory response syndrome
options.B: Transfusion-related acute lung injury
options.C: Multi-organ dysfunction syndrome
options.D: Disseminated intravascular coagulation
options.E: Acute respiratory distress syndrome

correct_answer: C. Multi-organ dysfunction syndrome
why_correct: Multi-organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS) is altered function of two or more organ systems in an acutely ill patient, such that homeostasis cannot be maintained without intervention. His respiratory failure needing ventilation and acute kidney injury needing renal replacement already meet this definition, and his low platelets and raised INR show that the haematological system is also affected. This follows the inflammatory 'second hit' of major trauma, massive transfusion and surgery, and is a recognised cause of late death after major trauma. Source: ACCP/SCCM Consensus Conference definitions for sepsis and organ failure (Bone et al., Chest, 1992).
why_wrong: A. SIRS describes the systemic inflammatory response (fever, tachycardia, tachypnoea, white cell changes), not failure of several organs needing support. B. TRALI starts within 6 hours of a transfusion and affects only the lungs; his last blood products were 3 days ago. D. DIC accounts for the coagulopathy but not the respiratory and renal failure. E. ARDS describes only his lung injury, which is one of three failing organ systems.
pearl: One failing organ is a diagnosis; two or more failing organs needing support is MODS — and mortality climbs with each extra organ.
thinking: Major trauma + splenectomy + massive transfusion  ↓  Day 4: ventilated with bilateral infiltrates (lungs)  ↓  Oliguria and rising creatinine needing haemofiltration (kidneys)  ↓  Low platelets and raised INR (clotting also affected)  ↓  Two or more organ systems failing, needing support  ↓  Multi-organ dysfunction syndrome
exam_trap: Choosing ARDS or DIC because one organ failure is the most striking — the question asks for the term that covers all of them.
takeaway: Dysfunction of two or more organ systems needing intervention after major trauma, burns or sepsis is MODS.
notes: No UK guideline (NICE NG39 major trauma included) defines MODS; the definition used is the ACCP/SCCM 1992 consensus (Bone et al., Chest 1992;101:1644-55), whose abstract was verified via Europe PMC; the definition wording is the standard one quoted from that paper. Presentation mapped to Deteriorating patient (P056) because the stem describes an ICU patient with new organ failures rather than the initial trauma (P121).

presentation: Schizoaffective disorder — family intervention to prevent relapse
stem:
A 26-year-old man with schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type, is seen in the community mental health clinic. He has needed two hospital admissions in the past 18 months, each with elevated mood and persecutory voices. He has taken lithium and aripiprazole regularly throughout, confirmed by therapeutic lithium levels, and is currently well with no psychotic or mood symptoms. He lives with his parents, who are very worried about him, and he says arguments at home about his illness are frequent and stressful. He agrees to his parents being involved in his care.

In addition to continuing his current medication, which is the most appropriate intervention to reduce his risk of relapse?

options.A: Switch his aripiprazole to clozapine
options.B: Family intervention with his parents
options.C: Add a benzodiazepine for stressful days
options.D: Long-term psychodynamic psychotherapy
options.E: Add a second regular antipsychotic

correct_answer: B. Family intervention with his parents
why_correct: NICE recommends offering family intervention to the families of people with psychosis (which includes schizoaffective disorder) who live with or are in close contact with them, and notes it is particularly useful after a recent relapse or when there is a risk of relapse. It should include the patient where practical, run over 3 months to 1 year with at least 10 planned sessions, and include problem solving or crisis management. CBT for psychosis should also be offered alongside medication. Source: NICE CG178 Psychosis and schizophrenia in adults, 2014 (last updated 2026).
why_wrong: A. Clozapine is for illness that has not responded to two adequate trials of antipsychotics; he is currently well and adherent. C. Benzodiazepines do not prevent relapse and add a risk of dependence. D. NICE recommends CBT for psychosis and family intervention, not psychodynamic psychotherapy, as treatments; psychodynamic principles are suggested only to help staff understand the person. E. Combining regular antipsychotics adds side effects without evidence of better relapse prevention, and NICE advises against it except for short periods such as when switching.
pearl: Medication plus family intervention plus CBT for psychosis — relapse prevention in psychosis is not a drug-only job.
thinking: Schizoaffective disorder = psychosis under NICE CG178  ↓  Relapsing despite adherence  ↓  Lives with parents, frequent conflict at home  ↓  Offer family intervention (at least 10 sessions, 3–12 months)  ↓  Also offer CBT for psychosis; continue medication
exam_trap: Reaching for clozapine or more drugs when the patient is adherent, currently well and the modifiable factor is family stress.
takeaway: For people with psychosis who live with family, offer family intervention alongside medication to reduce relapse.
notes: CG178 'Context' confirms the guideline's 'psychosis' includes schizoaffective disorder. Family intervention: 1.4.4.2, 1.5.4.2–1.5.4.3, delivery 1.3.7.2. Presentation X: routine review of a currently well patient with family conflict; no GMC presentation fits and the relapse symptoms are history only. Not a duplicate of MG044 (clozapine for residual voices) or MG046 (metabolic monitoring).

presentation: Acute bronchitis — evidence-based self-care
stem:
A 44-year-old man sees his GP with a 5-day history of cough productive of white sputum, a sore chest when coughing and a mild fever that has now settled. He has no long-term conditions, does not smoke and is not systemically unwell. His temperature is 37.2°C, heart rate 82 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 98% on air, and there are a few scattered wheezes with no focal chest signs. A diagnosis of acute bronchitis is made and he accepts that an antibiotic is not needed. He asks what he can take to ease the cough.

Which is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: Carbocisteine to loosen the sputum
options.B: A salbutamol inhaler when wheezy
options.C: Codeine linctus to suppress cough
options.D: Honey in warm drinks for the cough
options.E: A 5-day course of oral prednisolone

correct_answer: D. Honey in warm drinks for the cough
why_correct: NICE advises that acute bronchitis in people who are not systemically very unwell or at higher risk of complications should be managed without an antibiotic, with self-care and advice on when to seek help. Honey (in people over 1 year), pelargonium, and over-the-counter cough medicines containing guaifenesin or a non-codeine cough suppressant have limited evidence of some benefit for cough. Source: NICE NG120 Cough (acute): antimicrobial prescribing, 2019.
why_wrong: A. NICE advises against mucolytics such as carbocisteine for acute cough with a respiratory tract infection or acute bronchitis. B. Bronchodilators should not be offered for acute bronchitis unless there is underlying airways disease such as asthma. C. Codeine-containing cough medicines have not been shown to help cough and carry harms. E. Oral or inhaled corticosteroids should not be offered for acute bronchitis without underlying airways disease.
pearl: For acute cough, NICE's self-care list is honey, pelargonium, guaifenesin and non-codeine suppressants — not mucolytics, steroids or salbutamol.
thinking: Acute productive cough, no focal signs, systemically well  ↓  No comorbidity, not high risk  ↓  Acute bronchitis: no antibiotic  ↓  Self-care with limited evidence: honey, pelargonium, guaifenesin, non-codeine suppressants  ↓  Avoid mucolytics, steroids, bronchodilators and codeine
exam_trap: Choosing a salbutamol inhaler because of the wheeze — NICE advises against bronchodilators in acute bronchitis without asthma or COPD.
takeaway: Acute bronchitis in a well adult: no antibiotic; suggest simple self-care such as honey and explain when to return.
notes: Angle deliberately differs from DF039 (antibiotic request -> no antibiotic): here the antibiotic decision is settled and the question tests NICE's self-care and 'do not offer' recommendations (NG120 1.1.6, 1.1.7, 1.2.1, 1.2.2).

presentation: Lower respiratory tract infection — point-of-care CRP
stem:
A 52-year-old woman sees her GP with a 9-day history of cough productive of green sputum, tiredness and intermittent sweats. She has no long-term conditions and does not smoke. Her temperature is 37.8°C, heart rate 94 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, blood pressure 128/76 mmHg and oxygen saturation 97% on air. She is alert, and there are coarse crackles that clear on coughing with no focal chest signs. After assessment the GP is unsure whether an antibiotic is needed and performs a point-of-care C-reactive protein test, which is 58 mg/L.

Which is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Back-up prescription for doxycycline
options.B: Immediate 5-day course of doxycycline
options.C: No antibiotic; self-care advice alone
options.D: Same-day chest X-ray at the hospital
options.E: Refer for admission and IV antibiotics

correct_answer: A. Back-up prescription for doxycycline
why_correct: When it is unclear whether someone with a lower respiratory tract infection needs an antibiotic, NICE suggests a point-of-care CRP test: under 20 mg/L, do not routinely offer antibiotics; 20 to 100 mg/L, consider a back-up antibiotic prescription; over 100 mg/L, offer an immediate antibiotic. Her CRP of 58 mg/L falls in the middle band, so a back-up prescription with advice on when to use it is appropriate. Source: NICE NG237 Suspected acute respiratory infection in over 16s, 2023 (updated 2025).
why_wrong: B. An immediate antibiotic is recommended when the CRP is over 100 mg/L or the person is systemically very unwell, neither of which applies. C. 'No antibiotic' is the default for a CRP under 20 mg/L; at 58 mg/L NICE suggests considering a back-up prescription. D. She has no focal chest signs or features of pneumonia that would need urgent imaging. E. She has normal observations and no features of sepsis or severe illness that would warrant admission.
pearl: Point-of-care CRP in LRTI: under 20 no antibiotic, 20–100 back-up prescription, over 100 immediate antibiotic.
thinking: Adult with LRTI, systemically well, no pneumonia signs  ↓  Clinical doubt about antibiotics  ↓  Point-of-care CRP 58 mg/L  ↓  20–100 mg/L band  ↓  Consider a back-up antibiotic prescription with safety-netting
exam_trap: Treating green sputum or a raised CRP as an automatic trigger for immediate antibiotics.
takeaway: CRP 20–100 mg/L in an uncertain LRTI: back-up antibiotic prescription rather than immediate treatment.
notes: CRP thresholds verified in NG237 rec 1.3.4 (current). CG191, which held the original thresholds, is replaced by NG250, and NG250 1.1.1 points to NG237 for suspected LRTI at first presentation. NG120 rec 1.1.11 (old CRP reference) was removed in 2021. Doxycycline is NG120's first-choice antibiotic for adults.

presentation: Acute bronchitis — expected course and safety-netting
stem:
A 36-year-old woman sees her GP with a 4-day history of cough with clear sputum, a runny nose and a mild headache. She has no long-term conditions and is not pregnant. Her temperature is 37.4°C, respiratory rate 15 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 99% on air, and her chest is clear apart from a few scattered wheezes. The GP diagnoses acute bronchitis, and they agree that she does not need an antibiotic. She asks how long the cough will last and when she should come back.

Which is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: It should clear within a week; return if still coughing after that
options.B: It lasts about 10 days; return as soon as the sputum turns green
options.C: It can last 2 to 3 months; return only if she starts coughing blood
options.D: It should clear within 5 days; return for antibiotics if it does not
options.E: It may last 3–4 weeks; return if much worse or not better by then

correct_answer: E. It may last 3–4 weeks; return if much worse or not better by then
why_correct: NICE advises that acute cough is usually self-limiting and gets better within 3 to 4 weeks without antibiotics. Advice should cover the usual course, self-care, and seeking help if symptoms worsen rapidly or significantly, do not improve after 3 to 4 weeks, or she becomes systemically very unwell. Setting realistic expectations reduces unnecessary reattendance and antibiotic requests. Source: NICE NG120 Cough (acute): antimicrobial prescribing, 2019.
why_wrong: A. A cough after acute bronchitis commonly lasts well beyond a week, so this sets her up to return unnecessarily. B. Sputum colour does not distinguish bacterial from viral infection and is not a reason to return. C. Two to three months is far longer than expected, and limiting safety-netting to haemoptysis misses rapid worsening or systemic illness. D. Five days is too short, and failure to clear by then is not an indication for antibiotics.
pearl: Acute cough lasts up to 3–4 weeks — tell patients this at the start, and safety-net for rapid worsening or systemic illness.
thinking: Acute bronchitis in a well adult  ↓  No antibiotic  ↓  Usual course: up to 3–4 weeks  ↓  Return if rapid or significant worsening, systemically very unwell, or not better by 3–4 weeks
exam_trap: Underestimating the natural course (one week) or using green sputum as a reason to return for antibiotics.
takeaway: Tell patients with acute bronchitis the cough may last 3–4 weeks and to return if much worse or not settling by then.
notes: NG120 recs 1.1.1 and 1.1.5. Focus said 'about 3 weeks'; NICE wording is '3 to 4 weeks', used here.

presentation: Acute stress reaction with marked symptoms — trauma-focused CBT
stem:
A 27-year-old woman sees her GP 2 weeks after she was assaulted and robbed in the street. She was not seriously injured. Since then she has had intrusive images of the attack several times a day, nightmares, feeling cut off and 'unreal', a constant sense of being on guard and jumpiness at sudden noises. She avoids the area where it happened and has not returned to work. Her symptoms have not lessened since the first few days. She has no thoughts of self-harm, drinks little alcohol and has no previous mental health problems. A validated questionnaire shows her symptoms are above the clinical threshold.

Which is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Active monitoring with a review after 4 weeks
options.B: A single-session psychological debriefing
options.C: Individual trauma-focused CBT now
options.D: Sertraline 50 mg daily for 6 months
options.E: Diazepam 2 mg three times daily for 2 weeks

correct_answer: C. Individual trauma-focused CBT now
why_correct: Within a month of trauma, NICE recommends active monitoring only for people with subthreshold symptoms. Adults with acute stress disorder or clinically important symptoms of PTSD after a trauma in the last month should be offered an individual trauma-focused CBT intervention, such as cognitive therapy for PTSD or prolonged exposure therapy. Her persistent, above-threshold symptoms and loss of function put her in this group. Source: NICE NG116 Post-traumatic stress disorder, 2018.
why_wrong: A. Active monitoring is for people with subthreshold symptoms; her symptoms are above threshold, persistent and disabling. B. NICE advises against psychologically-focused debriefing for preventing or treating PTSD, as it shows no benefit and may worsen outcomes. D. NICE advises against drug treatment to prevent PTSD in adults; an SSRI is only considered for established PTSD when the person prefers drug treatment. E. Benzodiazepines should not be offered to prevent PTSD and carry a risk of dependence.
pearl: In the first month after trauma: mild, settling symptoms — watch and review; marked, persistent symptoms — trauma-focused CBT; never debriefing.
thinking: Trauma 2 weeks ago  ↓  Intrusions, dissociation, avoidance, hyperarousal, not settling, above clinical threshold  ↓  Acute stress disorder / clinically important symptoms within 1 month  ↓  Not for active monitoring (that is subthreshold)  ↓  Offer individual trauma-focused CBT
exam_trap: Defaulting to watchful waiting for every patient within a month of trauma, regardless of how severe or persistent the symptoms are.
takeaway: Severe, persistent symptoms within a month of trauma need individual trauma-focused CBT, not watchful waiting or debriefing.
notes: Focus sharpened to avoid duplicating GF032 (subthreshold, improving symptoms -> active monitoring, debriefing offered). This item tests the boundary of active monitoring: NG116 1.6.4 (active monitoring for subthreshold symptoms) vs 1.6.15 (offer individual TF-CBT for acute stress disorder / clinically important symptoms within 1 month); 1.6.5 (no debriefing) and 1.6.24 (no drugs to prevent PTSD) are tested as distractors. Condition mapped to Acute stress reaction (C013): DSM-5 acute stress disorder is the first-month post-trauma response and is coded with acute stress reaction (ICD-10 F43.0); the GMC list has no separate acute stress disorder and PTSD (C322) requires symptoms beyond 1 month. Reviewer may prefer X if acute stress disorder is judged outside 'acute stress reaction'.

presentation: Acute stress reaction versus PTSD — timing
stem:
A 45-year-old man sees his GP 4 days after escaping from a fire that destroyed his flat. He was not injured. Since the fire he has had nightmares, sudden vivid memories of the smoke, a racing heart when he smells burning and difficulty concentrating. He has avoided driving past the building. He says the symptoms were worst on the first night and are easing a little each day, and he is managing to stay with his sister and deal with his insurers. He has read about post-traumatic stress disorder online and is worried he has it.

Which is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Post-traumatic stress disorder
options.B: Acute stress reaction
options.C: Adjustment disorder
options.D: Generalised anxiety disorder
options.E: Panic disorder

correct_answer: B. Acute stress reaction
why_correct: Intrusive memories, nightmares, avoidance and arousal starting immediately after an exceptionally threatening event, and already easing day by day while he keeps functioning, fit an acute stress reaction: in ICD-11 this is a transient response to an extreme stressor that is considered normal given its severity and usually begins to subside within a few days. It is not the same as DSM-5 acute stress disorder, which needs at least 9 of 14 specified symptoms lasting from 3 days to 1 month and causing significant distress or impairment; his symptoms are fewer, improving and not disabling. Post-traumatic stress disorder can only be diagnosed when symptoms persist for more than 1 month after the trauma (DSM-5), and NICE structures care in the first month as active monitoring for settling symptoms or early trauma-focused treatment for acute stress disorder, rather than treatment of established PTSD. Source: NICE NG116 Post-traumatic stress disorder, 2018; WHO ICD-11 QE84 Acute stress reaction; DSM-5 criteria for acute stress disorder and PTSD.
why_wrong: A. PTSD shares these symptoms but needs them to persist for more than a month after the trauma; it is only 4 days. C. Adjustment disorder follows a stressful life change rather than an exceptionally threatening event and is not dominated by intrusive re-experiencing. D. Generalised anxiety disorder needs at least 6 months of excessive worry about many everyday matters, not trauma-specific symptoms. E. Panic disorder involves recurrent unexpected panic attacks; his palpitations are triggered by reminders of the fire.
pearl: Same symptoms, different clock: PTSD needs more than a month; a settling response in the first days is an acute stress reaction, while marked, persisting symptoms within the month suggest acute stress disorder.
