Note: the SoR CPD page says management is 'pain medication and antibiotics', which conflicts with the NHS trust leaflet (antibiotics rarely required) and healthdirect; the question follows the NHS leaflet.

presentation: Presumed mesenteric adenitis with evolving peritonism — surgical review
stem:
An 11-year-old boy was admitted overnight for observation with a working diagnosis of mesenteric adenitis after a cold. An ultrasound on admission showed enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes, but the appendix was not seen. Ten hours later the pain has become constant and is now in the right iliac fossa, worse when he coughs or moves. He has vomited twice and refused breakfast. His temperature is 38.4°C and heart rate 124/min. There is guarding and rebound tenderness in the right iliac fossa.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Request an urgent review by the surgical team
options.B: Discharge with paracetamol and safety-net advice
options.C: Start oral antibiotics and review again tomorrow
options.D: Repeat the abdominal ultrasound in 48 hours
options.E: Give stronger oral analgesia and observe on the ward

correct_answer: A. Request an urgent review by the surgical team
why_correct: Mesenteric adenitis is a diagnosis made only once appendicitis is reasonably excluded, and here the appendix was not seen on ultrasound. Pain that becomes constant and localises to the right iliac fossa, with vomiting, anorexia, tachycardia, guarding and rebound tenderness, indicates localised peritonism and probable appendicitis. He needs urgent surgical review (with IV access, fluids and analgesia) rather than continued observation. Source: Mesenteric lymphadenitis patient information, West Hertfordshire Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust; Appendicectomy without confirmation of appendicitis, Evidence-Based Interventions programme, Academy of Medical Royal Colleges, 2020.
why_wrong: B. Pain that localises with peritonism is exactly what safety-netting asks families to return for, so discharge is unsafe. C. Oral antibiotics without surgical review can mask progression to perforation. D. Waiting 48 hours for a repeat scan delays treatment of probable appendicitis. E. Masking worsening localised pain with stronger analgesia and continued observation delays definitive assessment.
pearl: A working diagnosis of mesenteric adenitis must be revised when pain localises and peritonism appears.
thinking: Presumed mesenteric adenitis, appendix not seen on USS  ↓  pain becomes constant and localises to RIF  ↓  vomiting, anorexia, fever, tachycardia, guarding, rebound  ↓  localised peritonism = probable appendicitis  ↓  urgent surgical review
exam_trap: Being falsely reassured by the enlarged nodes on ultrasound when the appendix was never visualised.
takeaway: Evolving right iliac fossa peritonism in presumed mesenteric adenitis needs urgent surgical review.
notes: Condition kept as Mesenteric adenitis (the working diagnosis being tested and revised); C028 Appendicitis would also be defensible since the scenario evolves into probable appendicitis. Distinct from GF050 (discharge safety-net advice for an improving child).

presentation: Traumatic eardrum perforation — flying and swimming advice
stem:
A 27-year-old woman has muffled hearing and mild pain in her right ear after being struck on the side of the head by a football 2 days ago. Otoscopy shows a small, dry perforation of the right eardrum with no discharge. There is no vertigo, no tinnitus and no facial weakness. Tuning fork tests suggest a mild conductive hearing loss on the right. She is flying abroad for a beach holiday in 4 days and asks for advice.

What is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: She must not fly until the eardrum has fully healed
options.B: She can swim if she uses antibiotic ear drops daily
options.C: She can fly, but should keep the ear out of water
options.D: She needs urgent surgical repair before she travels
options.E: She can fly and swim, as it will heal within days

correct_answer: C. She can fly, but should keep the ear out of water
why_correct: Most traumatic perforations heal on their own, usually within about 2 months, and hearing returns to normal. It is safe to fly with a perforated eardrum (the exception is after a myringoplasty). She should avoid swimming and keep water out of the ear until it heals, and should not put drops or cotton buds in the ear unless a doctor advises. Source: Perforated eardrum, NHS website (nhs.uk), reviewed 2023; Traumatic tympanic membrane perforation, NHS Greater Glasgow and Clyde Right Decisions.
why_wrong: A. Flying is safe with a perforated eardrum; the restriction applies after surgical repair. B. Antibiotic drops are not routinely needed for a dry traumatic perforation, and swimming risks introducing infection through the hole. D. Small traumatic perforations usually heal spontaneously, so early surgical repair is not indicated. E. Healing usually takes weeks rather than days, and water exposure should be avoided until it has healed.
pearl: Perforated eardrum: flying is fine, swimming is not — keep it dry until it heals.
thinking: Blunt injury to ear  ↓  small dry perforation, conductive loss, no vertigo or facial weakness  ↓  uncomplicated traumatic perforation, usually heals in weeks  ↓  flying safe  ↓  keep dry, no swimming, no drops unless advised
exam_trap: Advising against flying, which applies after myringoplasty, not to an unrepaired perforation.
takeaway: An uncomplicated traumatic perforation usually heals by itself; she can fly but must keep the ear dry.
notes: DF017 already tests 'keep dry and review' for a slap injury; this question shifts the angle to flying vs swimming advice to avoid duplication. NICE CKS (Perforated eardrum) could not be fetched (UK-only access), so NHS website and NHS GGC guidance were used.

presentation: Acute otitis media with perforation and otorrhoea — NICE NG91
stem:
A 6-year-old girl was brought to the GP after 2 days of right earache and fever. This morning the pain eased suddenly and yellow discharge began to leak from the ear. She is alert, playing and drinking well, with a temperature of 38.0°C. Otoscopy shows pus in the right ear canal and the eardrum cannot be fully seen. There is no swelling, redness or tenderness behind the ear and no facial weakness. She has no drug allergies. After discussion, her parents would like her to have an antibiotic.

What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Phenazone and lidocaine ear drops with oral amoxicillin
options.B: Ear syringing to clear the pus, then review in a week
options.C: Same-day referral to ENT for microsuction of the canal
options.D: Nasal decongestant and an oral antihistamine for a week
options.E: Regular paracetamol or ibuprofen with oral amoxicillin

correct_answer: E. Regular paracetamol or ibuprofen with oral amoxicillin
why_correct: This is acute otitis media with a perforation and otorrhoea in a child who is not systemically unwell. NICE NG91 lists otorrhoea as a group more likely to benefit from antibiotics, so an immediate prescription is reasonable when chosen after discussion; amoxicillin for 5 to 7 days is first choice. Pain should be treated with regular paracetamol or ibuprofen. Anaesthetic-analgesic ear drops should not be used when there is perforation or otorrhoea. Source: Otitis media (acute): antimicrobial prescribing, NICE NG91, 2018 (updated 2022).
why_wrong: A. NG91 restricts phenazone-lidocaine drops to children with no eardrum perforation or otorrhoea and no immediate oral antibiotic. B. Syringing an ear with a perforated eardrum risks forcing water and infection into the middle ear. C. Uncomplicated perforation from otitis media is managed in primary care; same-day referral is for complications such as mastoiditis or facial palsy. D. NICE advises that decongestants and antihistamines do not help acute otitis media symptoms.
pearl: Perforated drum or discharge: no anaesthetic ear drops and no syringing.
thinking: AOM, sudden pain relief then discharge  ↓  perforation with otorrhoea  ↓  not systemically unwell, no mastoiditis  ↓  otorrhoea group may benefit from antibiotics; parents choose immediate  ↓  amoxicillin 5–7 days + paracetamol/ibuprofen; no anaesthetic drops
exam_trap: Adding phenazone-lidocaine ear drops for pain despite the perforation and otorrhoea.
takeaway: In AOM with perforation, use oral analgesia (and amoxicillin if chosen), never anaesthetic ear drops.
notes: Under NG91 1.1.11, no antibiotic, back-up or immediate antibiotic are all options for otorrhoea; the stem fixes the parents' preference for an antibiotic so that one answer is clearly best. Condition C296 (perforation is present and drives the drop contraindication); C284 Otitis media would also be defensible.

presentation: Traumatic eardrum perforation not healed at 6 weeks — ENT referral
stem:
A 29-year-old woman returns to her GP 7 weeks after perforating her left eardrum while cleaning her ear with a cotton bud. She has kept the ear dry as advised. She still has muffled hearing on the left, but no pain, discharge, vertigo or tinnitus. Otoscopy shows a persistent dry central perforation of the left eardrum, about a quarter of its surface. Tuning fork tests suggest a conductive hearing loss on the left. Facial nerve function is normal.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Reassure her and review again in 6 months
options.B: Referral to an ENT outpatient clinic
options.C: Ciprofloxacin ear drops for 2 weeks
options.D: Same-day admission under the ENT team
options.E: Oral amoxicillin and review in 2 weeks

correct_answer: B. Referral to an ENT outpatient clinic
why_correct: Most traumatic perforations heal spontaneously within about 6 to 8 weeks. A perforation that has not healed by 6 weeks, particularly with persistent hearing loss, should be referred routinely to ENT for assessment, audiometry and consideration of repair (myringoplasty). There are no features needing urgent referral, such as vertigo, facial weakness, severe sensorineural loss or infection. Source: Traumatic tympanic membrane perforation, NHS Greater Glasgow and Clyde Right Decisions; Tympanic membrane perforation (paediatric ENT referral guidance), NHS Lothian RefHelp, 2025.
why_wrong: A. Waiting a further 6 months delays assessment of a perforation that has already failed to heal and is causing hearing loss. C. Topical antibiotics treat infection, and this perforation is dry and not infected. D. There are no red flags such as vertigo, facial palsy or sudden severe hearing loss, so emergency admission is not needed. E. Oral antibiotics have no role in a dry, uninfected perforation.
pearl: Not healed by 6 weeks, or hearing still down: refer to ENT.
thinking: Traumatic perforation 7 weeks ago  ↓  kept dry, no infection  ↓  still perforated with conductive hearing loss  ↓  failed spontaneous healing at 6 weeks  ↓  routine ENT referral (audiometry, consider myringoplasty)
exam_trap: Continuing to watch and wait because most perforations heal, despite 6 weeks having passed.
takeaway: A perforation not healed after about 6 weeks needs ENT referral.
notes: NICE CKS Perforated eardrum could not be accessed (UK-only); the 6-week referral threshold is confirmed by NHS GGC (routine ENT if not healed at 6 weeks with persistent hearing loss) and NHS Lothian (refer after 6 weeks if perforation persists).

presentation: Bitemporal hemianopia — imaging the chiasm
stem:
A 48-year-old man is referred by his optometrist, who found loss of the outer half of the visual field in both eyes on routine testing. He has recently clipped door frames with both shoulders and scraped both wing mirrors of his car. Visual acuity is 6/6 in each eye, the pupils react normally and the optic discs look healthy. Confrontation testing confirms a bitemporal hemianopia, more dense in the upper quadrants.

Which investigation is most appropriate to identify the cause?

options.A: CT scan of the head without contrast
options.B: Measurement of intraocular pressures
options.C: Duplex ultrasound of the carotid arteries
options.D: MRI scan of the brain and pituitary
options.E: Lumbar puncture with opening pressure

correct_answer: D. MRI scan of the brain and pituitary
why_correct: A bitemporal hemianopia localises the lesion to the optic chiasm, where the crossing nasal retinal fibres (serving the temporal fields) are compressed. The commonest cause is a pituitary adenoma growing up from below, which typically affects the upper temporal fields first. MRI of the brain and pituitary is the imaging of choice to show a sellar or suprasellar mass and its relation to the chiasm, alongside pituitary hormone tests. Source: Visual Field Deficits, Neuroscience 2nd edition (Purves et al.), NCBI Bookshelf; Pituitary tumours patient information, University Hospitals Coventry and Warwickshire NHS Trust.
why_wrong: A. Non-contrast CT shows the pituitary fossa poorly and may miss a mass that MRI would show clearly. B. Intraocular pressure checks for glaucoma, which causes arcuate defects that respect the horizontal meridian, not a bitemporal hemianopia. C. Carotid disease causes monocular visual loss or homonymous defects, not a chiasmal pattern. E. Lumbar puncture investigates raised intracranial pressure, which causes enlarged blind spots and swollen discs, and should not precede imaging.
pearl: Bitemporal hemianopia = chiasm = pituitary until proven otherwise; superior defects first suggest compression from below.
thinking: Loss of both temporal fields  ↓  crossing nasal fibres affected  ↓  optic chiasm lesion  ↓  upper quadrants worse = compression from below (pituitary)  ↓  MRI brain and pituitary
exam_trap: Choosing CT head as the quick first test, when MRI is needed to image the pituitary and chiasm.
takeaway: A bitemporal hemianopia needs MRI of the pituitary region to look for a chiasmal compressive lesion.
notes: Existing N4457 names the defect and N16494 localises it to the chiasm; this question tests the next investigation. Condition kept as Visual field defects because the question tests working up the field defect (no endocrine features given); C309 Pituitary tumours would be an alternative if the reviewer prefers labelling the likely cause.

presentation: Suspected visual field defect — formal characterisation by perimetry
stem:
A 52-year-old man tells his GP that for a month he has kept bumping into people and objects on his right side. Visual acuity is 6/6 in each eye, the pupils react normally and the fundi look normal. On confrontation testing he may be missing targets in the right half of the field of each eye, but his responses are inconsistent and the GP is unsure. He is referred to the eye clinic so that any field loss can be defined accurately and followed over time.

Which test will best define the extent and pattern of any visual field defect?

options.A: Formal automated visual field perimetry
options.B: Amsler grid testing of each eye in turn
options.C: Repeat confrontation testing using a red target
options.D: Ishihara colour vision plates for each eye
options.E: Optical coherence tomography of both maculae

correct_answer: A. Formal automated visual field perimetry
why_correct: Confrontation testing is a quick bedside screen, but it is insensitive and cannot map the shape, depth or exact edges of a field defect. Formal perimetry, usually standard automated perimetry (for example Humphrey testing), measures sensitivity at fixed points across the field of each eye and gives a reproducible chart that shows whether a defect is homonymous, respects the vertical midline, or spares the macula, which localises the lesion and allows monitoring. UK practice uses standard automated perimetry for formal field assessment, and the DVLA uses automated binocular (Esterman) field testing for licensing. Perimetry defines the defect but does not explain it, so it is not the end of his care. A new, persistent field loss needs timely ophthalmic or neurological assessment. If perimetry confirms a homonymous defect, as his symptoms suggest, the lesion is behind the optic chiasm and he needs neuroimaging to look for a stroke, tumour or other intracranial cause, with a stroke work-up (including checking for atrial fibrillation) if a vascular cause is likely. Sudden-onset loss or other neurological symptoms would need same-day stroke or emergency assessment. Source: Glaucoma: diagnosis and management, NICE NG81, 2017 (updated 2022); Assessing fitness to drive: visual disorders, DVLA, GOV.UK, current edition; Visual field defect, homonymous hemianopia (Community Eyecare Guideline 12.1), NHS Scotland.
why_wrong: B. An Amsler grid tests only the central 10 degrees or so for macular distortion and cannot map a peripheral or hemianopic defect. C. Confrontation testing is a screening tool, and repeating it will not give an accurate, recordable map of the defect. D. Ishihara plates test red-green colour vision, not the extent of the visual field. E. Macular OCT images retinal structure and does not measure the visual field.
pearl: Confrontation finds a field defect; formal perimetry defines it.
thinking: Bumping into things on one side  ↓  possible field defect on confrontation, but unreliable  ↓  need an accurate, reproducible map of each eye's field  ↓  standard automated perimetry (e.g. Humphrey)  ↓  pattern (homonymous, midline, macular sparing) localises the lesion  ↓  confirmed new defect = find the cause: neuroimaging ± stroke work-up
exam_trap: Choosing the Amsler grid because it is a familiar eye-clinic test, when it only assesses the central field.
takeaway: Suspected visual field defects are characterised with formal automated perimetry, but a confirmed new defect still needs investigation for its cause, including brain imaging.
notes: Replacement for MG086, which duplicated DR030 (the DVLA advice). New learning point: how a suspected field defect is detected and characterised (confrontation as a screen versus formal automated perimetry). NG81 is a glaucoma guideline, cited only for standard automated perimetry as the UK method of formal field assessment; the stem deliberately contains no glaucoma features.

presentation: Right superior homonymous quadrantanopia — left temporal lobe (Meyer loop)
stem:
A 58-year-old woman has noticed that she keeps missing objects in the upper right part of her vision, such as kitchen cupboards and road signs. For 2 months she has also had brief episodes of an intense feeling of déjà vu with a smell of burning rubber, each lasting about a minute. Visual acuity is 6/6 in both eyes and the fundi are normal. Formal perimetry shows a right superior homonymous quadrantanopia.

Where is the lesion most likely to be?

options.A: Right temporal lobe
options.B: Left parietal lobe
options.C: Left temporal lobe
options.D: Optic chiasm
options.E: Right occipital lobe

correct_answer: C. Left temporal lobe
why_correct: A homonymous defect means the lesion is behind the optic chiasm, on the side opposite the field loss, so a right-sided defect means a left-sided lesion. Fibres carrying the upper contralateral visual field loop forward through the temporal lobe (Meyer's loop), so temporal lobe lesions cause a superior quadrantanopia. Her déjà vu and olfactory aura are typical of focal seizures from the temporal lobe, supporting a left temporal lesion. Source: Visual Field Deficits, Neuroscience 2nd edition (Purves et al.), NCBI Bookshelf.
why_wrong: A. A right temporal lesion would cause a left, not right, superior quadrantanopia. B. Parietal lesions affect the upper optic radiation fibres and cause an inferior quadrantanopia. D. Chiasmal lesions cause a bitemporal, not a homonymous, defect. E. A right occipital lesion would cause a left-sided homonymous defect.
pearl: Temporal lobe: superior ('pie in the sky'); parietal: inferior ('pie on the floor'); always on the opposite side.
thinking: Homonymous defect = behind the chiasm  ↓  right-sided field loss = left-sided lesion  ↓  superior quadrant = Meyer's loop  ↓  Meyer's loop runs through the temporal lobe  ↓  déjà vu + olfactory aura support temporal lobe  ↓  left temporal lobe
exam_trap: Choosing the right temporal lobe by forgetting that the lesion is on the opposite side to the field defect.
takeaway: A superior homonymous quadrantanopia points to a contralateral temporal lobe (Meyer's loop) lesion.

presentation: Obesity in pregnancy — aspirin for pre-eclampsia prevention (BMI 35 or above)
stem:
A 30-year-old woman attends her booking appointment at 10 weeks' gestation in her first pregnancy. Her BMI is 37 kg/m². Her blood pressure is 116/74 mmHg and urine dipstick shows no protein. She has no medical problems and no family history of pre-eclampsia. She is already taking a pregnancy supplement containing folic acid 400 micrograms and vitamin D 10 micrograms daily.

Which additional medicine should she be advised to take?

options.A: Labetalol 100 mg twice daily from 20 weeks onwards
options.B: Metformin 500 mg twice daily throughout the pregnancy
options.C: Enoxaparin 40 mg daily by injection from 28 weeks
options.D: Ferrous sulfate 200 mg daily from the booking visit
options.E: Aspirin 75–150 mg daily from 12 weeks until birth

correct_answer: E. Aspirin 75–150 mg daily from 12 weeks until birth
why_correct: NICE lists nulliparity and a BMI of 35 kg/m² or more at the first visit as moderate risk factors for pre-eclampsia. A woman with more than one moderate risk factor should be advised to take aspirin 75–150 mg daily from 12 weeks until the baby is born. This woman has two (first pregnancy and BMI 37 kg/m²), so she needs aspirin even though her blood pressure is normal. Source: Hypertension in pregnancy: diagnosis and management (NG133), NICE, 2019 (updated 2023).
why_wrong: A. Labetalol treats established hypertension in pregnancy and is not used to prevent pre-eclampsia in a normotensive woman. B. Metformin is used for gestational or pre-existing diabetes, not for obesity alone or for pre-eclampsia prevention. C. Antenatal enoxaparin from 28 weeks is considered only with three VTE risk factors, and a BMI of 37 kg/m² in a healthy 30-year-old is just one. D. Iron is given for proven iron deficiency or anaemia, not routinely, and obesity is not an indication.
pearl: Two moderate risk factors (for example, first pregnancy plus BMI 35 or above) equal one high risk factor: start aspirin at 12 weeks.
thinking: Booking visit, first pregnancy  ↓  BMI 37 kg/m² (35 or above = moderate risk factor)  ↓  Nulliparity = second moderate risk factor  ↓  More than one moderate risk factor for pre-eclampsia  ↓  Aspirin 75–150 mg daily from 12 weeks until birth
exam_trap: Ignoring aspirin because her blood pressure is normal and she has no 'high-risk' condition, forgetting that two moderate factors are enough.
takeaway: Nulliparous with a booking BMI of 35 kg/m² or more: advise aspirin 75–150 mg daily from 12 weeks.
notes: Slot focus (5 mg folic acid for BMI 30 or above) was changed: NICE NG247 (2025) rec 1.1.6 now says people with BMI 25 or above do NOT need more than 400 micrograms unless they have another 1.1.5 risk factor, while RCOG GTG72 (2018) still says 5 mg. Because the guidance conflicts, this question tests a different, unambiguous obesity-in-pregnancy point (aspirin, NG133 1.1.3). Folic acid is deliberately absent from the options. Reviewer: existing bank items that teach '5 mg folic acid for BMI 30 or above' may need a note about NG247.

presentation: Obesity in pregnancy — booking BMI 50 or above, antenatal thromboprophylaxis
stem:
A 29-year-old woman attends her booking appointment at 9 weeks' gestation in her second pregnancy. Her first baby was born by uncomplicated vaginal birth 3 years ago. She weighs 125 kg and her BMI is 52 kg/m². She does not smoke, has no varicose veins, and has no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism (VTE). Her blood pressure is 118/76 mmHg, renal function and platelet count are normal, and she has no bleeding history.

Which is the most appropriate plan for VTE prevention?

options.A: No heparin now, with VTE risk reassessed at 28 weeks
options.B: Enoxaparin 60 mg daily from now until 6 weeks after birth
options.C: Enoxaparin 40 mg daily from 28 weeks until 6 weeks after birth
options.D: Enoxaparin 60 mg daily after the birth for 10 days only
options.E: Aspirin 75 mg daily from 12 weeks in place of any heparin

correct_answer: B. Enoxaparin 60 mg daily from now until 6 weeks after birth
why_correct: A booking BMI of 50 kg/m² or more now scores 4 on the RCOG VTE risk assessment, and an antenatal score of 4 or more means thromboprophylaxis should be considered from the first trimester. The RCOG's September 2026 position statement, in line with the NHS England Maternal Care Bundle, says women with a booking BMI of 50 kg/m² or more should be offered LMWH thromboprophylaxis during pregnancy and for 6 weeks postpartum. From booking, its weight-based dose table replaces the old GTG37a table, and 100–129 kg means enoxaparin 60 mg daily. Source: Reducing the Risk of Venous Thromboembolism During Pregnancy and the Puerperium (Green-top Guideline No. 37a), RCOG, 2015, and RCOG Position Statement on GTG 37a, September 2026.
why_wrong: A. Waiting until 28 weeks is for an antenatal score of 3, but BMI 50 or above alone scores 4. C. This is both too late and too low a dose; 40 mg is for women under 100 kg, and she needs prophylaxis from the first trimester. D. Postnatal-only prophylaxis leaves her unprotected through pregnancy, and with a BMI of 50 or above she needs 6 weeks after birth, not 10 days. E. Aspirin is not used for VTE prophylaxis in pregnancy and does not replace LMWH.
pearl: Booking BMI 50 or above: LMWH from booking until 6 weeks postpartum, with the dose set by weight.
thinking: Booking BMI 52 kg/m²  ↓  RCOG risk score: BMI 50 or above = 4 points  ↓  Antenatal score 4 or more = thromboprophylaxis from the first trimester  ↓  RCOG 2026 / NHS England bundle: during pregnancy and for 6 weeks postpartum  ↓  Weight 125 kg (100–129 kg band) = enoxaparin 60 mg daily
exam_trap: Using the older scoring (BMI 40 or above = 2 points) and delaying LMWH to 28 weeks or giving it only after the birth.
takeaway: A booking BMI of 50 kg/m² or more needs weight-adjusted LMWH from booking until 6 weeks after birth.
notes: Replacement for the rejected OGTT item. Antenatal, booking-stage point, different from GF001 (postnatal LMWH, BMI 42) and from MG090 (anaesthetic referral). Based on the RCOG GTG37a position statement (Sept 2026), which adds BMI 50 or above = 4 points and a revised weight-based dose table (100–129 kg: enoxaparin 60 mg daily). She is parous with a 3-year interval, so BMI is her only moderate pre-eclampsia factor (aspirin not indicated); aspirin appears only as a VTE distractor. Condition kept as Obesity in pregnancy (C272, the target) because her BMI is the deciding factor; VTE in pregnancy (C425) is also defensible. Primary source re-checked 8 Oct 2026 (RCOG position statement PDF): 'offered ... LMWH thromboprophylaxis during pregnancy and for 6 weeks postpartum'; Table 1 '100–129 kg: enoxaparin 60 mg daily*' (*may be given in two divided doses), applying 'From booking onwards'.

presentation: Obesity in pregnancy — booking BMI 40 or above, obstetric anaesthetic referral
stem:
A 33-year-old woman attends her booking appointment at 11 weeks' gestation in her second pregnancy. Her first baby was born by uncomplicated vaginal birth 4 years ago. Her BMI today is 44 kg/m² and her blood pressure is 124/78 mmHg. She has no medical problems. The midwife has already arranged an oral glucose tolerance test for 24–28 weeks and completed a venous thromboembolism risk assessment.

Which specialist referral should also be arranged during the pregnancy because of her BMI?

options.A: Dietitian for a calorie-restricted weight-loss diet in pregnancy
options.B: Bariatric surgical team for assessment for weight-loss surgery
options.C: Cardiologist for an echocardiogram before 20 weeks' gestation
options.D: Obstetric anaesthetist for an antenatal assessment
options.E: Endocrinologist for tests to exclude Cushing syndrome

correct_answer: D. Obstetric anaesthetist for an antenatal assessment
why_correct: The RCOG recommends that pregnant women with a booking BMI of 40 kg/m² or more are referred to an obstetric anaesthetist for consideration of an antenatal assessment. Very high BMI makes venous access, epidural or spinal anaesthesia, airway management and general anaesthesia more difficult. Planning ahead lets the team document risks, agree an analgesia and anaesthesia plan for labour and caesarean birth, and arrange suitable equipment. Source: Care of Women with Obesity in Pregnancy (Green-top Guideline No. 72), RCOG, 2018.
why_wrong: A. Pregnancy is not the time for a calorie-restricted weight-loss diet; advice should focus on healthy eating and limiting weight gain. B. Bariatric surgery is not done during pregnancy and does not address her antenatal risks. C. Obesity alone, with normal blood pressure and no symptoms, is not an indication for routine echocardiography. E. Nothing in her history or examination suggests Cushing syndrome, and obesity alone does not need endocrine testing.
pearl: Booking BMI 40 or above: think airway, back and veins — and refer to the obstetric anaesthetist.
thinking: Booking BMI 44 kg/m²  ↓  BMI 40 or above = higher anaesthetic risk (airway, regional block, venous access)  ↓  OGTT and VTE assessment already in hand  ↓  RCOG: refer to obstetric anaesthetist for antenatal assessment  ↓  Plan analgesia and anaesthesia before labour
exam_trap: Choosing dietitian-led weight loss, which is not recommended in pregnancy, instead of planning for anaesthetic risk.
takeaway: Every pregnant woman with a booking BMI of 40 kg/m² or more should be referred for an antenatal obstetric anaesthetic assessment.
notes: Different from GF003 (place of birth at 34 weeks, answer 'obstetric-unit birth after anaesthetic review'): this item is the booking-visit referral itself, with other BMI-related care (OGTT, VTE) already arranged. The full GTG72 text on Wiley returned 403; the BMI 40 anaesthetic referral is in the RCOG GTG72 key recommendations and was cross-checked against an NHS trust guideline based on it (Southern HSC Trust, 2025).

presentation: Simple ovarian cyst 50–70 mm in a premenopausal woman — yearly ultrasound
stem:
A 34-year-old woman has a pelvic ultrasound scan as part of investigation of heavy menstrual bleeding. The uterus and endometrium are normal. The scan also shows a 6 cm simple cyst in the left ovary: thin-walled, unilocular and anechoic, with no solid parts and no free fluid. She has no pelvic pain and no bowel or urinary symptoms, and abdominal and pelvic examination is normal.

Which is the most appropriate management of the ovarian cyst?

options.A: Repeat pelvic ultrasound scan in 1 year
options.B: Reassure and discharge with no follow-up
options.C: Laparoscopic left ovarian cystectomy
options.D: Serum CA125 and repeat ultrasound in 6 weeks
options.E: Pelvic MRI scan to characterise the cyst further

correct_answer: A. Repeat pelvic ultrasound scan in 1 year
why_correct: In premenopausal women, simple ovarian cysts are almost always benign and are often functional. The RCOG advises that asymptomatic simple cysts of 50–70 mm should have yearly ultrasound follow-up, because they are less likely to resolve than smaller cysts. Cysts under 50 mm generally need no follow-up, and simple cysts over 70 mm should be considered for MRI or surgery. She should seek review if she develops pain or other symptoms, and new symptoms, growth or any solid or complex features on follow-up would change management (further imaging or surgery). Source: Management of Suspected Ovarian Masses in Premenopausal Women (Green-top Guideline No. 62), RCOG/BSGE, 2011.
why_wrong: B. No follow-up is appropriate for simple cysts under 50 mm, not for a 6 cm cyst. C. Surgery is not needed for an asymptomatic simple cyst of 50–70 mm, and it carries operative risk and possible loss of ovarian tissue. D. CA125 is not needed for a simple cyst on ultrasound in a premenopausal woman, and a 6-week rescan does not follow the guidance. E. MRI is considered for simple cysts larger than 70 mm or cysts that cannot be fully assessed on ultrasound.
pearl: Premenopausal simple cyst: under 5 cm leave it, 5–7 cm scan yearly, over 7 cm consider MRI or surgery.
thinking: Premenopausal, asymptomatic  ↓  Simple cyst (unilocular, anechoic, no solid parts)  ↓  Size 6 cm = 50–70 mm band  ↓  RCOG GTG62: yearly ultrasound follow-up  ↓  Under 50 mm none; over 70 mm MRI or surgery
exam_trap: Reassuring and discharging because the cyst is simple, forgetting that the no-follow-up rule applies only below 50 mm.
takeaway: Asymptomatic simple cyst of 50–70 mm in a premenopausal woman: yearly ultrasound follow-up.
notes: Different from OG076 (4 cm simple cyst, answer no follow-up): this tests the 50–70 mm band. GTG62 (2011) is still the current RCOG guideline; RCOG notes a second edition is in development.

presentation: Postmenopausal complex ovarian cyst — RMI I of 200 or above
stem:
A 67-year-old woman saw her GP with bloating on most days for 2 months. Her CA125 was 25 IU/mL, and an urgent direct-access ultrasound scan was arranged. She is now seen in the gynaecology clinic. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a 6 cm left ovarian cyst that is multilocular with a solid area. There is no ascites, and the right ovary is normal. She has no other medical problems.

Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Repeat ultrasound and CA125 in 4–6 months
options.B: Laparoscopic salpingo-oophorectomy in the general gynaecology unit
options.C: CT abdomen and pelvis with gynaecological oncology MDT review
options.D: Ultrasound-guided aspiration of the cyst for cytology
options.E: Discharge to her GP as the CA125 is below 35 IU/mL

correct_answer: C. CT abdomen and pelvis with gynaecological oncology MDT review
why_correct: Her risk of malignancy index (RMI I = U × M × CA125) is high. She has two ultrasound features (multilocular and solid area), so U = 3. Postmenopausal status gives M = 3, so RMI I = 3 × 3 × 25 = 225. An RMI I of 200 or more means an increased risk of ovarian cancer, so the RCOG recommends CT of the abdomen and pelvis and referral to the gynaecological oncology MDT. Her CA125 of 25 IU/mL is below the old 35 IU/mL cut-off but meets the April 2026 NICE threshold for her age group (24 IU/mL or more at 60–69). Source: Ovarian Cysts in Postmenopausal Women (Green-top Guideline No. 34), RCOG, 2016 (amended 2025); Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (NG12), NICE, updated 2026.
why_wrong: A. Repeat assessment in 4–6 months is only for asymptomatic, simple, unilateral, unilocular cysts of more than 3 cm and up to 5 cm with a normal CA125. B. Laparoscopic surgery in a general gynaecology unit is for women with an RMI I below 200. D. Aspiration is not recommended for postmenopausal ovarian cysts, as cytology is unreliable and spilling a malignant cyst can upstage the cancer. E. A CA125 below 35 IU/mL does not exclude cancer; the RMI here is over 200, and her CA125 is above the NICE threshold for her age.
pearl: Do not trust a 'normal' CA125 alone: complex ultrasound features in a postmenopausal woman can push the RMI over 200.
thinking: Postmenopausal (M = 3)  ↓  Ultrasound: multilocular + solid area = 2 features (U = 3)  ↓  CA125 25 IU/mL  ↓  RMI I = 3 × 3 × 25 = 225 (200 or above)  ↓  CT abdomen and pelvis + gynaecological oncology MDT
exam_trap: Reassuring because the CA125 is under 35 IU/mL, without calculating the RMI or applying age-specific CA125 thresholds.
takeaway: Postmenopausal ovarian cyst: calculate RMI I; 200 or above means CT and gynaecological oncology MDT referral.
notes: GTG34 was amended in Dec 2025 (simple, unilateral, unilocular cysts 3 cm or less need no follow-up); this question does not depend on that change. CA125 25 IU/mL meets the NG12 April 2026 threshold for age 60–69 (24 IU/mL or more), consistent with the GP arranging the scan. Condition kept as Ovarian cysts (the target): the question tests risk assessment of a cyst, not management of confirmed cancer.

presentation: Ruptured haemorrhagic ovarian cyst — haemodynamically stable
stem:
A 23-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with sudden severe right lower abdominal pain that started 3 hours ago while she was playing netball. She is on day 24 of a regular 28-day cycle. A urine pregnancy test is negative. Her temperature is 36.9°C, pulse 92/min and blood pressure 116/72 mmHg. After intravenous morphine her pain settles to 4/10. There is right iliac fossa tenderness with mild guarding. Her haemoglobin is 121 g/L and is 118 g/L 2 hours later. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a 4 cm right ovarian cyst with internal echoes consistent with haemorrhage and a moderate amount of free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. The right ovary is not enlarged and Doppler flow is normal.

Which is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Emergency laparotomy and right oophorectomy
options.B: Urgent laparoscopy to untwist the right ovary
options.C: Intravenous ceftriaxone with oral doxycycline and metronidazole
options.D: Discharge with ibuprofen and a repeat scan in 6 weeks
options.E: Admit for analgesia, observation and serial haemoglobin

correct_answer: E. Admit for analgesia, observation and serial haemoglobin
why_correct: Sudden pain during exertion in the luteal phase, a negative pregnancy test, a haemorrhagic cyst and free fluid point to a ruptured haemorrhagic (corpus luteum) cyst. She is haemodynamically stable, so she does not need surgery now, but she should be admitted rather than discharged. She has a moderate haemoperitoneum, her pain needed intravenous morphine and she still has guarding, and her haemoglobin has already fallen from 121 to 118 g/L, so ongoing bleeding has not been excluded. Admission allows analgesia, regular observations, repeat haemoglobin and rapid laparoscopy if she deteriorates. Most stable women settle without surgery. Laparoscopy is needed if she becomes unstable, her haemoglobin keeps falling or her pain persists. Source: Kim JH et al., Successful conservative management of ruptured ovarian cysts with hemoperitoneum in healthy women, PLoS One, 2014.
why_wrong: A. Laparotomy is for haemodynamic instability with major bleeding, and removing the ovary would be inappropriate in a young woman. B. Torsion is less likely, as her pain has settled, the ovary is not enlarged and blood flow is normal, while free fluid and a haemorrhagic cyst suggest rupture. C. She has no fever or vaginal discharge and the pain began suddenly during exercise, which does not fit pelvic inflammatory disease. D. Discharge is unsafe with a moderate haemoperitoneum, as ongoing bleeding needs to be excluded with observation and repeat haemoglobin.
pearl: Stable patient + ruptured haemorrhagic cyst = observe; unstable or falling haemoglobin = laparoscopy.
thinking: Sudden pain on exertion, luteal phase, hCG negative  ↓  Haemorrhagic cyst + free fluid = ruptured cyst  ↓  Normal flow, ovary not enlarged = torsion less likely  ↓  Stable now, but moderate free fluid, IV morphine needed and Hb 121 → 118 g/L  ↓  Admit: analgesia, observation, serial haemoglobin
exam_trap: Sending a stable patient straight to theatre because of free fluid, or discharging her before excluding ongoing bleeding.
takeaway: Ruptured ovarian cyst in a stable patient: admit for analgesia, observation and serial haemoglobin; operate only if she deteriorates.
notes: Different from N9323 (diagnosis of ruptured cyst after intercourse): this tests management in a stable patient. No UK national guideline covers acute ovarian cyst rupture (RCOG GTG62 states it does not address the acute presentation), so the source is peer-reviewed evidence plus standard UK practice. Reviewer may wish to confirm against local acute gynaecology guidance.

presentation: Anterior vaginal wall prolapse after failed conservative treatment — anterior repair without mesh
stem:
A 58-year-old woman has a symptomatic anterior vaginal wall prolapse that reaches 2 cm beyond the hymen (POP-Q stage 3). She completed a 16-week programme of supervised pelvic floor muscle training without improvement. Several pessaries were tried, but each fell out within days. She has no urinary incontinence, no uterine descent and no bowel symptoms. She is fit for surgery, has completed her family and now wishes to have an operation.

Which is the most appropriate surgical procedure to offer?

options.A: A further 16-week course of supervised pelvic floor training
options.B: Anterior vaginal wall repair without mesh
options.C: Transvaginal mesh repair of the anterior vaginal wall
options.D: Anterior repair plus a mid-urethral sling to prevent leakage
options.E: Vaginal hysterectomy to support the anterior vaginal wall

correct_answer: B. Anterior vaginal wall repair without mesh
why_correct: NICE says surgery should be offered to women whose prolapse symptoms have not improved with non-surgical treatment, or who have declined it. For anterior vaginal wall prolapse, the procedure to offer is an anterior repair without mesh, after a shared decision-making discussion. Transvaginal mesh for anterior or posterior wall prolapse should be used only in research because of serious safety concerns. Source: Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse in women: management (NG123), NICE, 2019; Transvaginal mesh repair of anterior or posterior vaginal wall prolapse (IPG599, now HealthTech guidance HTG456), NICE, 2017.
why_wrong: A. She has already completed an adequate supervised programme without benefit, so repeating it delays the surgery she has chosen. C. NICE limits transvaginal mesh repair of anterior or posterior wall prolapse to research because of serious safety concerns. D. NICE advises against surgery to prevent incontinence in women having prolapse surgery who do not have incontinence. E. She has no uterine descent, and hysterectomy does not treat an isolated anterior wall prolapse.
pearl: Anterior prolapse surgery in the UK = native-tissue anterior repair; no transvaginal mesh, and no 'just in case' continence sling.
thinking: Symptomatic stage 3 anterior wall prolapse  ↓  Supervised PFMT and pessary have failed  ↓  Fit, family complete, wants surgery  ↓  NICE: offer surgery after failed non-surgical treatment  ↓  Anterior repair without mesh; no transvaginal mesh, no prophylactic sling
exam_trap: Adding a mid-urethral sling 'to prevent leakage' in a woman who has no incontinence, which NICE advises against.
takeaway: Anterior wall prolapse that has failed conservative treatment: offer anterior repair without mesh.
notes: Replacement for the rejected PFMT item. Tests a different learning point: surgery after failed conservative treatment (NG123 1.8.1, 1.8.3, 1.8.20 and IPG599 via the NG123 June 2019 note). Not covered by DF025, Q16587 or my MG095/MG096. Pelvic floor training appears only as a distractor (already completed). IPG599 (Dec 2017) has been moved to HealthTech guidance HTG456 with unchanged content (checked on nice.org.uk); research-only wording quoted in NG123.

presentation: Vaginal pessary in a frail woman — 6-monthly pessary clinic review
stem:
An 82-year-old woman who lives in a residential care home has a symptomatic stage 3 uterine prolapse. She has heart failure with an ejection fraction of 30%, COPD and mild dementia. After discussion with her and her daughter, a pessary was chosen because surgery and anaesthesia would carry a high risk. A ring pessary has now been fitted. It is comfortable, stays in place when she walks and coughs, and she can pass urine with it in place. She cannot remove or reinsert the pessary herself.

Which is the most appropriate follow-up arrangement?

options.A: Review only if she develops vaginal bleeding or discharge
options.B: Removal and replacement at her GP surgery every 2 years
options.C: Annual transvaginal ultrasound scan to check its position
options.D: Pessary clinic review with removal every 6 months
options.E: Removal by care home staff if it falls out, then reinsertion

correct_answer: D. Pessary clinic review with removal every 6 months
why_correct: A pessary suits women who prefer to avoid surgery or are at high surgical risk, as she is. NICE says a pessary should be removed at least once every 6 months to prevent serious complications such as erosion, fistula or impaction. Women at risk of complications, for example because a physical or cognitive impairment makes self-management difficult, should be offered a pessary clinic appointment every 6 months. Source: Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse in women: management (NG123), NICE, 2019.
why_wrong: A. Waiting for bleeding or discharge risks a neglected pessary causing ulceration, fistula or impaction, especially as she cannot report problems reliably. B. Two-yearly changes are too infrequent; NICE advises removal at least every 6 months. C. Ultrasound does not replace regular removal and inspection of the vagina. E. Care home staff are not trained to fit pessaries, and waiting for it to fall out means no planned removal or vaginal check.
pearl: A pessary is not 'fit and forget': remove it at least every 6 months, with clinic follow-up if she cannot self-manage.
thinking: Frail, high surgical risk: pessary is suitable  ↓  Ring pessary fitted and retained  ↓  Cannot remove or reinsert herself (dementia)  ↓  At risk of complications  ↓  NICE: pessary clinic review every 6 months, removal at least 6-monthly
exam_trap: Leaving a well-fitting pessary in place until a problem appears, which is how neglected pessaries cause fistulae.
takeaway: Pessary users who cannot self-manage need a pessary clinic review with removal every 6 months.
notes: Different from the existing pessary/vaginal oestrogen question: vaginal oestrogen is not mentioned. This tests who a pessary suits (high surgical risk) and the NG123 1.7.8–1.7.9 follow-up rules.

presentation: Anterior vaginal wall prolapse (cystocele) — voiding symptoms and a bulge
stem:
A 64-year-old woman who has had three vaginal births sees her GP with 8 months of urinary frequency, a slow stream and a feeling that her bladder does not empty fully. She sometimes has to push a soft bulge at the vaginal entrance upwards before she can pass urine. She has had two urinary tract infections this year. The heaviness is worse at the end of the day. Her bowel habit is normal, with no straining or need to press on the vagina to open her bowels. Urine dipstick today is negative.

Which is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Cystocele
options.B: Rectocele
options.C: Urethral diverticulum
options.D: Overactive bladder syndrome
options.E: Enterocele

correct_answer: A. Cystocele
why_correct: Anterior vaginal wall prolapse (cystocele) causes a bulge with urinary symptoms: frequency, slow stream, incomplete emptying and recurrent urinary tract infections from residual urine. Having to push the bulge back to start voiding is typical, because reducing the prolapse straightens the urethrovesical angle. Her normal bowel function makes a posterior wall prolapse unlikely. Source: Pelvic organ prolapse patient information, RCOG, 2022; Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse in women: management (NG123), NICE, 2019.
why_wrong: B. A rectocele causes bowel symptoms such as incomplete emptying and needing to press on the vagina or perineum to defaecate, which she does not have. C. A urethral diverticulum usually causes post-void dribbling, dysuria and a tender anterior vaginal swelling, not a bulge that she reduces to void. D. Overactive bladder causes urgency with or without urge incontinence and does not cause a vaginal bulge or voiding difficulty. E. An enterocele is small bowel bulging into the upper posterior vagina, usually causing dragging rather than voiding problems.
pearl: Bulge + bladder symptoms (and pushing it back to void) = front wall; bulge + bowel symptoms (and pressing to defaecate) = back wall.
thinking: Multiparous, vaginal bulge worse at end of day  ↓  Urinary frequency, slow stream, incomplete emptying, recurrent UTIs  ↓  Reduces bulge to void  ↓  Normal bowel function  ↓  Anterior wall prolapse = cystocele
exam_trap: Calling it overactive bladder because of the frequency, ignoring the bulge and voiding difficulty.
takeaway: A vaginal bulge with voiding difficulty and recurrent UTIs points to a cystocele.
notes: Q16587 also has the answer 'cystocele', but from an examination finding of anterior wall descent. This item gives no examination finding and tests recognition from voiding symptoms (reducing the bulge to void, incomplete emptying, recurrent UTI) versus bowel symptoms. Presentation mapped to Urinary symptoms (the main presenting feature); Vaginal prolapse P210 is equally defensible. Uterine prolapse left out of the options to avoid ambiguity.

presentation: Gender incongruence — low mood while awaiting the adult gender service
stem:
A 31-year-old trans woman sees her GP in England. She was referred to an NHS adult gender service 14 months ago and is still on the waiting list. Over the past 6 weeks she has had low mood, poor sleep and loss of interest in her hobbies, and her PHQ-9 score is 14. She has no thoughts of suicide or self-harm, is still working, and is not taking any hormones or other medicines. The GP uses her chosen name and pronouns.

What is the most appropriate management?

options.A: Defer treating her mood until the gender service has seen her
options.B: Start oestradiol in primary care to relieve her distress
options.C: Offer treatment for her low mood through primary care
options.D: Ask the gender service to bring her appointment forward
options.E: Refer her to psychiatry to confirm her gender identity

correct_answer: C. Offer treatment for her low mood through primary care
why_correct: Waits for NHS adult gender services are long, and the GP remains responsible for the patient's general health in the meantime, including co-existing mental health problems. Her depression should be assessed in the usual way, including its severity (a PHQ-9 of 14 fits less severe depression) and her risk of suicide or self-harm, and treated now (for less severe depression, for example, NHS Talking Therapies or guided self-help), with safety-netting and review, rather than being put off until gender care begins. GMC advice is that GPs should support trans patients while they wait and consider local mental health services if distress or risk increases. Source: GMC ethical hub, Trans healthcare (reviewed 2025); NICE NG222 Depression in adults, 2022.
why_wrong: A. Her depression is a separate, treatable problem, and putting it off until a gender service appointment that may be years away leaves her untreated. B. A GP should not start gender-affirming hormones without specialist advice; GMC guidance links any bridging prescription to local policy and advice from a specialist gender service. D. Gender services do not usually expedite appointments for low mood, and asking them to do so does not treat her depression now. E. Psychiatric assessment is not needed to 'confirm' gender identity before or during gender care, and she does not need secondary mental health care for depression of this severity.
pearl: While a trans patient waits for a gender service, the GP still owns everything else, including their mental health.
thinking: Trans woman on a long gender service waiting list  ↓  new depressive symptoms, PHQ-9 14, no risk  ↓  co-existing condition the GP can manage  ↓  treat depression now in primary care  ↓  safety-net and review
exam_trap: Thinking all of a trans patient's care, including mental health, must wait for the specialist gender service.
takeaway: Treat co-existing depression in primary care while a trans patient waits for gender services.
notes: Does not duplicate DF045 (referral). Learning point is GP care while waiting. NG222: PHQ-9 <16 = less severe depression. Hormone option worded as GP starting hormones on their own; GMC allows bridging only with local policy and specialist advice, and the stem gives no specialist advice and no self-medication.

presentation: Trans woman on oestrogen — reducing VTE risk
stem:
A 46-year-old trans woman has her annual hormone review at her GP practice in England. She was discharged from an NHS gender service to GP shared care 3 years ago and takes oral estradiol 4 mg daily, with estradiol levels in the target range. She smokes 15 cigarettes a day and is not ready to stop, although she will think about it. Her BMI is 29 kg/m², her blood pressure is 128/78 mmHg, and she has no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism.

Which change to her oestrogen treatment would most reduce her risk of venous thromboembolism?

options.A: Add cyproterone acetate to her current oral estradiol
options.B: Switch to oral ethinylestradiol at an equivalent dose
options.C: Stop oestrogen therapy permanently because she smokes
options.D: Add long-term prophylactic-dose enoxaparin injections
options.E: Switch to transdermal estradiol gel or patches

correct_answer: E. Switch to transdermal estradiol gel or patches
why_correct: Oestrogen therapy increases the risk of venous thromboembolism, and the risk is lower with transdermal estradiol than with oral estradiol because transdermal use avoids the first-pass effect on hepatic clotting factors. UK gender service shared-care guidance recommends offering transdermal preparations to people over 40 and to smokers, so she should be switched (with the gender service's advice where needed) while smoking cessation support continues to be offered. Source: Lancashire and South Cumbria MMG trans female prescribing information sheet, 2024; BAGIS Healthcare for Trans Adults: practical guidance for GPs, 2026.
why_wrong: A. Cyproterone acetate is an anti-androgen that does not lower thrombotic risk and has its own risks, including meningioma. B. Ethinylestradiol carries a higher risk of venous thromboembolism than estradiol, so switching would raise rather than lower her risk; UK shared-care protocols for trans women use estradiol, and international guidance (WPATH SOC8) advises against ethinylestradiol. C. Smoking is a reason to change to a safer route and to keep offering cessation support, not to withdraw treatment she relies on. D. Long-term anticoagulation is not indicated for someone with no previous venous thromboembolism, and it adds bleeding risk.
pearl: Trans woman over 40 or smoking: transdermal estradiol is the lower-VTE-risk route.
thinking: Trans woman on oral estradiol  ↓  aged 46 and smokes  ↓  higher VTE risk with oral oestrogen  ↓  transdermal route avoids first-pass liver effect  ↓  switch to gel or patches and keep offering smoking cessation
exam_trap: Stopping hormones altogether because she smokes, rather than changing to a safer route.
takeaway: Offer transdermal estradiol to trans women over 40 or who smoke to reduce VTE risk.
notes: Replacement for MG098 (previous version duplicated DF046 on cervical screening). New learning point: oral versus transdermal oestrogen and VTE risk in trans women. UK sources checked by R4: Lancashire MMG Dec 2024 ("Transdermal preparations should be offered to patients over 40 years, smokers or those with liver disease ... lower risk of thrombosis"), Sheffield GIC 2022 (risk greater with oral than transdermal; smoking not an exclusion), BAGIS 2026 GP guidance (transdermal for over 40, BMI over 35 or smokers). Ethinylestradiol: no UK NHS document found that states it verbatim; WPATH SOC8 statement 12.13 ("not prescribe ethinyl estradiol") and a 2023 review (PMC10081942: guidelines discourage ethinyl estradiol for GAHT because of VTE) support it, and UK shared-care protocols list only estradiol. Condition C149; C015 defensible. Presentation X (routine medication review).

presentation: Young person with gender distress — referral route and puberty blockers
stem:
A 14-year-old who was registered female at birth attends a GP practice in England with their mother. For the past 2 years they have identified as a boy, and they are increasingly distressed by breast development and periods. They ask to start puberty blockers. They are attending school, have friends, and have no history of self-harm or suicidal thoughts. Their mother supports them seeking help.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Refer to NHS paediatric or child mental health services
options.B: Refer directly to the NHS children's gender service list
options.C: Start a GnRH analogue and refer for specialist assessment
options.D: Advise a private UK clinic that can prescribe blockers
options.E: Reassure that the feelings will pass and review if needed

correct_answer: A. Refer to NHS paediatric or child mental health services
why_correct: There are two separate rules here. Referral route: since 1 September 2024, referrals to the NHS children and young people's gender services in England are accepted only from NHS paediatric services or NHS children and young people's mental health services, not directly from GPs. The GP should take the distress seriously, talk it through with the young person and their mother, and refer locally for a holistic assessment. Puberty blockers (a separate medicines policy): the NHS stopped routine prescribing of puberty blockers for gender incongruence in under-18s in March 2024, and restrictions on new private prescribing and supply to under-18s were made indefinite in December 2024 (due for review in 2027), with an exemption only for approved clinical research. A GP therefore cannot start them. Source: NHS England, Service specification: referral pathway for the specialist service for children and young people with gender incongruence (PRN01451), August 2024; DHSC, Ban on puberty blockers to be made indefinite on experts' advice, December 2024; House of Commons Library briefing CBP-10596, 2026.
why_wrong: B. Direct GP referral onto the national children's gender service waiting list has not been accepted since 1 September 2024. C. GPs must not start puberty blockers for gender incongruence; they are not routinely commissioned for under-18s, and use outside approved clinical research is restricted. D. The indefinite ban prevents private UK prescribers from supplying puberty blockers for gender incongruence to under-18s who are not already taking them. E. Dismissing two years of increasing distress is not appropriate; the young person needs a respectful, holistic local assessment.
pearl: In England the GP refers a young person with gender distress to local paediatric or CAMHS services, not straight to the gender service.
thinking: Under 18 with persistent gender distress  ↓  GP cannot refer directly to the CYP gender service (since Sep 2024)  ↓  refer to NHS paediatric or children's mental health services  ↓  separately, explain puberty blockers are not routinely prescribed and private supply is restricted
exam_trap: Referring directly to the national gender service waiting list, which was the route before September 2024.
takeaway: Young people with gender distress: GP refers to local paediatric or CAMHS services; puberty blockers are not routinely prescribed.
notes: England only (services devolved). Re-verified 8 Oct 2026. Referral rule: NHS England PRN01451 (published 7 Aug 2024, effective 1 Sep 2024): 'Referrals will only be accepted from two sources – CYPMHS or community/general paediatric services'. Puberty blockers: routine NHS prescribing stopped March 2024; private/overseas restrictions made indefinite Dec 2024 (review 2027), approved research exempt (Commons Library CBP-10596; Pendle Inside 4 Oct 2026: NC142 defeated 8 Sep 2026, Health Bill Lords second reading 13 Oct 2026). PATHWAYS trial: paused Feb 2026; REC favourable opinion on modified protocol 18 Jun 2026; recruitment 'not due to begin until 1 August 2026' (HRA). Whether recruitment has started could not be verified, so the question makes no trial-status claim. Recheck before release and at the 2027 review. Presentation X: gender distress has no matching GMC presentation.

presentation: Hypertensive retinopathy — what cotton-wool spots represent
stem:
A 58-year-old man is found to have a clinic blood pressure of 176/104 mmHg at his GP practice. He has no visual symptoms. Fundoscopy shows arteriovenous nipping and several small, pale, fluffy white patches with blurred edges near the optic discs in both eyes. There are no yellow, sharply defined deposits, and the optic discs are normal.

What do the fluffy white patches represent?

options.A: Lipid that has leaked from damaged retinal capillaries
options.B: Ischaemia of the retinal nerve fibre layer
options.C: Swelling of the optic nerve head from raised pressure
options.D: Extracellular deposits beneath the retinal pigment layer
options.E: Cholesterol emboli lodged in the retinal arterioles

correct_answer: B. Ischaemia of the retinal nerve fibre layer
why_correct: Fluffy white patches with indistinct edges are cotton-wool spots. They form when arteriolar narrowing causes focal ischaemia of the retinal nerve fibre layer, which interrupts axoplasmic transport in the ganglion cell axons so that axonal debris builds up. In hypertensive retinopathy they are part of the same severity grade as flame-shaped haemorrhages. Source: EyeWiki (American Academy of Ophthalmology), Hypertensive Retinopathy and Cotton Wool Spots, 2026; StatPearls, Hypertensive Retinopathy (NCBI Bookshelf), 2025.
why_wrong: A. Leaked lipid forms hard exudates, which are yellow with sharp edges, and the stem says there are none. C. Optic disc swelling (papilloedema) is at the disc itself, and his discs are normal. D. Deposits beneath the retinal pigment epithelium are drusen, which are seen in age-related macular degeneration. E. Cholesterol emboli (Hollenhorst plaques) are small, bright, refractile spots at arteriolar branch points, usually from carotid disease.
pearl: Cotton-wool spots are fluffy and ischaemic; hard exudates are yellow, sharp-edged and made of lipid.
thinking: Hypertension with fluffy white retinal patches  ↓  blurred edges = cotton-wool spots, not exudates  ↓  arteriolar narrowing causes focal ischaemia  ↓  axoplasmic flow in nerve fibre layer is blocked  ↓  ischaemia of the nerve fibre layer
exam_trap: Calling cotton-wool spots 'exudates' and thinking they are leaked lipid.
takeaway: Cotton-wool spots represent ischaemia of the retinal nerve fibre layer.
notes: Replacement for MG100 (the previous version duplicated Q1029 on papilloedema = grade 4). New learning point: what cotton-wool spots are, and how they differ from hard exudates. The bank has no question on this; cotton-wool spots appear only as findings in other questions. The option says 'ischaemia' rather than 'infarct' because StatPearls notes that the infarct label is debated. No UK guideline covers this point; StatPearls is the source checked. The stem avoids management so it does not overlap with DF019, DF020, MG101 or MG102. BP 176/104 is below NICE's same-day referral threshold (180/120).

presentation: Hypertensive retinopathy — looking for other target organ damage
stem:
A 56-year-old woman has a clinic blood pressure of 166/100 mmHg on two readings, and ambulatory monitoring has been arranged to confirm the diagnosis. She has no symptoms. Fundoscopy shows arteriolar narrowing and arteriovenous nipping, with no haemorrhages and normal optic discs. Blood tests for HbA1c, electrolytes, creatinine, eGFR and cholesterol have been sent, and a 12-lead ECG has been booked.

Which further investigation should be offered to look for target organ damage?

options.A: Transthoracic echocardiogram
options.B: Renal tract ultrasound scan
options.C: 24-hour urine protein collection
options.D: Urine albumin:creatinine ratio
options.E: Carotid artery duplex ultrasound

correct_answer: D. Urine albumin:creatinine ratio
why_correct: NICE recommends that everyone with hypertension is offered a set of tests for target organ damage: urine albumin:creatinine ratio and a urine dipstick for haematuria, HbA1c, electrolytes, creatinine, eGFR and cholesterol, fundoscopy for hypertensive retinopathy, and a 12-lead ECG. These should be started while waiting for the diagnosis to be confirmed. Her retinopathy is already evidence of target organ damage, and the remaining test is the urine albumin:creatinine ratio to look for kidney damage. Source: NICE NG136 Hypertension in adults, 2019 (updated 2026).
why_wrong: A. Echocardiography is not a routine test; left ventricular hypertrophy is screened for with the 12-lead ECG. B. Renal ultrasound is not part of routine target organ damage testing and is kept for suspected structural or renovascular disease. C. A 24-hour urine collection is cumbersome and has been replaced by the spot albumin:creatinine ratio. E. Carotid imaging is not part of hypertension work-up without symptoms of cerebrovascular disease.
pearl: Hypertension work-up for target organ damage: eyes (fundi), heart (ECG), kidneys (ACR, haematuria dipstick, eGFR), plus HbA1c and lipids.
thinking: New raised clinic BP  ↓  ABPM arranged  ↓  start target organ damage tests meanwhile  ↓  fundi done, bloods sent, ECG booked  ↓  missing kidney test = urine ACR
exam_trap: Ordering an echocardiogram or renal ultrasound rather than the simple NICE-recommended urine ACR.
takeaway: Every person with hypertension needs a urine albumin:creatinine ratio as part of target organ damage testing.
notes: Condition changed by R2 from C184 to C182 Hypertension because the question tests the NG136 target organ damage work-up; C184 Hypertensive retinopathy is a defensible alternative. Haematuria dipstick deliberately not offered as an option to keep a single best answer. Distinct from DF020 (whether retinopathy warrants drug treatment).

presentation: Hypertensive retinopathy — expected course with BP control
stem:
A 54-year-old man was diagnosed with hypertension 3 months ago. At diagnosis his clinic blood pressure was 174/108 mmHg, and fundoscopy showed arteriovenous nipping, a few flame-shaped haemorrhages and cotton-wool spots, with normal optic discs and normal vision. He has since taken his antihypertensive medicines regularly, and his home blood pressure average is now 132/80 mmHg. He asks what will happen to the changes in his eyes.

Which statement best describes the expected course of his retinal changes?

options.A: All the changes are permanent and his sight will slowly worsen
options.B: He needs retinal laser treatment to clear the haemorrhages
options.C: The nipping and haemorrhages will both fully clear in weeks
options.D: The changes will progress unless he has intravitreal injections
options.E: Haemorrhages and spots will fade; vessel changes may persist

correct_answer: E. Haemorrhages and spots will fade; vessel changes may persist
why_correct: Acute hypertensive retinal changes such as haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots and exudates usually resolve over weeks to months once blood pressure is controlled, and vision is generally preserved. Chronic arteriolar changes such as narrowing and arteriovenous nipping reflect longstanding sclerosis and often remain. Treatment is control of blood pressure; eye procedures are kept for complications such as macular oedema with visual loss. However, haemorrhages and cotton-wool spots at diagnosis were evidence of hypertensive target organ damage. They needed prompt clinical assessment, including NICE's target organ damage tests and a check for features needing same-day specialist referral (a clinic blood pressure of 180/120 mmHg or higher with retinal haemorrhage or papilloedema). They also needed active blood pressure treatment rather than reassurance alone, followed by sustained control and repeat fundoscopy. Source: NICE NG136 Hypertension in adults, 2019 (updated 2026); StatPearls, Hypertensive Retinopathy, 2025; MSD Manual Professional, Hypertensive Retinopathy.
why_wrong: A. With good blood pressure control, vision is generally preserved and the acute changes regress, so they are not all permanent. B. Laser treatment is not used for hypertensive haemorrhages, which clear with blood pressure control. C. Arteriovenous nipping reflects chronic vessel wall thickening and often persists despite treatment. D. Intravitreal injections are only considered for complications such as persistent macular oedema with visual loss, not for routine regression.
pearl: Blood pressure control clears the 'acute' signs (haemorrhages, cotton-wool spots) but not the 'chronic' ones (nipping, narrowing).
thinking: Retinopathy at diagnosis: AV nipping + haemorrhages + cotton-wool spots  ↓  BP now controlled  ↓  acute ischaemic and leakage signs regress  ↓  chronic arteriolar sclerosis remains  ↓  vision usually preserved
exam_trap: Assuming every retinal change will fully reverse, or that eye treatment is needed to clear haemorrhages.
takeaway: With BP control, haemorrhages and cotton-wool spots regress but AV nipping often persists; at diagnosis they signal target organ damage needing assessment and treatment.
notes: No UK guideline covers regression; StatPearls and MSD used. BP 174/108 is below the NG136 same-day threshold of 180/120, so no same-day referral was mandated — avoids overlap with DF019. Presentation P099 (follow-up of high BP).
